ON which Day, being the first Day of the Meeting of this Parliament for the Dispatch of Business, pursuant to a Proclamation hereunto annexed, and also to the Writs which had issued for that Purpose, the Right honourable William Earl Talbot, Lord Steward of His Majesty’s Houshold, who was then indisposed, having made aCom.irhffion or Deputation under his Hand and Seal, hereunto also annexed, empowering several Persons, therein named, to administer the Oaths appointed to be taken by the Members returned to serve in Parliament, before they go into the House of Commons} several of the said Commissioners came, about Ten of the Clock, into the Room belonging to the Clerk of the House of Commons, commonly called the Inner Court of Wards, where the said Oaths are usually taken; and 'Jeremiah Dyfott, Esquire, Clerk of the House of Commons; Mr. Hatfel, Clcvk-assistant; and other Clerks; attending according to their Duty; and the Honourable Charles Yorke and John Torke, Esquires, Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, having delivered to the said Mr. a Book, containing a List of the Names of such Members as had been returned to serve in this Parliament; the Right honourable Anthony Earl of Shaftesbury, the Right honourable George Henry Earl of Litchfield, and the Right honourable Henry Arthur Earl Powis, did, in the first Place, administer the said Oaths to the other Commissioners, being Members of the House of Commons; and then the said Commissioners administered the said Oaths to such other Members as appeared; which being done, the Members repaired to their Seats in the House of Commons, after which a Message was delivered by Sir Septimus Robinson, Gentleman Ulher of the Black.

Gentlemen,

The King commands this honourable House to attend His Majesty immediately, in the House ot Peers.

Accordingly the House went up to attend His Majesty in the House of Peers, wlitre the Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, by his Majesty’s Direction, said,

My Lords, and Gentlemen,'

His Majesty hath been pleased to command me to acquaint you, that he doth not think fit to declare the Causes of calling this Parliament, till there shall be a Speaker of the House of Commons.

It is therefore His Majesty’s Pleaftjre, that you, Gentlemen of the House of Commony1 do immediately repair to the Place where the Confmons usually fit, and there chuse a fit Person to be your Speaker; and that you present the Person who shall be lo chosen to His Majesty here, for His Royal Approbation, on Friday next, at One of the Clock. And the House being returned.

The Right honourable George Grenville, One of the Burgesses for the Borough and Pari 111 of Buckingham, in *7

the County of Buckingham, addressing himselt to the Clerk, (who Handing up, pointed to him, and then fat down,) spake to the Efiebt following,

Mr. Dfin,

We are no-.v assembled together, in consequence of the Di rest ions received from ills Majesty, and in pursuance of the ancient and undoubted Right of this House, to proceed to the Choice of a Speaker.

And, as the Bulir.els of this Day mult necessiirily renew our Concern lor the Absence of an honourable Person, whom we no longer fee amongst us, lo I am confident, that every Gentleman who hears me will join with Piealurc in paying the just Tribute of Praile, and of Gratitude, to that rood worthy, and mo, ft respedable Gentleman, whose eminent Virtues and Abilities, whilst he presided in the Chair, entitled him to the most distinguished Marks of the Regard ami Affection of this House, applauded by the unanimous Voice of his Country, and confirmed by the Royal Approbation of the beffc of Princes.

Upon this Occasion it hath been usual to point out the Qualifications for the due Discharge of that great Office, which is the Object of our present Consideration; and how can I do it more properly, or more effectually, than by recalling to your Minds the Character and Behaviour of Mr. Onslow.

There was in him, Experience, Knowledge, Authority, Firmness, Patience, and Industry, Dispatch without Precipitation, Vigour of Mind supported by the most unspotted Integrity, and tempered by the moll extensive Benevolence and Gent lends; equally free from the sordid Love of Money, and from the more dangerous Lull of Power; he was impartial to all, a constant Encourager of riling Merit, desirous to assist the most ignorant, and able to inltruct the moil knowing; Such were the Virtues, such were the Talents, which he exerted, during a long and unexampled course of Years, in this most honourable, but most difficult Station; and he left it, not too loon for his own Glory and Reputation, which were complete, too late I fear for his Health, worn out and broken in this painful Service, but much too loon for the publick Good, and for the Dignity of this House, to which he was so ardently devoted, and whose essential Rights, upon ail Occaliofts, lie most firmly maintained.

Nor is this the Language of Flattery and Exaggeration; I appeal for the Truth of it to the Witnesses of his Conduct, to every Gentleman who fat in any former Parliament; I cannot therefore entertain a Fear, that this genuine Testimony of public Gratitude, and of private Friendship, for both I feel most sensibly, offered to him in his Absence and Retirement, can ever be ascribed to any leis worthy or left honourable Inducement.

And let not this Recapitulation of his Services be deemed foreign to the Purpose of this Dav, as it mult " be

2 Geo. iir. 30

1

be the {lronc.cn: Incitement to others, to copy and to emulate his Example; and thus shall the Influence <;{ his Virtues and public Spirit, in feme Degree, supply his Place, and Gill continue to promote what were ever moll dear to him, the Honour, Welfare, and Security of the Commons of Great Britain.

In this Situation, after lb great a Loss, it is incumbent upon us all to consider what will be inofl conducive to the Authority and Credit of the Chair, upon which the Dignity, Order, and Dispatch of this great Assembly do most immediately depend.

And it is with this View, and with this View alone, free from every other Consideration, that I shall beg Leave to propol'e to the House a Gentleman, who, I hope, will be found equal to the Execution of this important Trust; a Gentleman of a very ancient and honourable Family, of an affluent and independent Fortune to support that high Rank and Station, of a fair and unblemilhcd Character to adorn it, free from Prejudices of every Sort, and of that known Temper and Moderation which are most likely to conciliate, and to preserve to the Chair, that Attention and Respect which are indispensably necessary.

To this let me add, a Gentleman of great Experience, Who hath lat many Years in Parliament, and, during that Time, hath attended to the Proceedings, and hath applied himself to the Business of the House, with more than common Afiiduity.

These and other Qualifications have induced me, with the Concurrence, and at the Request: of many worthy Members, to propose to you Sir John whole Presence, both for his Sake and my own, restrains me from expatiating more fully upon this Subject, as I feel it a more ingenuous and becoming Office to prail'e the abtent than the present, and therefore 1 shall conclude with moving you, that Sir John Cuji do take the Chair of this House, as Speaker.

Then the Right honourable William Lord Viscount Barrington, in the Kingdom of Ireland, One of the Burgesses for the Borough of P, in the County of Devon, addressing himself likewise to the Clerk, (who Handing up, pointed to him, and then fat down) spake to the Effect following, viz.

Mr. Dyson,

I have always great Pleasure in concurring with my Honourable Friend; but it gives me particular Satisfaction that I have the Honour to second him at this Time, and on this Occasion. I join with him in lamenting, most sincerely, that the present Parliament (peculiarly happy in many Respebts) will not have the Advantage which many preceding Parliaments have enjoyed, through the Care and Inlti uction of Mr. O who most dciervedly obtained the unanimous Approbation and Applause of the several Afl’elnblies in which he presided. Coming young to the Chair, called to it from an early Opinion universally conceived of his superior Fitness and Abilities for it, he equalled the most sanguine Expectations of his warmed Friends; and preserved inviolate to the lad, during more than Thirty Years, the hightd Reputation, to which a Member of this House can aspire. Educated in the Principles of Liberty and of Loyalty, (which, however incompatible in other Countries, should be ever in-leparable in this) he never deviated from them. He law and lamented the Rage and Violence of Parties, without being infefted by their Contagion; and he has had the Felicity of seeing them grow feeble in the lad Reign, and expire in this. Happy in the Justice done by his Country to the mature Virtues of the late King, and the well-founded Confidence placed in the riling Virtues of the present.

No Speaker ever preserved better the Dignity of this House, or the Decency requisite in its Debates and Proceedings: This he was enabled to do by the thorough Knowledge he acquired of the Conditution of Parliament, and of the Rules and Orders of the House of Commons. If there are not among us. Numbers expert in this useful, and indeed necessary Part of Parliamentary Knowledge, it mud not be imputed to him; for he was You. 29.

above the mean Arts of these who wiffi to keep Science to themselves, and he most readily imparted it to such as Were delirous to attain it. But, after what has been, with so much Truth and Justice, laid of that great Person, who filled that Chair for Thirty-four successive Years; when I rested upon hi» eminent Abilities, his extensive Knowledge in the constitutional Law of this Country, his inimitable Method of concluding the Bu-finess of this House; but above all, his Steadincfs and Vigour in supporting its Rights and Privileges, and in them the Rights and Privileges of all the Commons of Great Britain; how greatly must I be alarmed at the Difficulties which must attend any Successor to him ? I most ftneerely concur with tire noble Lords, and very honourable Gentleman, in lamenting that this excellent Person has chosen to be no more amongst us. Let not me, Sir, have so particular a Rcaton for lamenting his Lois beyond any other Member of this House.

These Reasons, however powerful, are yet personal, and respect only myself: There are other of a far higher, and more important Nature; the Honour of this House, — its Weight. — its Authority, — its Dignity. These cannot be l'upported, but by Abilities much superior to mine, nor can they suffer the least Diminution, without infinite Prejudice to the whole Nation, in its coliedive as well as representative Capacity; especially in the present arduous Conjuncture, when Affairs of the highest Concernment to His Majesty and these Kingdoms, must ne-ccffarily come under the Deliberation of this House: That these may receive no Detriment through my De-feds, I must beg Leave to repeat my Request to the very honourable Gentleman and noble Lords, that they will permit me to do the Duty of a private Member of Parliament, in this Place, and leave me in full Possession of the high Honour already conferred upon me, without a Possibility of its turning to the Disadvantage of this House, the Public, or myself.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker Elect, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty in the House of Peers, where Mr. Speaker Elect lpake to the Effect follow ing; viz.

Me (Tage so attend the King.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the SirJolmCuft Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, have, acquaints the in Obedience to Your Majesty’s Commands, and accord- King that b« ing to their ancient Right, proceeded to the Eiedion of Speaker!* One of their Members to be their Speaker; whom they now present to Your Majesty: But, Sir, with the utmost Concern must I acquaint Your Majesty, that out of many amon&lt them, eminently qualified for this important Station, their Choice has fallen upon me.

Under the Apprehensions of my Mind, arising from a Consciousness of my own Inability to discharge, as I ought, so great a Trust, I have this Satisfaction, that I can now be an humble Suitor to Your Majesty, that you would give your faithful Commons an Opportunity of rectifying this, the only inadvertent Step which they can ever take, and be graciously pleased to direct them to present Come other to Your Majesty, whom they may not hereafter be sorry to have chosen, nor Your Majesty to have approved.

I do not presume, Sir, to make this Request to Your Majesty, on my own Account; it is for the Sake of Your Majesty’s Service, the Sake of Your faithful Commons, and, what will ever be most dear to you, Sir, the Interests of Your whole People; that those arduous and urgent Affairs, which have induced Your Majesty to call this Parliament, may receive no Prejudice through my Dcfcds; nor the zealous Endeavours of Your faithful Commons, for the Service of Your Majesty and their Country, be in any wise obstruded through this their Partiality to me.

Henry Erskine, Mr. Curzon, Mr. Denis, Mr. Drake, Mr. Drummond, Mr. Duncomb, Mr. Evelyn, Mr. Gajhry, Sir Richard Glynne, Mr. Godolphht: And they are to meet upon Monday Sevennight at Five of the Clock in the Afternoon, in the Speaker’s Chamber; and to fit every nesday, Friday, and Monday, in the Afternoon; and all who come are to have Voices, and they are to take into Consideration’ all such Matters as shall or may come in Question, touching Returns, Elections, and Privileges; and to proceed upon double Returns in the first Place; and to report their Proceedings, with their Opinions thereupon, to the House, from time to time: And all Persons who will question any Returns, are to do it within Fourteen Days next, and lo within Fourteen Days next after any new Return shall be brought in: And the Committee are to have Power to fend for Persons, Papers, and Records, for their Information: And all Members who are returned for Two or more Places, are to make their Election by this Day Three Weeks, for which of the Places they will serve, provided there be ho Question upon the Return for that Place: And if any thing shall come in Question touching the Return, Election, or Matter of Privilege, of any Member, he is to withdraw during the Time the Matter is in Debate: And that all Members returned upon double Returns, do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Wu*l Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That, where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof; or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdeameanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this VOL.-9.

House do, from time to time, take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers that he shall see, or be informed of to be? in the House or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be dip charged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speakers Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take Care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every Day, before the.Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, of Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other Officers of Middlesex and Westminster do take Care, that, from Eleven of the Clock in the Morning to One in the Af* ternoon, and from Four till Six in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and Wefl shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstructions be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Paffuge of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westmitflerand that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, do take Care that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to waif in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending thirf House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House,

Ordered, That to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend, from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon, and for Two Hours at the least immediately after the Rising of the House; and also on every Monday, W, and Friday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take Care, during his Stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others bringing Notes under the Hands of the Members fending for the lame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

The King’s Mr. Speaker reported to the House, that, when the Speech House did attend his Majesty upon Friday last, in the repor e . jqoufe of Peers, his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne,' to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

At the Opening of the first: Parliament, summoned and dected under My Authority, I with Pleasure take Notice of an Event which has made Me completely happy, and given universal Joy to My loving Subjects. My Marriage with a Princes9, eminently distinguished by every Virtue, and amiable Endowment, whilst it affords Me all polEble domestic Comfort, cannot but highly contribute to the Happiness of My Kingdoms; which has been, and always shall be, My first Object in every Action of My Life.

It has been My earned Willi, that this first Period of My Reign might be marked with another Felicity, the restoring of the Blclfings of Peace to My People, and putting an End to the Calamities of War, under which so great a part of Europe differs: But though Overtures were made to Me, and My good Brother and Ally the King of Prussia, by the several belligerent Powers, in order to a general Pacification, for which Purpose a Congress was appointed, and Propositions were made to Me by France, for a particular Peace with that Crown, which were followed by an actual Negociation; yet that Congress hath not hitherto taken place, and the Negociation with France is entirely broken off.

The Sincerity of My Disposition to effectuate this good Work, has been manifested in the Progress of it: And I have the Consolation to relied, that the Continuance of the War, and the farther Effufion of Christian Blood, to which it was the Delire of My Heart to put a Stop,

cannot with Justice be imputed to Me.

Our military Operations have been in no Degree suspended or delayed; and it has plealed God to grant us

'9

farther important Successes, by the Conquests of the Islands of Belleijle and Dominica, and by the Reduction of Pondicherry, which hath in a Manner annihilated the

French Power in the East Indies. In other Parts, where the Enemy’s Numbers were greatly superior, their principal Designs and Projects have been generally difap- pointed, by a Conduct which does the highell Honour to the distinguished Capacity of My General, Prince Ferdinand of Brunswick, and by the Valour of My Troops

The Magnanimity and Ability of the King of Prvjjia have eminently appeared, in refilling such numerous Armies, and surmounting so great Difficulties.

In this Situation, 1 am glad to have an Opportunity of receiving the truest: Information of the Sense of My People, by a new Choice ol their Reprdentatives. I am fully persuaded you will agree with Me in Opinion, that the steady Exertion of our moll vigorous Efforts, in every Part, where the Enemy may Hill be attacked with Advantage, is the only Means that can be productive of such a Peace as may with Reason be expected from our Successes. It is, therefore, My fixed tlcsolution, with your Concurrence and Support, to carry on the War in the moll effectual Manner, for the Iniereft and Advantage of My Kingdoms; and to maintain, to the utmofc of My Power, the good Faith and Honour of My Crown, by adhering firmly to the Engagements entered into with My Allies. In this I will persevere, until My Enemies, moved by their own Losses and Distretfes, and touched with the Miseries of so many Nations, shall yield to the equitable Conditions of an honourable Peace; in which Cafe, as well as in the Prosecution of the War,

I do allure you, no Consideration whatever shall make Me depart from the true Interests of these My Kingdoms, d the Honour and Dignity of my Crown.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I am heartily sorry, that the Necessity of large Supplies appear so clearly, from what has already been mentioned. The proper Estimates for the Services of the ensuing Year shall be laid before you; and I desire you to grant Me such Supplies, as may enable Me to prosecute the War with Vigour, and as your own Welfare and Security, in the present critical ConjunClure, require; that we may happily put the last Hand to this great Work. Whatsoever you give, shall be duly and faithfully applied.

I dare say, your affeClionate Regard for Me and the Queen, makes you go before Me in what I am next to mention; the making an adequate and honourable Provision for Her Support in case She should survive me. This is what, not only Her Royal Dignity, but Her own Merit, calls for; and I earnestly recommend it to your Consideration.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I have such a Confidence in the Zeal and good Affections of this Parliament, that I think it quite luperlluous to ule any Exhortations to excite you to a right Conduct: I will only add, That there never was a Situation in which Unanimity, Firmness, and Dispatch, were more necessary for the Safety, Honour, and true Interest of Great Britain.

To express our just Sense of that affeClionate Regard which His Majesty has shewn for His People, by consulting, on this moll important and intereiling Occasion, as on every other, their Happiness, and that of their Pollerity.

THE Earl of Thomond reported to the House, That His Majesty, having been waited upon, pursuant to the Order of Saturday last, humbly to know His Majesty’s Pleasure, when he would be pleased to be attended by this House, had been pleased to appoint to be attended this Day, at Three of the Clock in the Afternoon, at His Palace of Saint James.

chard Harris, the Portreeve, and Returning Officer for the said Borough, contrary to the Duty of his Office, rejected the Votes of several unquestionable Freeholders, who offered to vote at such Election for the Petitioner, and admitted a great Number of Persons to vote in favour of the said John Harris, who were no Freeholders, many of them Servant* and Dependants of the said John Harris, claiming and received to vote, as having really, and, bona fide, purchased the Freehold of certain Lands and Tenements within the said Borough, from the said John Harris and others, when, in Truth, no such Purchases were ever made, and the Title of such pretended Voters was well known to the Portreeve to be fictitious; it being notorious in the said Borough, that many fraudulent Practices had been made use of, previous to the said Election, by the said J Harris and others, in order to multiply Voices at the said Election, and to enable Strangers to the said Borough to out-vote whatever might happen to be the Number of real Freeholders, offering themselves to vote at the said Election; and as to many of such Voters, the said Portreeve having, previous to the Election, himself drvised and prepared the Conveyances, which, at the Election, he admitted to be sufficient Evidence of their Title, although such Conveyances were, and he knew' them to be, coilufive, not calculated to work an Alteration of Property, but merely to create occasional Votes, in defiance of the Laws, and to bear down the free Choice of the bona fide Electors; and that by means of thelc, and other arbitrary, corrupt, and illegal Practices of the Portreeve, and of the said John Harris, and his Agents, a colourable Majority appeared upon the Petitioner’s Poil, in favour of the said John Harris, again (I the Petitioner; under Pretence whereof the said John Harris hath procured hini-self to be returned with the said Thomas Walpole, a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough, in the Room of the Petitioner, in Violation of the Rights and Franchises of the Electors, and to the great Prejudice of the Petitioner: And therefore praying the House to take the Petitioner’s same into their Consideration, and to grant him such Relief in the Premises as shall seem meet.

Majority,- took upon them to reject the Votes of a very great Number of the Petitioners, and others, who voted for the said Sir Gerard Napier and Mr. Haldane, under various Pretences, all either void of Foundation in Truth, ,or, though true, insufficient, as the Petitioners humbly conceive, to support any solid Objection to the Votes lo rejected; particularly, it was pretended, that. Inhabitancy being among the Requisites to a Qualification to vote, several of the Voters rejected, who had been absent in the Service of their Country, some at Sea, others in the Militia, had forfeited their Franchises by such Absence, though they had never any settled Habitation out of the said Borough; and had returned, and been actually resident within the said Borough some Months before the said Election; and alledging, that the Petitioners were the more confirmed in thinking the several Pretences, under Colour of which the said Votes were rejected, of no Weight, even in the Opinion of the said Bailiffs; for that the said Bailiffs, during the said Poll, admitted many others in favour of the said Mr. Coventry, under the same Circumstances; and for that the Petitioners, whole Votes were so rejected, had been repeatedly lblicited foi; the fame, in Behalf of the said Mr. Coventry, by divers Members of the Corporation, and some of them by the said Bailiffs themselves, as well as by the said Mr. Coventry and his other Agents; and that the said Bailiffs, though regardless of the just Rights of the Petitioners, permitted several Persons, who had no Right, to poll for the said Mr. Coventry; and that by these, and divers other partial, corrupt, and illegal Practices of the said Bailiffs, and of the said Mr. Coventry, a colourable Majority was obtained for the said Mr. Coventry, against the said Mr. Haldane-, and the said Bailiffs have unduly returned the said Mr. Coventry, with the said Sir Gerard Napier, to the Prejudice of the said Mr. Haldane, who was duly eledecl, and ought to have been returned; and that the Petitioners, many of them being thus unjustly stript of their Franchises, and all of them, with the Electors in general, deprived of the Representative-eftheir Choice, and having another impoied on them, whom they have not chosen, can have no adequate Redress but from this House: And therefore praying, that the Petitioners ancient Rights and Privileges may be preserved to them; and that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and do therein as shall seem meet

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petitions b'e heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petitions be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Tuesday the 16th Day of February next.

A petition of the several Persons, whole Names are theryunto subscrilxd, being common Burgesses of the Boiiongh of Jivefiani, in the County of on

behalf qfthertdelyes, and other common Burgesses and Inhabitants of the said Borough, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the said Borough is an ancient Borough, and has sent Two Members to Parliament everfince CheThird Year of the Reign of King James:the First. And that by Charter granted i i the Third Yf4t>: of tlradaid Reign, the Right of electing Burgesses, to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was vested in the then M.'y°r> Aldermen, and Burgesses of the said Borough, and their Successors; and by the same Charter Power was given to Twenty-one Persons therein named, called capital Burgesses, and their Successors; and to the major Part of them, to nominate and choose such and so many Persons, as well resident without as within the said Borough, to be Burgesses thereof, as they should think most- conducive to the Public Good arid Welfare of the said Borough; and that by ancient and invariable Usage in the said Borough, for Time immemorial, the eldest Sons of Burgesses, living at the Death of their Father, and Persons who have served regular Apprenticeships to Burgeflesin the said Borough, upon making Proof thereof to the Mayor, Aldermen, and capital Burgesses, in Council assembled; have been admitted to," and enjoyed, all the Rights and Privileges of Burgesses of the said Borough; and that in the Year 1669, the then Mayor, Aldermen; and capital Burgesses of the said Borough, assumed to themfe'Ves‘the foie Right' of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and having returned Sir Thomas Hanmore as duly defied by them for that Purpose, upon Application made to the then House of Commons again (I the fold ‘Return, the House resolved, That the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, was in the Common Burgesses; and that the select Election, made by the Mayor, Aldermen, and chief Burgesses, was not good; and alledging, that in order to defeat the Intent of the said Reforution, and to acquire the like Power of determining Elections, the Mayor, Aldermen, and capital Burgesses have, from time to time, but more particularly of late Years, nominated and admitted many Persons of Distinction and Fortune, and others, not bred to any Trade or Profession, and who never resided

in or were possessed of any Property in, the said Borough, to be Burgesses (hereof, with no other view than to multiply Votes in favour of particular Candidates; and the said Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, uithlnrent to prevent disinterested and impartial Persons from voting at such Elections, have of late Years held Meetings so lel-dom, and upon such short Notices, that many Persons, duly qualified, and delirous to be admitted Burgeflls of the said Borough, have not had proper Opportunities allowed them for that Purpose; by which illegal and arbitrary Practices the Rights and Privileges of the Petitioners have been infringed, and the Freedom of Elections of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough is endangered; and that the Petitioners apprehend, and are advised, that by the said Resolution of the House of Commons, the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, is, in the Mayor, Aldermen, and finch common Burgesses of the said Borough, as are, or shall be admitted Burgesses thereof, by Birth, Servitude, or Eieftion, in order to trade in the said Borough, and have not received Alms or other Charity: And further setting forth, That at the last General Eieftion for Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, Seven hundred Persons were admitted to poll for such Burgesses, one Half of whom had not, as the Petitioners apprehend, any Right of voting at such Eieftion, being either Honorary Burgesses, or Freemen Paupers, or never admitted, or entitled to be admitted, Burgesses of the said Borough; And further alledging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that the Majority of legal Votes, at the said Eieftion, were given in favour of Sir John Rushout, Baronet, and William Bay* lies, Esquire, Two of the then Candidates; and that the said William Bay lies ought to have been returned, as duly defied: And therefore praying the House to take the Mattefs aforesaid into Consideration, and to do therein as they shall think meet.

A Bill to repeal so much of an Act passed in the first Year of the Reign of His present Majesty King;

thrThird, intituled, An Act for the Relief of insolvent Debtors, as relates to Creditors compelling Prisoners charged in Execution to deliver up their Estates, and to such Prisoners being thereupon discharged, was. read a Second Time.

Resolved, That; the Bill be committed.

Resolved, That the Bill be committed to a Committee of the whole House. ‘

Resolved, That this House - will, upon Monday Corning next, resolve itself into a - Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson, according to Order, reported

from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider that Part of His Majesty’s most gracious ^pejxh to both Houses of Parliament, which relates to a Provision to be made for the Queen, the Re-' solutions which the Committee had'directed him to report to the-House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at thei Clerk’s Table: Where the same were.read; and are as followeth; viz.

, Resolved, IfhaL it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That a Provision be made for the Queen, in case She shall survive His Majesty, of One hundred thousand Pounds per Annum, during her Life,. to support Her

Royal Dignity, together with His Majesty’s Palace of Somerset House, and the Lodge and Lands at Richmond Old Park. ’

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that His Majesty be enabled to charge the said One hundred thousand Pounds per Annum, upon all or any Part of such of the Revenues, which, by an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Support of His Majesty’s Houshold, and of the Honour and Dignity of the Crown of Great Britain, were directed to be, during'His Majesty’s Life, carried to, and made Part of the Aggregate Fund, as shall be subsisting after His Majesty’s Demise; and to charge all, or any Part of ►the Aggregate Fund", as a collateral Security for making good the said Annuity.

The First Resolution being read a second Time;

_ Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That this House doth

agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That a Provision be made for the Queen, in case She shall survive His Majesty, of One hundred thousand Pounds per Annum, during Her Life, to fu^ort Her Royal Dignity, together with His Majesty s Palace of Somerset House, and the Lodge and Lands at_ Richmond Old Parki

The Second Resolution being read a second Time, Resolved, Nemine Cotitradicente, That this House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That His Majesty be enabled to charge the said One hundred thousand Pounds per Annum upon all or any Part of such of the Revenues, which, by an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the liipport of his Majesty’s Household, and of the Honour 4 '15 1

and Dignity of the Crown of Great Britain, were directed to be, during His Majesty’s Life, carried to, and made Part of the Aggregate Fund as shall be subsisting after His Majesty’s Demise; and to charge all, or any Part, of the Aggregate Fund, as a collateral Security for making good the said Annuity.

Ordered, That a Bill be brought in, pursuant to the said Resolutions: And that Mr. Alderman Dickinson, the Lord Barrington, Mr. Attorney General, Mr. Solicitor General, Mr. Htiffey, Mr. West, and Mr. Samuel Martin do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker re fumed the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow Morning.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, that they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.-

A Petition of the Owners, and Occupiers of Houses Halifax, and Tenements in the Town of Halifax, in the County of ’"atcr York, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth.

That the Watercourse issuing from the public Spring called Well Head, near Halifax aforesaid, and whenfe the Inhabitants of the said Town used to be principally supplied with Water, is of late so much obstructed and polluted with Filth and Rubbish in its ancient Course to the said Town, that the said Inhabitants are obliged, at a great Expence of Labour, Time, and Money, to fetch Water for domestic Uses in Carts, from the Head of the said Spring; and that the said Town being of late Years increased in Trade and Number of Inhabitants, the said Spring is not now sufficient to serve the said Town* nor, by reason of its Situation, can the Water thereof be conveyed in PipesintotheDwellingHouseslituate in the upper Part of the said Town; and alledging, that it would be ajj Advantage to all Persons residing in, and resorting to the said Town, if a sufficient Supply of wholesome Water was conveyed in Pipes into the Dwelling Houses therein, which, the Petitioners apprehend may be done by the Assistance of the several other Springs of Water arising ip Ovendin, in the said County, and in several other Parts in the Neighbourhood, which lie higher than the said Spring called Well Head-, and that the Petitioners having with that view made Proposals for the Purchaseof Two of the said'Springs which lie higher thanihe said Spring called Well Head, and for an Authority to convey the Water in Pipes, or otherwjfe, from thence and the said Spring called Well Head, through the interjacent Grounds, are desirous that such Purchase may beperfefted, and the same veiled in Trustees, and Power given to raise Money fdr defraying the Expences thereof, and of the said Undertaking: And therefore praying, that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the several Persons whose Names are thereunto subscribed, being Merchants, and extensive Dealers in Butter, Cheese, Salted Beef, Bacon, Pickled Pork, and all other Provisions, in Behalf of themselves, and all others concerned in the said Branches of Trade and Merchandize throughout this Kingdom in general, Were severally presented to the House, and read; reciting, That, by several Acts, the Importation of Salted Beef, Pork, and Butter, from Ireland into this Kingdom, has been permitted; and, by the last of the said Acts, is to have Continuance until the 24th Day of December 1761; and alleging, that the Petitioners, in the Course of their respective Dealings and daily Correspondence, havedif-covered to a Certainty, that, from the Mildness of the last Winter, and the abundant Plenty of the last Summer, all Sorts of Provisions, both for Man and Cattle, are become exceeding cheap, especially in the Northern Counties of this Kingdom, and Principality of Wales, the Produce of which the said several Acts more essentially affect; and all the good Purposes for which the said Acts were passed, have been fully answered: Therefore praying, That the said Acts, permitting the Importation of Irish Provisions into this Kingdom, which will expire on the 24th of December next, maybe discontinued from that Time, and a total Stop put thereto; Or that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act to continue, for a limited Time, the Importation of Salted Beef, Pork, and Butter, from Ireland.

A Petition of Alexander Esquire, was

presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, feme Time before the last General Election, Vice Admiral Francis Holborne, and the Petitioner, severally declared themselves Candidates to represent the Five Boroughs of Stirling, Dum/erline, Culrofs, and keithing, as Members in the present Parliament; and that Admiral Holborne, after he had so declared himself a Candidate, endeavoured, by Violence, and other undue and illegal Influence, to overawe, interrupt, and subvert the Freedom of Election, and thereby procured himself to be returned: And that, at the last General Election for this District of Boroughs, when the said Admiral and the Petitioner were Candidates, the Delegates, or Commissioners, for the said Five Boroughs, who were, David Gourlay, George Cockburn, Esquire, John Erjline, Esquire, Mr. James Montgomery, and Mr. James Hardie, voted as follows; viz. George , Esquire,

and John Erskine, Esquire, Delegates for Dum/erline and Culrofs, voted for the Petitioner; David Gourlay and Mr. James Montgomery voted for Admiral Holborne-, and Mr. James Hardie, the Delegate for Inverkeithing, having tendered his Commission to the Town Clerk ot Stirling, who was the Returning Officer, gave his Vote for the Petitioner; but the Town Clerk refused to receive such Vote; and the Delegate for Stirling, the presiding Borough, having thereupon taken upon him to give his calling Vote for Admiral Holborne, in the same Manner as if there had been an Equality of Votes, the said Admiral Holborne hath procured himself to be returned as a Commissioner to serve in Parliament for the said District, though not duly elected, to the manifest Prejudice of the Petitioner, who had the Majority of legal Votes: And therefore praying the House will take the Petitioner’s Cale under Consideration, and order the Return for the said District of Boroughs to be altered, by inserting therein the Name of the Petitioner, instead of the Name of Vice Admiral Francis Holborne, or that the House will give to the Petitioner such Relief as so extraordinary a same shall appear to deserve.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Titefday the 27th Day of April next.

A Petition of Hulthifon Mure, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Honourable Archibald Montgomerie, Esquire, and the Petitioner, having declared themselves Candidates for representing in Parliament the District of Boroughs in North Britain; which coniifts of the Burghs of Whithorn, New

Galloway, and Stranraer: Alexander Earl of Galloway, a Peer of Great Britain, did, in Person, and by his Agents, influence the Voters, and attack the Freedom of Election of the Delegates for the Burghs of Wigtown and Whithorn, on behalf of the said Archibald Montgomerie, Esquire: And that the said Alexander, Earl of Galloway and John Lord Garlics, his eldest Son, in open Defiance of the Law's and Freedom of Election, took upon them to attend and vote at the Election of Delegates for the said Two Boroughs of Wigtown and Whithorn, whereby they procured Two Persons in the Interest of the said Archibald Montgomerie, to be elected Delegates for these Boroughs. And that, at the General Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for this District, the Delegates for Wigtown and Whithorn, the Eieftions of whom were brought about by the undue Influence of the said Alexander Earl of Galloway, and by the V otes of him the said /

Earl, and of his eldest Son John Lord Garlics, voted for Archibald Montgomerie, Esquire; and the Delegates of the other Two Boroughs, Ne Galloway and Stranraer, voted for the Petitioner. The Voices being thus equal, the Delegate of Wigtown, the presiding Borough, took upon him to give a calling Vote to

Esquire, who has accordingly been returned Member to serve in Parliament for this District, notwithstanding that the Merits were for the Petitioner, who had the only Two legal Votes in the Election: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give him such Redress therein, as to the House Lhall seem just.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House;

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Eieftions; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Zetland;

44

Zetland \ the Petitioner, together with John Mack ay, Thomas Barkie, Samuel Hitche/jon, and David Esquires, were all duly inroiled as Freeholders of the said Shire or County; and that at the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the said County, on the 30th Day- of April last, John Sheriff Clerk,

who by Law is obliged to call over the Roll made up at the last Michaelmas Meeting, in case of the Absence of the former Commissioner, did most unwarrantably refuse, though legally required, to call over the said Roll of Freeholders, or to allow the Petitioner and the Four other Freeholders, before named, to vote for the Choice of a Praefes and Clerk: And that in the same Manner Colonel James Haliburton of Pit cun, who was unduly chosen Praefes of this Meeting, did refuse, though required, to allow the Petitioner, and the Four other Freeholders before named, to give any Vote in the Election erf a Member of Parliament for the said County; and that the Petitioner at the said Meeting did, in Terms of the Act of the 7th of King George the Second, require the said Colonel James Robert

Andrew Young, George Trail, Mungo Grahame and Andrew Ross, all pretended Freeholders, of the said County, to take the Oath of Trull prescribed by the said Act, but that was refused, whereby all of the Six before-named Persons were, in Terms of the said Act, absolutely disqualified from voting at the said Election, and ought to have been struck off the Roll of Freeholders: And that the Petitioner, and other Freeholders adhering to him, did enter regular Protests against every Step of these illegal Proceedings j and after declaring their Votes for the Choice of a Praefes and Clerk, they did vote for the Petitioner to be the Commissioner to serve in this present Parliament for the said County: and required John -dock, the Sheriff Clerk, and Clerk of the said Meeting, to certify the Petitioner to die Sheriff of the said County, that he might be returned as the Member duly elected: All which will appear from the Instruments of Protest taken on this Occasion j and that notwithstanding the re-

A, 1761,

of, the Clerk of the said Meeting did certify Sir James Douglas, of Saint Gila, to be the Member duly elected to

serve in Parliament for the said County, and Sir Andrew Mitchell, the Sheriff Depute of the said County has returned him accordingly: The Petitioner therefore prays it may be found and declared, That the Proceedings in the Election and Return of the said Sir James Douglas, as Member to serve in Parliament for the County of Orkney and Zetland^were illegal and unwarrantable, whereby

the said Election itself was absolutely void; and that the Petitioner, as having the Majority of unquestionable Votes at the said Election, ought to have been certified and returned, as the Member duly elected for the said Counties; and that such other Relief may be given to the Petitioner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections; and that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

That, in the Lift of the Names of the Members returned to serve in this present Parliament, which was delivered to the Clerk of this House by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery, Richard Earl of Til-ney, in the Kingdom of Ireland, is certified to be returned as One of the Burgesses for the Borough of Malmesbury in the County of Wild;

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do attend this House immediately with the Return for the said Borough of Malmesbury.

And he attended accordingly with the said Return.

And the faief Return was read.

And it appearing to the House, by the Information of One of the Members of the House, who was present at the late Election of Burgesses for the said Borough, that John Earl of Tilney, in the Kingdom of Ireland, and Thomas Conolly, Esquire, who is also returned for the said Borough, were the only Candidates at the said Election, and that the said John Earl of Tilney was the Person elected, and deligned to be returned, together with the said Mr. Conolly, for the said Borough;

Ordered, That the said Return be amended, by rafing out the Word " Richard," and inserting the Word " John," instead thereof.

And the Deputy Clerk of the Crown amended the said Return accordingly.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson, according to Order, report* ed from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to confide-r further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee." That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred Seventy-two Thousand Two hundred Twenty-six Pounds Nine Shillings and One Penny, be granted to His Majesty, for the Ordinary' of the Navy, including Half-pay to Sea Officers, for the Year 1762.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, for completing the Chapel ordered to be built for the Use of the Hospital for Sick and Wounded Seamen, at Haflar, near and such other Works as may be afterwards found proper to be performed, before the whole Work is put out of Hand.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum not exceeding Six thousand Pounds be granted to His Majesty, for completing the Works of the Hospital for Sick and Wounded Seamen, building near Plymouth.

Resolved, That- it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Two hundred thousand Pounds, be granted to His Majesty, towards the Buildings, Rebuildings, and Repairs, of His Majesty’s Ships, for the Year 1762.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceedingOnc Million, be granted to H is Majesty, towards paying o.Tand discharging the Debt of the Navy.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Speech of Mr. Speaker, this Day, upon presenting to His Majesty the Bill, for enabling His. Majesty to make Provision for supporting the Royal Dignity of the Queen, in case She shall survive His Majesty; when it passed the Royal Assent.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

IT has been the first Care of Your faithful Commons, to take into their Confederation what Your Majesty most affectionately recommended to them from the Throne, namely, the enabling Your Majesty to make that Provision for the Queen, in case She shall survive You, to which Her Royal Dignity, and Her own Merit, give Her the justest Claim.

On such an Occasion, I should ill discharge the Trust which has lately been reposed in me by the Commons, and most graciouflyconfirmed by Yrour Majesty, if I omitted to allure you, that they feel the warmed Sentiments of Gratitude to Yrour Majesty, who have made their Happiness, and that of their Posterity, Your principal Object: Ofthis Your Majesty has given abundant Proof, by Your Royal Nuptials with a Princefe, whose illustriousAnceftors were early AiTertors of the civil and religious Liberties of Mankind; and, in Consequence, closely attached to

Mr. Jenkinson, from the Office of One of His Majesty’s Principal Secretaries of State, accordingly presented to the House, another Copy of a Convention between His Majesty and the Reigning Duke of Brunswick Luneburg, concluded and signed at Brunswick, the 10th of August 1761; and Translation.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation were read.

The said. Copy is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session; and the said Translation is as followeth; viz.

Translation of a Copy of a Convention, between His Majesty and the Reigning Duke of Brunswick Lune-hurg, concluded and signed at Brunswick, the 10th August 1761.

His Majesty, the King of Great Britain, having thought fit to propose to his most Serene Highness, the Reigning Duke of Brunswick Luneburg, an ulterior Augmentation to be made to the additional Body of his Troops; and his moll Serene Highness having entered . i with Zeal into His Majesty’s Views, the High Contracting Parties have transmitted their Orders thereupon to their respective. Ministers: That is to say. His Britannic Majesty, to Colonel John Clavering, a Captain of His i Guards, and One of His Majesty’s Aides de Camp; and the most Serene Duke of Brunswick Luneburg, to Henry Bernard de Schliejledt, his most Serene Highness’s Minister of State, hereditary Cup Bearer of the Duchy of Brunswick, Lord of Schliejledt, Kublingen, and Hauffnein-dorffy Knight of the Order of Dannebrog; who, after the

Exchange of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the following Articles:

Article I.

The same Conditions, by virtue whereof the additional Body is engaged, in Consequence of the Treaty of Mar-pitrg, and the Convention of Paderborn, shall be applied to this ulterior Convention.

Article II.

This Augmentation shall be of 361 Men, and shall consist in 118 Hussars, iai Chasseurs mounted, and 122 Chasseurs on Foot.

Article III.

The Levy Money for this Augmentation shall be paid, agreeably to the Stipulations in the 3d Article of the Treaty of Marpurg: The Subsidies shall be augmented, in Proportion to the said Augmentation: The Explanation given to the Term Immediatementy inserted in the 10th Article of the Treaty of Marpurg, shall be applied to this ulterior Augmentation, in the same Manner as it was done with Regard to the Augmentation agreed on for the Convention of Paderborn: Lastly, the ordinary and extraordinary Pay of this ulterior Augmentation, shall be the same as that which has been granted to the whole additional Body of Brunswick Troops, which ought to enjoy, as well with Regard to the Pay, as with Regard to the other Advantages, an intire Parity with the Hejftan Troops.

Article IV.

Towards defraying the Expences, which the Maintaining of the Men and Horses composing this ulterior Augmentation, has already occasioucd to H. M. S. H. and, in Consideration that this Body of Troops has been now near Three Months raised and equipped. His Britannic Majesty consents, that the Payment of the Subfi-dies, and of the Pay for this, ulterior Augmentation, shall commence from the ift of May, of the present Year.

Article V.

The Corps of Chasseurs, as well Infantry as Cavalry, confiding, # after this ulterior Augmentation, of above 630 Men, *it has been necessary, for the Good of the Service, to add a Second Staff Officer: This Officer shall belong to the Cavalry of this Corps,-and shall command it as Major of Horie.

Article VI.

This Convention shall be ratified; and the Ratifications thereof shall be exchanged on each Side, within the Space of Four Weeks, if it can be done. In Witness whereof, We, the under written, Ministers of His Majesty the King of Great Britain, and of his most Serene Highness the Reigning Duke of Brunswick Lunebttrg, by Virtue of our full Powers, have signed the present Convention, and have thereto put the Seals of our Arms.

Done at Brunswick, the 10th of August 1761.

(J. Clavering) (L. S.) H. B. de SchlieHedt.

Spiritiious ported from the Committee of the whole House, to Ijquon. whorii it was referred to take into Consideration an Act made in the 33d Year of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act -for preventing the excessive Use of Spirituous Liquors by laying additional Duties thereon; for shortening the Prohibition of making Low Wines and Spirits from Wheat, Barley, Malt, or other Grain; and from MeaJ, Flour, and Bran; for encouraging the Exportation of British'made Spirits; and for more effectually securing the Duties payable upon Spirits, and preventing tjje fraudulent Re-landing or Importation thereof; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report so the House; which he read in his Place; and af-. terwands delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Method of subjectng Spirits, made for Exportation, to the Payment of Duties, and, in ConsiderMiort thereof, granting Drawbacks or Allowances to be paid upon the Exportation of such Spirits, has been found to be attended with many Inconveniences.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That certain Regulations be established for the making of Spirits for Exportation; and that Spirits made under such Regulations, be not subject to the Payment of any of the present Duties, nor intitled upon Exportation to any of the present Drawbacks, Allowances, or Bountifes.

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That,1 foPencouraging the Exportation of Spirits made in Great Britain from Corn, a Bounty of Three Pounds Vol. 29.

Decembris. 6 5

Twelve Shillings- per Ton be allowed upon the Exportation of such Spirits made from Corn.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Provision contained in the Act of the 33d Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, by which the Distillers of Spirits from Corn are retrained from rectifying or compounding Spirits, as it tends to enhance the Price of Spirits made for Exportation, equally with that-of Spirits made for Home Consumption, is inexpedient, and ought not to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in order to prevent the increatc of the Use of Spirits for Home Consumption, an additional Duty be laid upon all Spirits made in Great Britain, other than those which shall be made for Exportation, under the Regulations above mentioned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Low Wines or Spirit*, of the first Extradion, tnade or drawn in Great Britain, for Home Consumption, from any Sort of Drink or Wafti, brewed or made from any Sort of Malt or Corn, or from Brewers Wash or Tilts, or any Mixture with such Brewers Wash or Tilts, there shall be granted and paid to His Majesty One Penny, over and above all other Duties, charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Strong Waters, or Aqua Vitae, made for Sale for Home Consumption, of the Materials aforesaid, there shall be granted and paid to His Majesty Three Pence, over and above all other Duties, charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Low Wines or Spirits, of the first Extradion, made or drawn for Home Consumptfon, from any foreign or imported Materials, or any Mixture therewith, there shall be granted and paid to His Majesty Three Pence, over and above all other Duties charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Spirits, made or drawn in Great Britain, for Home Consumption, from any foreign or imported Materials, or any Mixture therewith, there shall be granted and paid to His Majesty Two Pence,

over and above all other Duties, charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Low Wines or Spirits, of the first Extradion, made or drawn for- Home Consumption, ' from Cider, or any Sort or Kind of British Materials, except those before mentioned, or any Mixture therewith, there shall be granted and paid to Mis Majesty One Penny Three Farthings, over and above all other Duties, charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers or Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Spirits made for Sale, for Home Consumption, from Cider, or any Sort or Kind of British Materials, except those before mentioned, there shall be granted and paid to His Majesty Two Pence, over and above all other Duties, charged or chargeable thereon, to be paid by the Distillers 01.Makers thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this. Committee, That, for every Gallon of Single Brandy, Spirits, or Aqua Vitae, imported into Great Britain from beyond the Seas, not being the Produce of our own Colonies, there be paid by the Importer, before Landing, Six Pence.

Rejoived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for every Gallon of Brandy, Spirits, or Aqua Vitae, above Proof, commonly called Double Brandy, imported into Great Britain from beyond the Seas, not being the Produce of our own Colonies, there be paid by the Importer, before Landing, One Sliilliner.

in the County of Wilts; was committed; That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendments were once read throughout; and then a Second Time, One by One; and, upon the Question severally put thereupon, were agreed toby the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendments, be irgrofied.

- Sir John Glyntte reported from the Committee, to whom the Bill for naturalizing John Berens was committed, That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true; and that the Committee had directed him to report the Bill to the House, without any Amendment: And he delivered the Bill in at the Clerk’s Table.

Ordered, That the Bill be ingrafted.

A Petition of Sir Edward Turner, Baronet, Lord of the Manor of Merten, in the County of Oxford, and Proprietor of Lands in the open and common Fields in the Township of Merton aforesaid; and of Richard Harrington, Esquire, a Proprietor likewise of Lands in the said open and common Fields; was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Lands of the Petitioners lie dispersed in the said open Fields; and being intermixed with the Glebe Lands belonging to the Rector and Fellows of Exeter College, in the University of Oxford, are, in their present Situation, in a great Measure, incapable of Improvement; and alleging, That if the said Fields were divided, and inclosed, and fe -parate Allotments made to the Proprietors, in Proportion to their respective Properties and Interests therein, it would tend to the Benefit of the Parties concerned, as well as to the public Advantage; but that the feme cannot be efleded, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, for dividing and inclosing the said open Fields, in such Manner, and under such Regulations, as to the House shall leem proper.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring.in a Bill, pursuant to the Prayer of the said PetitionAnd that the Lord Strange, Mr. Coventry, and Mr. Morton, do prepare, and bring in, the feme.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the Electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament

And the iaft Determination of the House, made upon the ioth.Day of February 1670, concerning the Right of electing Barons to serve in Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex (whereby it was resolved, that the Bailiff, Jurors, and Freemen, had not only Voices in the Election, but that the Election was in the Populacy) was allb read.

And the Standing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel at the

Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament, for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the lait Determination in the House of Commons, was also read.

And One of the Counsel for the Petitioners was heard; and infilled, that in the said Determination of the House, the Words "Bailiff, Jurors, and Freemen," mean such Bailiff, Jurors, and Freemen only, as are resident within the said Town and Port; and that the Word " Populacy* means " Inhabitants at large of the Town and Port of Seaford,

" being Mailers of Families, and not receiving Alms.’* Then One of the Counsel for the Sitting Members was heard.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

They were again called in.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having proposed to produce Evidence, in order to shew that the Words " Bailiff, Jurors, and Freemen," mentioned in the said Determination oif the House, of the 10th Day of February 1670, mean only such Bailiff, Jurors, and Freemen, as are resident within the said Town and Port;

And the Counsel for the Sitting Members having ob-jeded to the Ad million of that Evidence, as being contrary to the said Determination of the House: And having been heard upon their said Objection;

The Counsel for the Sitting Members were heard in Answer thereto; and infilled that the Word " Populacy" in the said Determination of the House, means Inhabitants, Housekeepers paying Scotland Lot.

And the said Counsel examined a Witness, in Support of their said Construction.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having been heard by way of Reply;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Rejoived, That in the last Determination of this House, of the Right of Election of Barons to serve in Parliament for the Town and Port of Seaford, in the County of Sussex, made the 10th Day of February, in the Year 1670; which is as followeth; "That the Bailiff, Jurors, and Freemen, had not only Voices in " Election, but that the Election was in the Populacy," the Word " Populacy" therein mentioned, extended only to the Inhabitants, Housekeepers of the said Town and Port, paying Scotland Lot.

Then the Counsel on both Sides were again called in; and Mr. Speaker acquainted them therewith.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners acquainted the House, that the House having come to the said Resolution, he had nothing further to offer in Behalf of the Petitioners.

Then the Counsel on both Sides were again directed to withdraw.

Anthony Gardner, being examined, said, That he is well acquainted with the River Severn, between Bridge and Bewdley Bridge, which is navigable for Boats and other Vessels: That the Method of haling upon that Part of the River, is by Men only, for which Purpose they have. Time out of Mind, claimed a Path, a Foot and an Half wide on each Side of the River, in what Part they please; which they have always enjoyed, without Interruption, or the Payment of any Toll or Imposition whatibever.

That sometimes Vessels are drawn by 40 or 45 Men, and sometimes no more than Five.

That they are obliged to go in a Variety of Paths, by Reason of the Riling and Falling of the River; that the Paths are, in many Places, 30 or 40 Yards wide, iti others, not more than Four Feet; and that, in (hors Turnings of the Fiver, they are obliged to go 60 Yards into the Land; and don’t make any Satrsfaction for this, though it should happen to be in Gtafs fit for mowing.'

Mr. James Berresford, being examined, laid, He knows that Part of the River very-well; that it is the Custom to tow Vessels with Men; that the Men cannot draw all in One Line, which occasions the Paths to be very broad in some Places; but that he never heard any Complaint of Trel’palTes on that Account, or any Satisfaction demanded.

That he has surveyed this Part of the River, and finds the Paths, upon an A verage? N in* or Ten Feet broad.

Mr. Richard Tasterfall, being examined, Hid, That he knows the River Sever,/, between Worcester Bridge artd Bewdley Bridge-, that Vessels navigating the said River are towed by Men; that they never make Satisfaction for the Damage done by towing, although they go in fotne Places throng!) Com Fields.

Then the Agent for the IV't'o^rs produced an Act: of the 23d Year o( Ile/ry the Lvgh'h. by which it appeared, that Persons navigating the 'a:-.! Rivet, have a Right to Towing Paths on each Side, a Foot and an Halt wide.

Mr. Anthony Gardner, being again examined, (-.id,'

That Carnage on the said Riv-r is much inrreased, tying near doubled vvii.iin t - is Time; so that it is difficult to fin i Men to vv the Y’edbls; and that at le.ift Nine Tenths of the Good., brought up the River from Wcr-c-ferarc landed at Bewd/rv: That Vessels < sten wait Three or Four Days at Wor refer t -r want of Men; and that sometimes the Water tails during the Interval, so that they cannot proceed fir Want of Water.

That the Waiters of Vessels choose to employ Men uled to the Bhliness; but that they are frequently obliged to hire Husbandmen, at the Rate of Two Shillings a Day and their Victuals, besides Three Halfpence, which they give them the Night before; and that, within hii Memory, they gave but 18 d.

That the Water falling while Vessels are waiting for Men, sometimes detains Merchandizes for a Month; during which Time they are liable to be damaged by being kept on board, or to be stolen if put on Shore.

Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Berresford and Mr. Tat ter fall.

And all the Witnesses further said, That they cannot at present tow with Horses, as there are many Stiles irt the Way, and they want proper Bridges over the Brooks: That, if they could make Ule of Horses, it would be a Saving of more than rjs. in 20, as they apprehend One Horle would draw more than Seven Men (though they never (aw the Experiment tried) and may be hired for Three Shillings a Day.

Rcfo/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

A Petition of the Rector and Scholars of Exeter College in Oxford, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That the Petitioners observe by the Votes of the House, that a Bill has been brought in for dividing and inclosing the Common Fields of the Parish of Merton, in the County of Oxford-, and alleging, that the Rectory of the said Parish, conlifting of the Tythes of the whole, and- also a considerable Glebe, whereof Eighty-six Acres lie intermixed and dispersed within the Common Fields of the said Parish, are Part of the Inheritance and Endowment of the said College; and that, if the said Bill should pass into a Law, the same would be very detrimental to the Rights and Revenues of the Petitioners and their Successors: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and that the Petitioners may be heard by themselves or Counsel against the said Bill^ and that the same may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields in the Township of , in the County of Oxford, be read a Second Time; and that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be then heard by their Counsel upon their said Petition.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente,

That an humble Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House, for His most gracious Speech from the Throne; and for His having been pleased to communicate to this House the Motives which have obliged His Majesty to declare War against Spain; a Measure which hath been rendered unavoidable by the offensive Conduct of that Court, the great Armaments made in Spain, both by Sea and Land, and by the repeated Denials of those Explanations, and of that just Satisfaction which His Majesty, for the Security of His Kingdoms, had so much Reason to demand: To declare, That this House fees, with Concern, that Influence which hath unhappily prevailed in the Court of Spain, and which hath determined them no longer to disavow their hostile Intentions, but to come to Extremities, contrary to the real Interest of both Nations: To acknowledge, with the warmed Sentiments of Gratitude and of Duty, the many signal Instances of His Majesty’s Moderation, and of His tender Concern for His People, in His constant Endeavours to prevent this Rupture, if it had been possible; and to express the highest Satisfaction at the Preparations which His Majesty, in His Royal Wisdom, hath in the mean time directed to be made for that Event:

To assure His Majesty, That, thoroughly sensible of the Dangers with which the ambitious Designs, and Union of the House of Bourbon, theaten the Commerce and Independency of these Kingdoms, and of the rest of Europe, His faithful Commons will, with the utmost Firmness and Vigour, steadily support His Majesty in the Prosecution of this just and necessary War, and for the Attainment of an honourable Peace.

Coalheaver*. A Petition of several Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and all other industrious Coalheavers, employed in the unloading Ships and Vessels bringing Coals into the River Thames, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That, in pursuance of the late Act, for the Relief of the Coalheavers working upon the River Thames, and for enabling them to make Provision for such of themselves as shall be sick, lame, or past their Labour, and for their Widows and Orphans, about Fifty Gangs of Coalheavers, with a Foreman to each Gang, were formed

and registered in Manner directed by the said Act; which Regulation, had it been continued, the Petitioners apprehend, would have proved of great Benefit to rlie Coal Trade in general, and also to the Coalheavers and their numerous Families; but that soon after the establishing of the said Gangs, which the Petitioners prelume were a greater Number than all the Buyers of Coals could supply with Lighters and other Craft to receive the Coals from the Ships, a Combination was set on foot by certain Persons called Coal Undertakers, who agreed among themselves to give the Preference of the Work to such of the Gangs as would promise not to pay the Poundage, which, by the said Act, is directed to be paid, to be applied toward a Provision for such of them as should be sick, or otherwise incapable of working, and toward the Maintenance of their Widows and Children; and that the said Undertakers, by many other Artifices, have decoyed the said Gangs from the Office; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Prices of Coalheavers Labour were settled by Act of Parliament, it would be very advantageous to the Coal Trade in general, and to the Petitioners, and the rest of the Coalheavers; and that the above-mentioned Act is, in many other Respects, defective: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for rendering the said Act more effoftual, for the Purposes thereby intended, under such Regulations as shall be thought most fit; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief in the Premises as to the House fin 11 seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

The Counsel on the Behalf of the Sitting Member rested their Defence on the Evidence of the Witnesses produced by the Petitioner, and infilled, that neither the Agency of Joseph Hannan, nor the Partiality of Simon Ranee, the Returning Officer, was any ways proved

by the Evidence, on the Behalf of the Petitioner; and therefore thought it needless to call any Evidence.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; videlicet.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That William Matthezv Burt, Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, at the last Election of Burgesses to serve for Great Marlow, in the County of Bucks, in this present Parliament, Joseph Harman was guilty of Bribery, and other corrupt Practices.

The First Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

Mr. Burt withdrew.
