To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Act of the ioth Year of the Reign of King George the First was read; whereby the said Commissioners are impowered to make a new Cut or Channel from Winchelsea Water to the Sea, and heighten the Walls of the Channel of Winchejeaand Breads, from the said

new intended Cut to the Town of and from the said Cut to the present Harbour of; and to do . all other Works necessary for effecting the Purpose of the said Act: And,

Mr. William Green, Engineer, being examined, laid, That a Cut is already made from Winchelsea Wall to the Sea, Part of which is planked or wharfed, and the rest rice-headed or faggot-headed; and that Two Piers are erected, and a Sluice made, and the Walls of the Cut are wharfed, and that the Sea may now be let in without any Danger to the adjoining Lands: That the Walls are-Three Feet above the highest Spring Tides, and where lpweft, are higher than the highest Part of Wall; and that the highest Spring Tides don’t come over the Winchelsea Wall: That the Walk are 90 Feet broad in the weakest Part, and extend to Feet above High Water Mark at the highest Tide: That the Wall is of Earth dug from the Canal, which is the properest Material, and that they are quite sufficient to keep out the Sea, being able to bear Nine Times more Weight than will be against them.

That the Stone Piers are 36 Feet wide, 60 long, and about Two Feet above the highest Tide: That there is a wooden Pier at the Head of the western Pier, which ip nearly finished, the same Width of the Stone Pier, and which will be 200 Feet long.

That the Sluices and Flood Gates are completed, and; that there is a Stone Dam cross the Harbour in which they are fixed, 1 Rods from the Stone Pier Heads: That there are Two Stone Piers to the Gates, Forty Feet Five Inches long; and another in the Center 24 Feet wide and 58 long; which, with the Timber upon, them, are 10 Inches above the highest Tides.

That the Sluice Gates are 35 Feet wide, and the Water on the Sill of the Gate 16 Feet deep at Neap Tides, which is sufficient to carry in Merchant Ships of above 300 Ton Burthen, and Government’s Ships of 400 Tons.

That the Gates for scouring the Channel are 30 Feet wide between Pier and Pier: That they arc divided into rive Gates, and that the Bottom of them goes to the Bottom of the Sluice.

That 256 Sail of ryelTds may lay entirely safe in the Canal, and have funicient Room to swing with Safety.^ That there is Six Feet Diffe.cncc between Neap Tides juid Spring Tides; the Neap Tides riling Two Fathom, and the Spring Tides Four; and that there will bp con-?

City of Sir Robert Ladbroke reported from the Committee, to l^xidon whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and treeu' Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In support of the Allegations of the said Petition, the Agent for the Petitioners produced an Act of the 33d Year of his late Majesty, whereby the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of are im-

powered to widen and render more convenient several Streets, Lanes, and Passages, described in a Schedule annexed to the said Act; and also to make and open such new Streets, Ways, and Passages, as are described in another Schedule annexed to the said Act: And

Mr. George Dance, Surveyor to the City of London, informed your Committee, That he was employed to make Designs for opening the Streets in pursuance of the said Act, and that some Progress hath been made therein; but that the Powers of the Act have been found deficient to answer the Purposes thereby intended; — that they proceeded to make a Street from Crutched Friars to the Minories, which was ordered to be Fifty Feet broad, but found they could purchase no more Ground than was necessary to be laid into the Street, and consequently could not build Houses on each Side thereof; and that they are always limited to the intended Breadth of the Street, without any Regard to the Houses on each Side.

And that the said Act is also deficient, or doubtful, with regard to laying Timber in Party Walls.

That if the Powers of the said Act were extended to > the opening of a new Street from to the Man-

Jion House, it would be of great public Utility.

That the Ground on which the said Street is intended to be made, is a great Part of it covered with Rubbish; that the Owners of lome Part of it are not known, and is a Receptacle for Persons of ill Fame.

Mr. Robert Taylor, Surveyor, confirmed Mr. Dance’s Evidence, and said. That he should have purchased Ground in some of the intended Streets, had not the City been so confined that they had not Power to fell enough.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging and rendering more effectual the Powers granted by an Act made in the 33d Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for widening certain Streets, Lanes, and Passages, within the City of London and Liberties thereof; and for opening certain new Streets and Ways within the feme; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; and for extending the same to certain other Streets and Passages within the said City and liberties thereof: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke, Mr. T1 icier, Sir Richard Glynne, Mr. Alderman Mr. Alderman Harley, Mr. Alderman Dickinson, Sir

William Baker, and Me Palerson, udo prepare, and bring in, the fame. '

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That several Butchers, not only keep open Shops in the public Streets, within the said City and Liberties thereof, but daily llaughtef their Cattle, to the great Annoyance of the neighbouring Inhabitants, and all Persons passing the said Streets; and that the said Practice is not only inconvenient, but detrimental to the Health of the Inhabitants of the said City; and alleging. That the Petitioners conceive, that the foie Exercise of the said Trades ought to be confined to the several public Markets; and representing to the House, That the Practice of driving live Cattle through the Streets of the said City, has of late Years become an intolerable Grievance to the Petitioners, and all other Persons passing the public Streets: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to prevent the fiaughtering of Cattle, except in Places appointed for that Purpose, and for confining the Exercise of the Trade of Butchers to the several Markets, and for regulating the driving of Cattle within the said City and Liberties, under such Provisions and Restrictions as to the House shall seem meet.

The House being informed, That the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the Door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House

Sir Henry Erjk'me reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of James Earl of Lauderdale, and the humble Petition of George Baillie, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of FaCl contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House: and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

By the Evidence of Robert Reid, Engineer, it appeared, that the Road from Carfrae Mill, through New-biggin, 7 her fane, and Greenlaw, in the County of Berwick, is much the nearest, and best Communication between Newcastle and Edinburgh; and that the present

Road from Newcastle to Edinburgh, through Berwick is almost impassable for Carriages, and absolutely so for Artillery; but that, in order to render the said first mentioned Road of Use to the Public, it is necessary to build a Bridge over the River Tweed, at or near;

for, without such Bridge, it is impossible that the Road should produce a Toll sufficient even to keep the same in Repair.

And the said Mr. Reid, and Mr. Smeaton an Engineer, severally produced to your Committee Designs for the said intended Bridge, with Estimates of the Expence of perfecting the fame, which they had severally drawn, and computed, without any previous Communication with one another: and Mr. s Design amounted

to £.2500 and Mr. Reid’s to £.2583 1 od.

Then an Act passed in the 33d Year of His late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Road from Deatiburn Bridge, through Greenlaw, and Part of the Jedburgh Road, by Lauder, in the Shire of Berwick, to Cornhill, in the County of Durham; and for building a Bridge over the Tweed, near Cold-fir earn, was read.

And the said Mr. Reproduced to your Committee an Account of the whole Produce of the Tolls, from the 29th Day of September 1760, the Time of the Commencement of the Ad, to the 3d Day of January 1762, by which it appeared that the Tolls had produced £.283 ior. nd. and that the Money disbursed was 1,370 1 os. 8 d.so that there remained a Debt of £.1000 to certain Persons who had advanced the said Money on their own private Credit, besides a Debt of £.86 19J. 9 d.and, considering the necessary Expences of gathering the Toll, it would be Six Years before the Debt could be paid off, without producing any thing towards the Repair of the Road or building the said Bridge.

Then Mr. Reid produced to your Committee a particular Survey of the Road directed to be repaired by the said Act, together with an Estimate of the Expence of repairing the same; by which it appeared that the Sum of £.3140 14 s.6d. would be necessary to repair the said Road, which is 25 Miles in Length; exclusive of the Expence of building 17 small Bridges thereupon, of which Bridges he produced an estimate to the Committee, amounting to £.954 u. od.

James Pringle, Ei'quire, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Reid, as to the Road from Edinburgh to Morpeth, by

VOL. 29.

Coldstream, being much hearer, and more convenient, than the Road through Berwick; which was likewise confirmed by l'everal Members present at your Committee.

It appeared by the Evidence of Colonel Caulfield, Inspector of the Roads in Scotland, that the present Road by Berwick is very difficult to be passed for Troops and Carriages; and that feme Part of it, particularly from Berwick to Bellford, and at a Place called the he thinks almost impassable for heavy Carriages, or Artillery; and that it would require a very large Sum of Money to put it in tolerable Repair.

Major Roy, Engineer and Deputy Quarter-master General, said. That the Hill called the Pees, on the Berwick Road, is one of the worst Pafles for Artillery that he ever saw.

Major Stewart laid, He had often made out the Routs for T/roops from England to Scotland; and that he always understood that the drawing Artillery by the Pass of the Pm, was almost impracticable; and that One Day’s March in Six is laved when the Troops can march by Coldstream.

And all the Witnesses concurred, I hat the completing the Road by Coldstream, and building a Bridge there over the Tweed, would be of great public Utility, particularly in the March of Troops, and the Carriage of Artillery; which was confirmed by several Members present.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Mr. Speaker.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for charging certain Annuities, granted in the Year 1760, on the Sinking Fund; and for carrying the Duties therein mentioned to the said Fund; and for making forth Duplicates of Exchequer bills. Tickets, Certificates, Receipts, Annuity Orders, and other Orders loft, burnt, or otherwise destroyed, without any Amendment.

Mr. John Watkinson, being examined, said. That the Trustees, appointed by the said Act, have made great Progress in repairing the said Road; and for that Purpose have borrowed the Sum of 2,568, which dill remains unpaid.

That the Road described in the Petition is very ruinous and dangerous, and in many Places narrow; and that it cannot be repaired and widened by the Laws in being.

That the Petitioners have borrowed a considerable Sum of Money, on the Credit of the said Act, which still remains due; and have caul'ed the greatest Part of the said Roads to be amended and widened; but that, of late, they have been greatly in jured by Waggons and other Carriages; and alleging, that the Tolls now paid for fuel) Carriages, upon those Roads, are by no Means a sufficient Recompeuce for the Damage they do to the Roads; and that, without an IncreafeofToll upon such Carriages, it will not be in the Power of the Petitioners to keep the said Roads in tolerable Repair; and that the said Acts are, in many other Respects, ineffectual: And therefore praying. \\ hereupon your Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Bringing of Fish by Land Carriage to the Cities of London and Westminster, will contribute to the more plentiful Supply of the Markets there with Fish, and reduce the present exorbitant Price thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons, whether brought up in the Trade of a Fishmonger or not, ought to be at Liberty to buy Fish in any Parts of Great Britain, to sell the same again, and

to carry the Fish they shall so buy as they shall think fit, and without Lett orlnterruption, by Land Carriage or otherwise, to the Cities of London or Westminster, or any other Place, to be sold again; under proper Reflric-tions and Regulations against Regrating, Forestalling, and Engrossing thereof; and also touching the Selling thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Carriages which shall be used to carry Fitli as aforesaid, may be permitted to be drawn on Turnpike Roads, by a certain Number of Horses, although the Wheels of such Carriages shall be under the Breadth of Nine Inches.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Carriages to be employed in the Bringing of Fish to the Cities of London and , or else-

vvliere, be put under proper Regulations and Restrictions, as to their travelling on Turnpike Roads, and the Weight of Filli to be carried therein.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all such Fish Carriages ought to be marked on the Outside thereof; and that such Carriages may be permitted tobedrove on the Roads on Sundays or Holidays, and under proper Restrictions, to prevent Drivers thereof carrying Passengers , or any Game or other Things, except Fish, therein.

That, for several Years pad, only Four Persons have annually been nominated to the Office of Overseers of the Poor of the said Parish, whose Duty it is to collect the Poor’s Rates quarterly, and to relieve, employ, and take care of the Poor; and that, from the Extent and Variety of Affairs belonging to their Office, as Overseeds, it is not possible for them to execute it in a proper Manner, although they should employ their whole Time in their Office.

In Support of the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, t lie several Acts of the 8th Year of her late

said Town has, of late Years, very much increased: That, in consequence of this Increase of Trade, the Merchants have been induced to build much larger Vessols than heretofore, and which require so great a . Draught of Water that they are ofren obliged to unlade their Goods before they can get into the Docks, there not being a sufficient Depth of Water to carry them in, except upon the Height of Spring Tides; and that there is a Neeeflity of building a new Dock, with proper Piers, and other Accommodations, capable of admitting Ships of greater Burthen, which is very practicable; a Plan whereof he produced to your Committee:

That he has surveyed the Coast, for a great Distance, on both Sides; and that the Navigation into the Harbour is very dangerous, occasioned by the many shifting Sands at the Mouth thereof; that frequent Accidents happen to Shipping, which the Witness apprehends might in a great Measure he prevented, if Light-houses were erected, or floating Lights placed in a proper Manner.

Mr. William Hutcliinfon, Dock Master of

being examined, said, That the present Docks are in-sufficient for the Shipping using the said Port; and that they cannot get Births for discharging their Ships:

That the Ships are now built 1b large, that they cannot get into the Dock; and that it is necessary to build a Dock capable of receiving Ships of greater Burthen:

That many Accidents have happened to Shipping at the Mouth of the said Harbour, for Want of Light-houses, or moving Lights; and that the present Duties are insufficient for building the necessary Docks and Works; and that there is no Fund applicable to the Building of Light-houses, or defraying the Expence of Lights.

Mr. Joseph Valens, being examined, said, That he had been Receiver of the Dock Duties at Liverpoole upwards of 30 Years; that a new Dock, with proper Piers and Works, and also a Light-house, or moving Lights, are very much wanted; hut that he apprehends the Amount of the present Duties are insufficient to answer the Expence of such new Works; and that no Money can be applied for a Light-house or Lights, by virtue of the present Acts of Parliament.

Mr. John Eyes, being further examined, said, That the Navigation within the Limits of the Port of Liverpoole, has of late Years been very much obit rafted by laving down Yards or Coups for Fish, 225 of which the Witness saw on the Lancq/hirc Side of the said Port, and

Mr. Henry Mart, Pilot and Fisherman, being examined, said, That he is well acquainted with the River Mersey-, and that he had tiled the Method of fithing with Fifti Yards for Seven Years; and, during that Time, taken great Quantities of small Fry of Cod and Whitings, from Three to Five Incites long; that he apprehends thi- Method of fishing is very destructive to the Fifttery, for that he believes that sometimes not less than 3000 Weight a Dav is destroyed by this Means; that he grounds this Opinion from the Number of Fifti Yards in the River, and the Fifti destroyed in One; that he apprehends the Number destroyed in each Fifti Yard to be pretty near alike, and that persons feed their Flogs and Ducks with the small Fry:

That the Fifti Yards obstruct the Course of the River, being set at Low Water in Rows, where they collect Sand; that the Course of the Channel near the Rocks called Red Noses, is not so good as it used to be, which lie imputes to the Fifti Yards fixed there; that they never remove them after they are once fixed, but, if they, are sanded up, they let them go to Ruin.

Mr. Staunton reported from the Committee, to Avhom Journals,

the Report was re-committed, which was made from the Committee avIio were appointed to consider of the reprinting a lutTicient Number of the Journals of this House, for the Use of the Members thereof; That the Committee had considered further of the Matter to thenj referred; and had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee, in the first place, took into their Consideration the several Rel'o'utions and Orders of the House, made upon the 5th Day of May 1742, the 31st Day of May 1742, the 3d Day of March 1748, the 16th Day of January 1752, the 26th Day of May 1756, the lit Day of June 1759, and the 13th Day of March 1761, in relation to the printing of the Journals of the House; from which it appeared, that 1,000 Copies of the said Journals had beeu ordered to be printed for the Use of the Members.

They then proceeded to inquire what had been done in pursuance of the said Orders, and were informed by the Clerk of the House, that 1,000 Copies of the Journals, consisting of 28 Volumes each, had been printed accordingly; and that by far the greateli Part thereof had been delivered for the Use of the Members.

That of such Copies there are now not more than Two complete Sets remaining; but that, as in consequence of the great Length of Time taken up in fmiftiing the Work, many of the Persons avIio had received the former Volumes, were uot, at the Time of delivering the latter Volumes, entitled to the fame, having, ceased to be Members of the House, a great Number of the latter Volumes, in very different Proportions, are frill remaining; a general Account whereof having been stated to your Committee, it appeared to them, that by reprinting a proper Number of Copies of the former Volumes, which may he done at a very moderate Expence, a proportionable Number of entire Sets of the whole Journals might be made lip for the Use of the Members, out of the broken Sets now remaining.

Upon the whole Matter your Committee came to the following Resolution;

liefolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to complete such imperfect Sets of the printed Journals of this House, as are now remaining in the Hands of the Clerk, Three hundred Copies of the First Fourteen Volumes of the said Journals, together with the Indexes thereto, be reprinted for the Use of the Members of this House; by the Appointment, and under the Direction, of Jeremiah Esquire,

Clerk of the House of Commons.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was prnpoferi to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words "Three hundred," and in-farting the Words " Two hundred and Fifty " instead thereof.

Aud the Question being put. That the Words "Three hundred" Hand Part of the said Resolution;

It pasted in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the Words "Two hundred and Fifty" be inserted instead thereof}

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the last Determination of the House, made upon the 12th Day of April 1628, concerning the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Bridport, in the County of Dorset (whereby it was resolved, that the Commonalty in general ought to have Voices in the Election of the Burgesses for the Parliament) was read:

And the Handing Order of the House, made the 16th Day of January 1735, for restraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port, or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons; was also read:

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners were heard; and infilled. That, in the said Determination of the House, the Word " Commonalty" means " all those who, at the " Time of the Election, and for Forty Days before,

" have been Housekeepers, and Inhabitants, legally " settled, and not receiving Alms."

Which being denied, by the Counsel for the Sitting Member; who infilled, that the Word, " Commonalty" means " Inhabitants, Householders, paying Scotland " Lot;"

The Counsel for the Petitioners proceeded to give Evidence, in Support of their Construction of the said Word.

And a Copy of a Charter, granted by King Richard the Second to the Borough of dated the 13 th

Day of May, in the Second Year of his Reign, containing an Inspexiraus of a Charter, granted by King Henry the First, to the said Borough, was produced, and read.

Then a Copy of an Indenture of Return of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in the 17th Year of the Reign of King Edward the Fourth, made by the Bailiffs and Burgesses of the said Borough, under their Common Seal, was produced and read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having referred to, and Hated, a Charter granted by King James the First, incorporating the said Borough, by the Name of Bailiffs and Burgesses;

The same was admitted by the Counsel for the Sitting Member.

Then the Entry in the Journal of the House, of the 12 th Day of April 1628, of the Report of the Proceedings before the Committee of Privileges, touching the Election for the Borough of Bridport, was read.

And the Entries in the Journals of the House, of the 24 th Day of March 1689, and of the 3 ill Day of March 1715, of several Petitions, complaining of undue Elections and Returns for the said Borough, were also read.

And the Journal of the House, of the 5th Day of May 1715, in relation to the Proceedings of the House, upon hearing the Merits of the Election for the said Biorough; and also the Minutes taken of the Evidence given at the Bar of this House, upon the said Hearing, were also read.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners examined several Witnesses, in order to prove that the Inhabitants at large have, by Usage, voted at Elections of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough.

And Copies of several other Indentures of Return of Members to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, dated the 12 th Day of December 1746, the 15th Day of April 1754, and the 28th Day of March 1761, being produced;

The Copy of the said Indenture of Return, of the 12th Day of December 1746, made by the Bailiffs and Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the said Borough, under their Common Seal, was read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners examined aWit-ness, and produced Evidence, in order to prove that several of the Persons, whose Names are subscribed to the said Indenture, were not Persons paying Scotland Lot.

And the said Counsel having gone through their Evidence;

The Counsel for the Sitting Member were heard; and proceeded to give Evidence in Support of their Construclion of the Word " Commonalty," in the said Determination of the House.

And the Entries in the Journals of the House, of the First Day of February 1727, and of the 3d Day of February 1728, of several Petitions complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, were read.

And the Journal of the House, of the 12th Day of February 1729, in relation to the Proceedings of the House, Upon the Petitions which had been presented to the House, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the said Borough, was also read.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member examined a Witness, in further Support of their Construction of the Word " Commonalty," in the said Determination of the House.

And the said Counsel having summed up their Evidence;

The Counsel for the Petitioners were heard by way of Reply.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

To prove the Allegations of the first-mentioned Petition, Mr. Michael Baxter and Mr. Robert Hutchins, being severally examined, said, That they are well acquainted with the Roads leading from the New Inn, in the Parish of Burbach, in the County of Leicester, through the several Places described in the Petition, to Fafeley Bridge, in the County of Warwick -, and from Fieldon Bridge to Bourn Bridge-, and from the Cross Lanes in Over Whitacre, to the Guide Post on Nuneaton Common; and from the Arbour ,at Lane

End, to the South Eall End of a Street, called the Abbey End, in Nuneaton, in the said County of Warwick-, that the said Roads are in a ruinous Condition, and in many Places very narrow and incommodious, and cannot be repaired and widened by the ordinary Course of Law; that there are many Collieries and Lime Works on the said Roads; and that if the same were repaired, it would be of great Advantage to the Vo l.29.

Martii. 213

Inhabitants of the feveraj Towns lying hear the said Roads, by supplying them with Coals and Lime at all Seafous, at a reasonable Price.

To prove the Allegations of the second-mentioned Petition,

Mr. John Hewitt, being examined, said, That the Road leading from Coventry to the Cross Lanes in Oter W hit acre, and from thence to Common, by the

Coal Pits on the said Common, into the Waiting Street Road, by Birch Coppice, to Pin the County of Warwick, is in a ruinous Condition; that the repairing the said Road would be a considerable Advantage to the City o (Coventry, by supplying them with

Coals, at a cheaper Rate, from the different Coal Pits lying near the said Road, where Coals are sold at per Cwt. and prevent a Monopoly at Colliery,

which is the nearest Colliery to Coventry, and from whence they are at present supplied, where Coals are now sold at near 7 d.per Cwt. at the Pit.

That there are great Numbers of Teams kept on the said Road, and in the Neighbourhood of the Collieries, which are confined in the Winter by the Badnels of the Road, but would be employed in carrying Coals to Coventry, and bringing Lime, as Back Carriage, to manure the Lands, if the said Road was repaired.

To prove the Allegations of the third-mentioned Petition,

Mr. Robert Hutchins, being examined, said. That the Road from the North West Eud of the Church Street in Nuneaton, to Wolvey Heath, in the County of

zoick, is in a ruinous Condition; and in many Places very narrow'; and cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law; that there are several Collieries and Lime Works on the said Road; and if the said Road was repaired, Persons residing near the same might be supplied with Coals and Lime at all Seasons, at a reasonable Price:

That the Road from Nuneaton to Mancester Church, being Part of the Road described in the first-mentioned Petition, is the Market Road between Nuneaton and Atherfone, and leads to several Commons and Collieries in the Parish of Nuneaton-, and though narrow' in many Parts, wants but very little Repairs; and therefore it would be a Burthen to the Inhabitants of Nuneaton, if a Gate should be erected between that d own and Mancester Church, or on any Part of Nuneaton Common.

That the Trade of the City of London is much prejudiced by the said Tolls; and that Quarrels do frequently arise between the Toll-takers and Carmen, on Account thereof; by which the Passage on the said Bridge, and in several Streets adjacent, has been greatly obstructed; and that the Petitioners believe, that the Bridge House Estate is more than sufficient, without the said Tolls, to keep t he said Bridge in Repair; and that the Citizens of London, in particular, and the Public in general, will be benefited by abolishing the said Tolls: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief therein, as to the House ilia.Il seem meet.

And the Question being proposed. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to restrain Butchers from slaughteringCattle, or keeping open Shops within the City of London, except in the Markets; and to prevent the Mischiefs that arise from driving Cattle within the said City and Liberties;

The Amendments following were severally proposed to be made to the Question,

To leave out the Words " restrain Butchers from," and insert the Words " regulate the;" after " slaughtering" to insert " of;" to leave out " or keeping open Shops," and insert " and Sale of Meat;" and to leave out " except in the Markets," and insert " and Liberties thereof."

And the Question being put. That the Words " restrain Butchers from" Hand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " regulate the" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the Question being put. That the Word "of" be inserted after the Word " slaughtering

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " or keeping open Shop" Hand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the Words " and Sale of Meat" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " except in the Markets" Hand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put, That the Words " and Liberties thereof" be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the main Question, thus amended, being put;

Mr. Alderman Harley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled (relating to the Testimony of Freemen of the said City, in Suits concerning the Corporation) was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had, directed him t6 report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as followefh;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, William Hu fey, Esquire, the City Solicitor, informed the Committee, That no Freeman can be admitted as a Witness on the Part of the Corporation whereof he is a Member; to remove which Iuconvenience, Witnesses are admitted in Courts of Law, who bave been disfranchised in the Mayor’s Court by a fictitious Judgment; and who are again admitted to their Freedom, as soon as they have given their Evidence:

That this Method is attended with great Trouble and Expence to the City; and it often has happened, that necessary Witnesses have refused to be disfranchised, by which the City have been deprived of their Testimony.

Jonathan Co/ston, Esquire, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Hujfey; and both the W7itnesses added. That, in their Opinion, the Intej-el! of an individual Freeman, in a Corporation of which he is a Member, is so very small, That it cannot possibly have any Influence upon his Testimony.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for admitting Freemen of the City of London, as competent Witnesses on Trials in which the Corporation of the City is concerned: And that Mr. Alderman Harley, Mr. Alderman Dickinson, and Mr. Alderman Bedford, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Walkers Works into back Water; that Lands through which the Cut made by Messrs. Being asked tile Question, he/aid; He believed the Waste Water, after serving the Mills, might be returned into the Navigation, or that A New Ciit thight be mdde upon the same Level With that of Messrs: Walkers; without prejudicing their Mills; And that before the neifr Cut and Mills were made, he never heard of any Boats being flopped hi Ickles Data; which did not get clear in 24 Hours.

Being asked, Hoiv many Locks there are between Walker's Works and the Head of the Navigation ? He said, there are 3 above Rotherham arid 2 above Holmes.

Mr. John Cockjhiit;being examined; said; That he

knows the River Dun, within the Limits described in the Petition, and has kno writhe 10 or iz Years, at which Time there was only One Slitting Mill there; and that 3 or Years Ago it new Slitting Mill and a Rolling Mill were eroded; that there is also a Blast Furnace for melting Iron Ore, and a Gri nding Mill; and that the Rolling Mill arid Slitting Mill appear to be much larger and stronger than before, and believes the present Mills have greater Power than the former.

That about 3 Years since a Navigable Cot was finished from the Tail of the Works on Holme's Go4t to Ickles Dam, which supplied the said Dam with Water, and thereby rendered it navigable; that then a Dam was made at about the Distance of 100 Yards from Holme's Green, for the Purpose of flopping the Water from running down the New Cut into Ickle's Dam; that afterwards, in August 1760, (as the Witness thinks) Flood Gates were erected for the same Purpose; that the Dafn was to keep the Water from running down into Bromley Sands Cut, and the Flood Gates are eroded for the same Purpose, only that they may be opened And flint occasionally, and they throw the Waite Water down the Tail of the old Goit into BotherhOm Dam; that when

the Witness saw the Flood Gates, which was in Summer* they were shut; the Consequence of which whs, the pinching the Navigation of Water in fd

Being asked, Whether if the Flood Gates next the River were to be left open in Times of Floods, it would not lay the Works in back Water ? He said, That those Gates are so conllrufted as to shut themselves, and by that Means prevent any back Water: but if the lower. Gates were taken away, the Floods would flop the Works:

That if the Owners of the Works were to fill up the new Cut, the Water would go the same Course it for-pierly did, and the Works would use the same Quantity of Water.

Mr Cockjhut, being further examined, said. That he

bas surveyed the River Dun from Holm's Goit along Jckle's Dam, to the Tail of the Works; that the Fall of Water from Bromley Sands Lock to Rotherham Dam is 6 Foot 11 Inches at the upper Flood Gate, in the New Cut, is 10 Inches, and the Water stood 2 Inches deep upon Holm's Mill Sheeting; so that the whole Fall from Holm's Mill to Rotherham Dam is 7 Foot 7 Inches; and that the Fall on Holm's Goit is nearly equal; that the Water run 8 Inches deep over the Dam, which is 12 Foot wide.at Holm's Goit, and that the Mills were then (landing dill.

That a new Cut might be made out of Holme Goit, from any Part above the Dam made by the Navigators,* into Bromley Sands Cut, which would answer the Purpose of the Navigation as well as the New Cut, and could be no Prejudice to the Works of Mefirs. Walkers and C\ but that such a Cut could not be made below that Dam without raising the Banks, to prevent overflowing the Lands; and that by raising Banks on Holm's Goit, it would be practicable to bring the Water into Bromley Sands Cut, from the Distance of about 400 Yards, without Prejudice to the Works.

Being cross examined, he was asked, Whether the Water from the W orks on Holm's Goit would flow into the Navigation when the main River is fresh or high ? He said, It could not; for then the Gates (hut thein-selves; and that in Times of Flood, it is necessary that the Old Tail Goit be kept open to prevent back Water in the Works; and that if the Blast Furnace is laid in back Water, it would be a great Damage to the Own-. ers; that when he surveyed the River, the Dam made in the Old Goit, by the Company, was 6 Inches lower than Melfrs. Walkers Works, and consequently could be no Obstruction to them; that the Ground where the Company have raised their Dam, in Holme Goit, is . higher than the Ground of Jckle's Dam.

Being asked, Whether if a new Cut was made below Mr. Walker's New Cut, into Ickles Dam, from the Goit, it would not be necessary to make a Dam in the Goit, in order to throw the Water into Ickle's Dam ? He said, It would , but that that Dam might be 6 Inches . lower than the Sheeting of the Mills; and that the Works could not receive any Injury from thence by the back Water.

Westminster Mr. Whitworth reported from the Committee, who Street*, were appointed to consider of proper Methods for the better Paving, Enlightening, and Cleansing the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Alleys, of the City and Liberty of Westminster, the Parillies of Saint Mary Le Bone, Saint Giles in the Fields, Saint George the Martyr, Saint George Bloomsbury; that Part of the Parish of Saint Andrew's, Holbourn, which lies in the County of the

several Liberties of the Rolls and Savoy-, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster which lies in the County of Middlesex-, That the Committee had considered the Matters to them referred; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

Upon reading several of the Acts of Parliament hitherto paired, relating to paving and cleansing the Streets within the City and Liberty of and

upon the Examination of several Persons whom your Committee called before them; and also upon considering the several Accounts relative to the Matter referred to the Consideration of your Committee, and whichyour

233

Committee had directed to be laid belore them, and have hereunto annexed; your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Alleys, of the City and Liberty of Westminster, the Parishes of Saint Mary le Bone, Saint Giles in the Fields, Saint George the Martyr, Saint George Bloomsbury-,that Part of the Parish of Saint Andrew's, Holbourn, which lies in the County of Middlesex; the several Liberties of the Rolls and Savoy; and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster which lies in the County of Middlesex; are, in general, very ill paved and cleansed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Method of taking Care of the Pavements, by the Annoyance Jury, is ineffectual to answer the Purposes intended by the Legislature.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the present Method, of the Inhabitants paving before their own Houses, without being limited, either in Time, Materials, or Method of doing it, is One Cause of the bad Pavements of the Streets.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the respective Companies who furnish Water to the Inhabitants, or any other Person or Persons whatsoever, being permitted to take up the Pavements by their own Workmen, and not being obliged to lay down the Dime in a proper and effect uni Manner, is another Cause of the bad Pavements of the Streets.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Alleys, are not duly and properly lighted.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the future, the Paving, Cleansing, keeping in Repair, and Lighting the said Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Alleys; and also removing Nuisances thereout, and making the same more ornamental and commodious; be put under the Management of Commissioners.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That from the present bad, irregular Paving, both as to Manner and Materials, it will be absolutely necessary to lay in most Places a new Pavement, instead of repairing and amending the old one.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Expence of new paving any Square, Street, Lane, or Alley, will be too great to be borne wholly by the Inhabitants of such Squares, Streets, Lanes, or Alleys.

That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Inhabitant of any Square, Street, Lane, or Alley, shall be liable to contribute or pay towards the new Pavement of such Square, Street, Lane, or Alley, until the Pavement of such Square, Street, Lane, or Alley, shall be completed.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Squares, Streets, Lanes, or Alleys, which shall remain not paved under the Direction of the said Commissioners, shall continue to be kept in Repair, lighted, and cleansed, according to the Laws now in being for those Purposes.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards New Paving, Cleansing, Lighting, and keeping in Repair, the said Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Allej's, a Pound Rate should be laid on every Inhabitant thereof, so soon as any such Square, Street, Lane, or Alley, shall be new paved under the Direction of the said Commissioners.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the said Inhabitants, paying to such Pound Rate, should be exempted from the Charge of Paving, Cleansing, Lighting, and keeping in Repair, the said Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Alleys; and from all Penalties incurred by neglecting the fame.

To the Committee of the honourable House of Commons, appointed to consider of proper Methods for the better Paving, Enlightening, and Cleansing the Squares, Streets, Lanes, and Alleys, of the City and-Liberty of Westminster, See. and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster adjoining the reto:

In Obedience to your Order of the 3d of March instant, for the proper Officer to lay before the said Committee the Total of the yearly Rent Charge to the Poor and Scavenger’s Rates, of the Parish of St. Mary le Strand, for the Year lad pad (which Parish is but finall, and lies partly within the Liberty of Westminster, and partly in the said Duchy of Lancaster) I do humbly certify. That the total Rent Charge to the Poor and Scavenger’s Rates, of the said Parish, the last Year, amounted to £. 5,443, which, at in the Pound, that was charged the last Year to the Poor’s Rate of the said Parish, came to £.367. ijs. 4 and at 3d. in the Pound to the Scavenger’s Rate, came to £.68. or. gd. but, by reason of several of the Tenants leaving their Houses, and Houses Handing empty that Year, there was collected and received the Sum of£. 359. 6s. only, of the said Poor’s Rate; and the Sum of £.64. os. gd. only, of the said Scavenger’s Rate; the Palace of Somer/el House, within the said Parish, being not charged, either to the Poor’s or Scavenger’s Rates, His Majesty allowing a Bounty of £. 30 a Year-to the said Parish, in lieu thereof; and the Pavement before the same is kept in Repair by His Majesty’s Board of Works.

March 8th, 1762.

Robt Bygrave,

Vestry Clerk of the said Parish,

Sir John Philipps reported from the Committee, to-whom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled (relating to the Improving of an Avenue of l/mdon Bridge) was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-rested him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, made in the 29th Year-of his late Majesty, was read; whereby the Ix>rd Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, are impowered to purchase and take-down such Houses, or Buildings, {landing on don Bridge, or contiguous or adjoining thereto, as they should judge necessary, for Enlargement or Improvement of the Passage over, and the Avenues leading to and from, the said Bridge. And,

Mr. Dance, Surveyor, being examined, said. That great Progress hath been made in executing the Powers given by the said Act; and the Passage over the said Bridge, for Foot Passengers, on the Eastern Side, is finished, and secured by a Balustrade, which ranges Northward, almost in a Line, upon the Steeple of the Parish Church of the United Parishes of Saint Magnus and Saint Margaret, NewFish Street Hill:

That if Part of the Fabric, on the North and South Sides of the said Steeple, was taken down, and a Passage made through the said Steeple, it would not only render the Easteru Side of the said Bridge more safe and commodious for Foot Passengers, but would tend to prer vent the frequent and dangerous Delays arising from the Number of Carriages eroding each other in their Passage over the said Bridge, to and from Fish Street Hill, and the Upper and Lower Thames and that this will

not be any Injury to the said Church, in Point of Safety, Ornament, or Utility.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for fenlarging and improving the North East Avenue to London Bridge: And that Sir John Philipps, Mr. Alderman Dickinson, Sir Robert Ladbroke, Sir Richard Glynne, Mr. Alderman Beckford, and Mr. Alderman Harley, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That the Petitioners observe, that a Bill is depending to enlarge the Term and Powers of an Act, passed in the 11 th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty,.for continuing several Acts, relating to the Harbour of Liverpool, and for enlarging the said Harbour, by making an additional Dock, and building a Pier in the Open Harbour there; and for enlightening the said Dock; and for erecting Light-houses. or proper Lights, within the said Port; and for the Preservation and improvement of the Navigation and Fishery of the River Mersey, within the said Port and Harbour of Liverpool; and repre-fenting to the House, That several of the Powers and Provisions, contained in the said Bill, will be very prejudicial to the PetitionersEfiates and Intcrefls, and will deprive them of certain Rights, to which they apprehend they are legally intitled; and that no Public Meeting has been held of the Inhabitants of the Counties of Lancaster or Chester, to consider of Application for the said Bill, or any Notice given to the Persons interested in the Lands adjoining to, or the Fisheries, or other Properties, in the said River, nor any Plan or Scheme of the intended Regulations produced, or any Information, with respect to the Purport or Prov ifions of the said Bill, given to the Petitioners, or others interested therein, whereby they could form any Judgment how, or in what Manner the said Regulations may afi'efl their respectivelnterefts and Properties: And that as no Meeting was called, whereby the Sense of the Public, and of the Parties particularly interested, could he taken, with respect to this Matter; and as the Petitioners were unacquainted with the Powers contained in the said Bill, until the same was presented to the House; and as several of the Persons interested have not yet, as the Petitioners

3 S have

*54

have the greatest Reason to believe, been apprized of , the Purport of the said Bill; the Petitioners hope that the same will not pals, until the Traders, Manufacturers, and Inhabitants of that Part of the Country, and all the Parties whose Properties are likely to be affected, have had, as is nfual in Matters of this Kind, proper previous Notice of the Nature of the Scheme, in order that a Judgment may be formed, whether the most effectual Provision is made for the Advantage of the Public, and such Individuals, as may think themselves affected, may have reasonable Time to lay their same before the House: And therefore praying the House to take the Matter into Consideration, and to give such Relief as to the House shall seem necessary.

" Resolved, That the present Method of taking Care €l of the Pavements, by the Annoyance Jury, is ineffeftual to answer the Purposes intended by the " Legislature.

" Resolved, That the present Method of thelnhabitants Paving before their own Houses, without being 1 " limited either in Time, Materials, or Method of " doing it, is One Cause of the bad Pavements of the ^Streets.

" Resolved, That the respective Companies, who furnish Water to the Inhabitants, or any other Person or " Persons whatsoever, being permitted to take up the " Pavements, by their own Workmen, and not being " obliged to lay down the same in a proper and effectual " Manner, is another Cause of the bad Pavements of " the Streets.

" UcJ'olved, That the said Squares, Streets, Lanes,

" and Alleys, are not duly and properly lighted.

" Resolved, That the Expence of new Paving any " Square, Street, Lane, or Alley, will be too great to <c be borne wholly by the Inhabitants of such Squares,

" Streets, Lanes, or Alleys.

" Resolved, That no Inhabitant of any Square,

he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

Thomas Sewell, being examined, said, That the Road leading from Hesket Newmarket, in the County of Cum-

berland, by Haves Bridge, to C; and from thence, by Lorton, over Whinlatter, to Keswick, in the said County; and from Keswick, by Dummail Rays, and

Ambleside, to Kirkby in Kendale, in the County of West-

moreland; and also the Road from Cross,

near Kirkby in Kendale, to the Lake called Windermere, in the said County of Westmoreland; and also the Road from Hesketh aforesaid, over Hutton Moor, to Penrith, in the said County of Cumberland; are in many Places very narrow, and become so ruinous and bad, as to be dangerous to Persons and Carriages travelling thereon; that the said Roads lie chiefly over very high and steep Mountains, and through the most barren Parts of the said Counties; and that the repairing and widening the said Roads would be a great Advantage to that Part of the Country in particular, and to the Public in general; but that the same cannot be done by the ordinary Course of Law.

A Member present at the Committee confirmed the above Evidence, with regard to the bad Condition of the Roads.

hyment of was referred, That the Committee had examin-

a£2n ed the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, anil afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegat ions of the Petition, the Agent for the Petitioner laid before your Committee a Report from the Commissioners of the Salt Duties, in Consequence of an Order of Reference from the Lords Commissioners of the Treasury, upon the Petition of the said William Earle, praying Relief in his Cafe, containing the following Particulars; viz.

That on or about the Tenth Day of December 1759, there was thipped at Liverpoole 720 Bushels of White Salt, on Board the Drake, James Master,

for the North Seas; the Duties of which being £. 120. was f .'cured by the Bond of and James Mackenjiei/, dated 12th October, 1759:

That it appears, that Proof was made, at the Quarter Sessions at Liverpool, that the said Vessel, the Drake, going into the Harbour of Dublin, was made an intire Wreck, and no Part of the Salt saved:

And that the Certificate of the Loss of this Salt was laid before the said Commissioners; and they were desired to permit their Collector to accept of the Certificate of the Loss of the Salt, in Discharge of the Bond given for the Duty on the Salt loll; to which the Commissioners answered, that they could not give an Order to their Collector to discharge the said Bond, the Proof of the Loss not having been made within Nine Months after the Loss happened, as required by the Act 12 Anme, cap. 2.

But that the said Commissioners had no doubt of the Reality of the Loss of the Salt in question, the Negative put upon the Certificate arising purely from the Proof of the Loss not having been made within the Time prescribed by Law; and therefore they have no Objection to the suspending any Prosecution upon the Petitioner’s Bond, until such Time as he shall have an Opportunity of applying to Parliament for Relief.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

That the moll convenient Places for building Light- Liverpool Iioufes would be at, or near, Milje and Harbour.

Hall, which lie within a Mile of High Water Mark:

N*. I.

To the Worshipful John Blackburn Esquire, Mayor, the Aldermen, Bailiffs, and Council of Liverpool.

Gentlemen,

We, the underwritten, Mailers of the Coasting Vessels trading to Liverpool, having a grateful Sense of your generous Endeavours to support the Floating Light, by the Expence of a large Sum out of the Dock Tonnage, do hereby return our moll sincere Thanks, for your great Attention to the public Interests, &c. and as the Continuance thereof would be attended with such large Expences, (as Ihe hath parted her Moorings so often, which made her at same Time but an uncertain Guide); we therefore beg Leave humbly to offer it as our Opi-

Liverpool

Harbour.

nion, that Four lights, properly placed on Shore, would be more constant, and more conducive to the good Ends proposed; viz. One large and high Light, to be placed on or about Mockbeggar's alt; another low, and less Light, at the Edge of the Strand thefeTwo to be kept in a Line, for Leading Marks along 7/iy/r, by the North West Buoy, which might be run by in going out, or incoming in, till we bring other Two Check Lights in a Line, to lead into Hyle Lake-, the higher and larger of which to be placed on, or near, the Land Mark; the lower, and less, at the Strand Edge-, the Meeting of these Two Lines would direct to a proper Place for anchoring, to wait for the Liverpool Tide, as may be fcen in the Draft', Sic. these Lights would likewise direct how to go into Hyle Lake, when there is no other Place of Refuge; as at the Six o’CIock Tides in the Winter, which are the Dead of the Neap, and consequently little Water to run round the Rock with, and no Day Light to run for either Channel with a flowing Tide; in such Cases these Hyle Lake Lights may serve to run by, from one Channel to the ether, to keep clear of the West of Burbo: We think ourselves in equal Danger coming in or going out, as we are often catched upon a Lee Shore, by the Wind’s coming about all at once from the Southward to the North Welt, and blowing strong when in the Night, we are close to the Backs of these dangerous Banks which are so deeply imbaved; the many fatal Losses, where the Crew's and Passengers have suffered, with the Ships and Cargoes, are but too well known, to shew the Necessity of these Lights; to support which we are willing to pay a reasonableTonage, to be regulated as other Lights of the same kind are paid for.

This Scheme examined and approved of by.

A Petition of several of the Trustees, for patting in execution an Act of the 20th Year of his late Majesty, for enlarging the Term and Power granted by an Act of the 13th Year of King George the First, for repairing the Roads leading from Bromsgrove to Dudley, and other Roads therein mentioned) was presented to the House, and read; Alleging, That great Part of the Road between Bromsgrove and Dudley is a deep Clay, and that the gross Tolls, One Year with another, do not exceed Two hundred Pounds, which being chiefly collected from heavy Carriages with Coal and Lime, arc hardly sufficient to keep the Road in Repair; and that the said Trustees have been obliged to take up at Interest, upon their own Personal Security, the Sum of Four hundred Pounds, towards repairing the said Road, which is still unrepaired^ and that the Petitioners are informed, a Petition has been prdented for annexing to a Bill now depending, a certain Road branching out of the said Turnpike- Road, at a Place called Dudley Wood, by Witheij Moor Mill, along Poke Lane, and other Places therein described, through the Parish of Franhhry and North field, and Rednall Green, in the Parish of King's Norton, for the Purpose of making the same Turnpike; and that in case the same thou Id pass into a Law, it would greatly lessenthe Tolls on the before'mentioned Turnpike Road, and be prejudicial to the Petitioners: And therefore' praying, That the Petitioners may be heard against the before mentioned Petition, and that they may have such Redress as to the House shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the last preceding Petition is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. James Wadefon, being examined, said, That he knows

the Road described in the Petition very well; that the same is extremely narrow all the Way, inso much that a Cart, with a single Horse, cannot pass along it; and that it cannot be repaired by the ordinary Course of Law.

Being asked. Whether a Gate set on that Road would produce Tolls fulBcient to repair it ? He said. He rather thought it would not; and he did not know whether any Person would advance Money on the Credit thereof.

Mr. Secretary at War reported from the Committee, who were appointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered to rot;en an

the Lords at aConference, for disagreeing to the Amend- America* ments made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled.

An Act for naturalizing such foreign Protestants as have served, or shall serve, for the Time therein mentioned, as Officers or Soldiers in His Majesty’s Royal American Regiment, or as Engineers in America, That the Committee had drawn up Reasons accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To the first Amendment made by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, "An Act for naturalizing such foreign " Protestants as have served, or shall serve, for the " Time therein mentioned, as Officers or Soldiers in " His Majesty’s Royal American Regiment, or as Engineers in America," which is in Press 2, Line 33, to leave out the " Royal American Regiment," and, instead thereof, to insert " His Majesty’s Armies;" the Commons disagree; First, Because it is by no Means correspondent with the Design of the Bill, which was intended to gran t the Benefit of Naturalization to those Foreigners only who having been enabled, by the Act of the 29th Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, to serve under certain Restrictions in one particular Regiment, or as Engineers, in America, should have since served for Two Years, according to the Terms of the said Act, to which Purpose alone the whole Frame of the Bill is adapted;. whereas the Amendment, made by your Lordships, would establish military Service in general as a Handing and ordinary Mode of Naturalization; aProvision which the Commons cannot but look upon as far too extensive and important to be introduced, Liy way of Amendment, to a Bill of so limited an Extent as the present.

Secondly, Because if the Establishment of such a Method of Naturalization could, with any Propriety, be inserted in this Bill; yet, for want of such a Provision, for enabling the Crown to grant Commissions to the Persons who are the Subject of the Amendment, as was made by the Act of the 29th Year oP his late Majesty’s Reign, with respect to those who are the Subject of the Bill, the Amendment proposed must be ineffectual; unless indeed it could be understood to convey indirectly, and by Implication, to Foreigners at large, a Capacity of holding military Commissions: Which, we fully persuade ours elves, your Lordships would be as unwilling to propose as the Commons themselves to admit.

To the second Ainendment made by your Lordships, which is in the Title of the Bill, to leave out " Royal American Regiment," and insert " Annies," the Commons disagree; because it intirely ^depends upon the former Amendment.

The said Reasons, being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Captain John ltolwjbn produced toyour Commitfeea Plan of the present Harbour, which contains the Works already done, and those proposed to be further added, in Consequence of the present Application to Parliament, whereby it appeared. That the Trustees have made very considerable Improvements to the said Harbour, in Consequence of the Act of the 13th of his late Majesty, by adding several Works to the said Harbour, and'by ereciing several new, large, anti extensive Moles; in order to perform which, they had expended upwards of £.26,000, and had borrowed the Sum of £ 5,985, whereoi £. 2,970 still remained unpaid, as appeared by the Accounts signed by the Treasurer of the said Harbour, and produced by the Witness to your Committee.

Then the Witness proceeded to explain to your Committee the Nature and Conveniency of the Extension of the said Harbour, and of the new Works proposed to be erected in Consequence thereof; and said, That if the said Port and Harbour was extended, and a new Mole erected on the North East Side thereof, and the old Moles further extended and enlarged, it would prevent the Roughness of the Sea caused by a N. W. W ind, which renders the said Harbour dangerous and incommodious, to the great Detriment of Shipping, and Loss of the Petitioners; and it would likewise facilitate the Pafl’ageof Ships into a Place of Safety; but that it will be impossible to make the proposed Additions and improvements, which are estimated at £.25,000, or thereabouts, without a further Continuation of the said Harbour Duties:

That if the said additional Works were made, and the Limits of the said Port and Harbour enlarged, it

Then the said Act of the 7th of Queen Anne being again read, it appeared, That several Duties were granted thereby, upon Several Goods in the said Act particularly enumerated; but that no mention was therein made of Battery, Rice, or Deer Skins, by which means the said several Goods are subjected to pay the Duty ad.

valorem, which amounts to so large a Sum as to tend al-moll to a Prohibition; and that it will be necessary to lay a small Duty on those several Species of Goods: That there is a small Rivulet called the Poe, which runs through the Market Place of the Town of Whitehaven into the said Harbour, which at present is very detrimental thereto; for, though all Persons are by the said Acts prohibited from throwing any Filth, Rubbish, or other Things, into the said Harbour yet they constantly do it into the said Rivulet, and it is washed down into the said Harbour, to the great Detriment thereof; and that, if the Trustees of the said Harbour were impowered to cover the said Rivulet, and to open, widen, deepen, or pen up the fame, it might be made very useful, in cleansing the said Harbour from Filth and Rubbish, which, in its present Situation, it contributes to bring into the same; and would likewise prevent several Accidents which frequently happen in its present State, and likewise prevent a public Nuisance:

That there is likewise another small Rivulet, called Branjy Beck, which at present runs jull without the intended Limits of the Harbour, and would be useful lor the fame Purpose; and it is of the utmost Consequence to keep the said Harbour clear from Rubbish, Ballad and other Obdruftions:

That the Town of Whitehaven is greatly increased, and at present very populous, and very ill supplied with fresh Water, the Water being generally biackilh; and there is no Method of supplying the Town with Water, but by a Reservoir, which may be supplied from eer* tain Springs, at about or 5 Miles Didance; that this would not only be a very great Convenience to the Inhabitants, for their daily Ufc, but would likew’ife be the Means of furnishing the Shipping with Water, who now have no other Way of being supplied, but by bringing the Water in Carts, in a very tedious and expensive Manner:

That, if Provision was made for enlightening (he said Town, it would be a great Convenience to the Inhabitants, and particularly to the Shipping in the Harbour, where Fires are not allowed for Fear of Accidents, and consequently the Sailors are put to great Inconveniences, when attending the Tides by Night, which would in a great measure be remedied, if Lamps were put up near the said Harbour; but that there is no Power vested in the Petitioners, nor any Fund for those Purposes:

That a Regulation of the Drivers of Carts and Carriages in the said Town would be very advantageous, and greatly contribute to the Preservation of the Lives and Limbs of His Majesty’s Subjects; for that it is a common Practice with the Carmen, as soon as they have delivered their Loading at the respective Warehouses, to drive as fall as possible down to the Harbour, which frequently occasions very melancholy Accidents.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the several Parishes of Weriminfttf St. Margaret's, St. John the Evangelifi, St. Martin in the Street*. Fields, St. Clement Danes, St. Mary le Strand, St. Anne,

St. Paul Covent Garden, in the City and Liberty of Wefi-minster-, and of the Parishes of St.George the Martyr-, that Part of the Parish of St. Andrew's, which.

lies in the County of Middlesex; the several Liberties of the Rolls and Savoy-, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster which lies in the County of Middlesex-, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves, and of the rest of the Inhabitants within the said several Parishes and Places; was presented to the House,-and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners find, by the Votes of the House, That a Bill is now depending for Paving, Cleansing, and Lighting, the squares.

Streets, and Lanes, within the City and Liberty of Westminster, the Parishes of St. Mary le Bone, St. Giles in the Fields, St. George the Martyr, St. George Bloomsbury; that Part of the Parish of St. Andreio's, Holbourn, which lies in the County of Middlesex; the several Liberties of the Rolls and Savoy-, and that Part of the Duchy of Lancaster which lies in the County of Middlq-sex-, and for preventing Annoyances therein; and alleging, That the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Laws now in being were enforced by a due Execution thereof, the Inconveniences complained of would be removed at a much less Expence, than the Petitioner* may be liable to under the Provisions in the said Bill; and that the Petitioners hope they shall not be subject to the Burthen of this additional Expence, at a Time when, with the utmost Difficulty, they endeavour to discharge the Taxes and Rates already imposed upon them; and that, for these and other Reasons, the Petitioners submit the Consideration of the Premises to the House: And pray.

That they may be heard by their Counsel against the said Bill, so far as the same affects the Petitioners; and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the said Bill be read the Third Time; and that the Petitioners be then heard by their Counsel, upon their said Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That the said Bill be read the Third Time* upon this Day Sevennight, if the said Bill shall he thenf ingrossed.

Sir George Montgomery Mreported from the Committee, who were appointed to draw up Reasons, to be offered to the Lords at a Conference, for disagreeing to the Amendment made by their Lordships to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend, and render more effectual, several Arts made for cleansing and enlightening the Streets of the Town of Kingston upon Hull, and for preventing Annoyances therein, That the Committee bad drawn up Reasons accordingly, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To the Amendment made by your Lordships to the Bill, intituled, "An Act to amend, and render more " effectual, several Arts made for cleansing and enlightening the Streets of the Town of Kingston upon " Hull, and for preventing Annoyances therein," which

is in Pr. 7. L. 26. to leave out from " thereof," to " and, " in the 37th Line of the same Press, the Commons disagree;

Because, by a Statute 9® Georgii iml, Cap. 7. Sert. 6. it is enarted, " That no Person shall be taken to have " any legal Settlement, in any City, Town, Parish, or " Hamlet, by reason of his being rated, and paying to " the Scavenger’s Rate, or Repairs of the Highways:" By the present Bill, Power is given to the Mayor and Aldermen of the Town of Kingston upon to make

a Rate upon the Occupiers of houses in the said Town, and Liberties thereof, which is directed to be applied to Purposes, which must otherwise have been supplied b7 a Scavenger’s Rate.

The Clause which, by your Lordships Amendment, is proposed to be left oat, was insertod by the Commons; that this Bill, which is intended for private and particular Purposes, may not beconiirued to imply any Alteration of the general Law, in regard to the Settlement of the Poor, antecedent to this Bill; the Payment of such a Rate as is directed to be levied by virtue thereof could have intit led no Person to a Settlement, by reason of the Act g° Georgii iml: And the Commons therefore apprehend it is necessary to retain the Clause left out by your Lordships Amendment, the Effect of which Clause is, to provide, that the Qualifications which intitle a Person to a Settlement shall remain the same as they would have been, independent of this Bill, in which the Settlement of the Poor was not an Objefil under the Consideration of Parliament.

The Commons decline, at this Time, offering any other Reason, believing this may be sufficient to prevail with your Lordships, not to infill upon the Amendment, that a useful Bill may not be loft.

The House proceeded to the further Hearing of the Matter of the several Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the City of Durham.

And the Counsel were called in.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member proceeded in their Evidence.

v And they examined several Witnesses, in order to dif-prove the Evidence brought by the Counsel on the other Side, with respect to the Time of giving Notice of a Meeting of the Company of Dyers, on the Second of November last, to One of the Members of the said Company.

Then several ancient Books, belonging to the Corporation of the City of Durham, were produced.

And several Parts thereof were read, in order to prove a continued Usage of admitting Freemen by Redemption, from 1575 to 1677.

And a public Book, belonging to the Company of Dyers of the said City, having been produced;

The Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

They were again called in.

And One of the Wardens of the said Company was examined, in relation to the said Book.

And Part of the said Book was read;.in order to prove. That, in 1707, a Person was admitted, by Redemption, to be free of the said Company.

'J? VoL. 29.

Then the public Books belonging to the Company of Barbers, and to the Company of Mercers of the said City, were severally produced; and Parts thereof read j in order to prove, that, in the Year 1707, several Persons had been admitted, by Redemption, to be free of the said Companies of Barbers and Mercers respectively.

And, in order to prove that the said Persons, so admitted free, by Redemption, of the said several Companies of Dyers, Barbers, and Mercers respectively, had signed the Return of Members to serve in Parliament for the said City at the next ensuing Election;

A Copy of the Return of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said City, dated 10th May 1708, was produced; and the Names of those who had signed the said Return were read.

Then the public Books belonging to the Company of Masons of the said City were produced.

And several Parts thereof were read; in order to prove, that several Persons were, in the latter End of the Year 1721* admitted, by Redemption, to be free of the said Company; and to prove, that several of the Persons, so admitted, had polled at the ensuing Election of Members to serve in Parliament for the said City, in 1722.

The original Poll, taken at the said Election in 1722, was produced, and Part thereof was read.

Then an Entry in the Book of By-laws of the Corporation of the City of Durham, (which Book had been produced on Tuesday last) containing the Form of the Oath to be taken by Freemen, with a special Direction in the same of the Admission of Foreigners, or Freemen by Redemption, was read.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member having gone through, and summed up their Evidence;

The Counsel for John Drake Bainbridge Esquire, Returning Officer at the last Election of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the City of Durham, did, in part, sum up his Evidence.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were again di-rested to withdraw.

Ordered, That the further Hearing of the Matter of the said Petitions be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

The Lord Barrington acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker; (all the Members of the House being uncovered) and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty relying on the known Zeal and Affection of His faithful Commons, and considering, that in this Conjuncture Emergencies may arise, which maybe of the utmost Importance, and be attended with the most pernicious Consequences, if proper Means should not immediately be applied to prevent, or defeat them: And His Majesty also taking into His most serious Consideration the imminent Danger with which the Kingdom of Portugal, an ancient and natural Ally of His Crown, is threatened by the Powers now in open War with His Majesty, and of what Importance the Preservation of that Kingdom is to the Commercial Interests of this Country, is desirous that this House will enable Him to defray any extraordinary Expences of the War, incurred, or to be incurred, for the Service of the Year 1762, and to take all such Measures as may be necessary to disappoint or defeat any Enterprises or Designs of His Enemies, against His Majesty, or His Allies; and as the Exigency of Affairs may require.

R.
