Mr. Alderman Dickinson, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of One hundred Fifteen thousand Pounds, granted by an Act made in the Second Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, upon Account of Arrears of his late Majesty’s Civil List Revenues, and now, by His Majesty’s Direction, replaced and refunded out of the Arrears of the said Revenues, which were Handing out at the Time of his late Majesty’s Demise, be issued and applied towards railing the Supply granted to His Ma-efly in this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Twenty thousand Pounds, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer, being part the Sum of One hundred thousand Pounds, granted to his late Majesty in the Year 1758, upon Account, towards defraying the Charge of Pay and Cloathing for the Militia for the Year 1758; and for defraying such Expences as were actually incurred upon the Account of the Militia in the Year 1757, be issued and applied towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty in this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Eighty thousand Pounds, remaining In the Receipt of the Exchequer, which was granted to his late Majesty in the Year 1760, upon Account, towards defraying the Charge of Pay and Cloathing for the unembodied Militia for the Year ended the 25th of March 1761, be issued and applied towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty in this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Seventy thousand Pounds, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer, which was granted to His Majesty in the last Session of Parliament, upon Account, towards defraying the Charge of the Pity of the Militia of that Part of Great Britian called England, when unembodied; and of the Cloathing of the Part of the Militia then unembodied, for One Year, beginning the 25th Day of March 1761; be issued and applied toward raising the Supply granted to His Majesty in his Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Seventy-three thousand Six hundred Seventy-eight Pounds, remaining in the Receipt of the Exchequer, being the Surplus of the several Duties on Malt, eliabJished by an Act made in the 33d Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for paying Annuities granted in the Year 1760, alter satisfying all Charges and Incumbrances thereupon to the 5 th Day of January 1762, be issued and applied towards making good the Supply granted to His Majesty in this Session of Parliament.

Resolved, That'it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of One million Nine thousand Two hundred Seventeen Pounds Two Shillings, and Eight Pence Halfpeny, out of such Monies as shall or may arise, of the Surpluses, Excess'es, or overplus Monies, and other Revenues, composing the -Fund commonly called the Sinking Fund. ’ Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards making good an Pfecuring the Payment . of the.Sums of Money directed by an Act made in the 3zd Year of the Reign' of his late Majesty, to be ap-

Slieil in Augmentation of the Salaries of the Judges and uliices‘therein mentioned, within England and JEales, . there be granted to His Majesty an additional Stamp: 19

Duty of Two Pounds, upon every Piece of Velhim or

Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrossed or written any Admission into any of the Four Inns of Court.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards making good and securing the Payment of the said Sums, there be granted to His Majesty an additional Stamp Duty of Two Pounds, upon every Piece of Vellum or Parchment, or Sheet or Piece of Paper, on which shall be ingrossed, or written, any Register. Entry, Testimonial, or Certificate, of the Degree of Utter Barrister, taken in any of the Four Inns of Court.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Sum of One million be raised by Loans or Exchequer Bills, to be charged on the First Aids to be granted in the next Session of Parliament.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Several Members present took the Oaths, and made and subscribed the Declaration; and took and subscribed the Oath of Abjuration, according to the Laws made for those Purposes: And such of the said Members, as

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I found, on my Accession to the Throne, these My Kingdoms engaged in a bloody and expensive War. I resolved to prosecute it with the utmost Vigour; determined, however, to consent to Peace, upon just and honourable Terms, whenever the Events of War should incline the Enemy to the same pacific Disposition.

A Negotiation was accordingly begun last Year, which proved ineffectual: the War became afterwards more general, by the Resolution of the Court of Madrid to take Part with My Enemy, notwithstanding My best Endeavours to prevent it.

This, with the unexpected Attack of My natural and good Ally the King of Portugal, greatly affected our Commerce, multiplied the Objects of our Military Operations, and increased our Difficulties, by adding to the heavy Burthens under which this Country already laboured.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty the moll humble and hearty Thanks of this House, for Your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

Permit 11s. at the same T*ime, to congratulate Your to which we greatly owe the Sttcceflcs of the War, in

Majesty on the auspicious Birth of His Royal Highness the Prince of H ales, and the Recovery of Your Royal Consort, endeared to this Country, not only by this important Event, but by her own personal Virtues.

We acknowledge, with the utmost Gratitude, Your Majedy’s great Attention to the Welfaieof Your People, in the vigorous Prosecution of the War, and congratulate Your Majesty on that happy Effect of it, the Prof-pcCl of such a Peaces may give Stability and Permanency to the Blessings we promise ourselves under Your Majesty’s most auspicious Reign.

AVe allure Your Majesty, That Your faithful Commons are truly sensible of the Wil'dom with which Your Plans have been concerted, as well as of the successful Zeal with which they have been carried into execution by your Fleets and Armies.

The Resolution and Intrepidity of Y’our Majesty’s Army in Germany, and the Military Skill and distinguished Activity of Your General, Prince Ferdinand of Brun/'wick, which have obtained so many signal Ad-

vantages over an Enemy so superior in Numbers, are Objects of our highest Admiration: The Stopping the Frogress of the French and Arms in Portugal,

and the Preservation of that Kingdom, by the Firmness and Resolution of its Sovereign, and by the superior Talents and able Conduct of the reigning Count La Liype, Seconded by the Valour of the Troops under his Command, are Events of the highest Importance to this Nation and its Commerce: The Reduction of so glorious to your Majesty’s Arms, and the ltill more glorious and important Conquest of the by

Which great Treasure, and a very considerable Part of the Navy of Spain are fallen into Your Majesty’s Hands, speak the Wisdom of Your Councils and the Valour of those employed in the Execution of these great Commands, and fill our Hearts with Gratitude and Satis-:

faction.

The public Testimony which Your Majesty has there-> fore graciously given to the unwearied Perseverance and unparalleled Bravery of Your Officers and private Men, by Sea and Land, to which, under-God, these glorious Achievements are to be attributed, is a no less honourable than deserved Reward of their Sendees, and muff: be an additional Recommendation of them to the Esteem and Gratitude of their Country.

Allow us. Sir, to thank Your Majestyfqr havingpro-miled todireetthe Preliminary Articles of the Peace to be laid before us. And we receive, with the greateftSatisfaction, the Information which Your Majesty has conde-icended, in the mean time, to afford us; from which we promise ourselves, that, with Your Ala jesty’s Dominions, our Trade will be increasqd; and that allOccasions of future Disputes being removed, the Blessingsof Peace will be thereby rendered permanent and secure.

We return your Majesty our moil sincere and humble Thanks for Your great Goodness and tender Regard for the Welfare of Your Subjects, in proceeding without Delay to the Conclusion of the Negociation of Peace, so expedient for this Country; and for Your gracious Intentions, as foonas itffiall be concluded, to reduce the public Expences.

Your Majesty may be allured, that Your faithful Commons will cheerfully affili in the Support of such Expences as may be Hill necessary, with due Regard to that Economy which Y’our Majesty recommends to us, as far as may be confident with Wisdom and true Policy.

We will not fail to considerof the most efteflua] Methods of settling oar new Acquisitions, of feenring those Countries to us, and of improving our Commerce and Navigation. And, lamenting the Loss of those many brave Men who have fallen in this glorious War, we will pay all due Attention to the Services of those who yet remain, by whose Valour those Acquisitions have been made. And we will continue to cultivate that Union Vox.. 29.

order thereby to make the bed Advantages of Peace, and lay the Foundation of that Economy which we owe to ourselves, and to our Poderity.

Resolved, That, where the House shall judge any Petition touching Elections to he frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity aguinli such Person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing or giving Evidence, the same is declared to he a high Crime and Misdemeanor; and this House will proceed with the utmost Severity aguinli such Offender.

Resolved, That it is a high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Britain,

for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That in all Cases of controverted Elections for Counties in England and Wales, to be heard at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Petitioners do, by themselves or by their Agents, within a convenient Time, to be appointed either hv the 1 Ioufe or the Committee of Privileges and Elections, as the Matter to be heard shall be before the House or the said Committee, deliver to the Sitting Members, or their Agents, Lists of the Persons intended by the Petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the Sitting Members, giving, in the said Lifts, the several Heads of Objection, and distinguishing the same against the Names of the Voters excepted to; and that the Sitting Members do, by themselves or by their Agents, within the same Time, deliver the like Lifts, on their Part, to the Petitioners or their Agents.

Mr. Speaker reported to the House, that, the House Ring's attended His Majesty on Saturday last, with their Ad- Answtr dress, to which His Majesty was pleased to give this to Addrefi. most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen,

I return you My hearty Thanks for this very dutiful and affectionate Address; and I receive your Congratu-latjonSHm the Birth of the Prince, My Son, as a fresh Proof of your Attachment to My Person, and* of your Regard for the Queen.

The Afluranees of your ready Support in such Expences as may be still necessary, afford Me the highest Satisfaction; and the Ratification of the Preliminary Articles gives Me the pleasing Hope of soon easing My faithful Subjects, by a safe, honourable, and permanent Peace, of the heavy but unavoidable Burthens they have so cheerfully borne during the War.

Translation of the Preliminary Articles of Peace, signed at Fontainebleau, November 3d 176?, by the Plenipotentiaries of Great Britain, France, and Spain.

In the Name of the Mod Holy Trinity The King of Great Britain, and the Moll Christian King, animated with the reciprocal Desire to re-establish Union and good Understanding between them, as well for the Good of Mankind in general, as for that of their respective Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, having reflected soon after the Rupture between Great Britain and Spain, on the State of the Negotiation of last Year (which unhappily had not the defin'd effect) as well as on the Points in dispute between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, Their Britannic and MoltChrittian Majesties began a Correspondence, to endeavour to find Means to adjust the Differences fubfiliing between Their said Majesties: At the same time the Molt Christian King having communicated to the King of these happy

Dilpofirions, his Catholic Majesty was animated with the same Zeal for the Good of Mankind and that of Ins Subjects, and refolded to extend and multiply the Fruits of Peace by his Concurrence in such laudable Intentions; Their Britannic, Molt Christian, and Catholic Majesties, having, in consequence, maturely considered all the above Points, as well as the different Events which have happened during the courseof the present Negotiation, have, by mutual Consent, agreed on the following Articles, which shall lerve as a Bafts to the future Treaty of Peace; for which Purpose His Britannic Majesty has named and authorized John Duke and Earl of Bedford, Marquis of Tavijtock, Sec. Minister of State of the King of Great Britain, Lieutenant General of His Forces, Keeper of his Privy Seal, Knight of the Moll noble Order of the Garter, and His Britannic. Majesty’s Minister: Plenipotentiary to his Moll Christian Majesty; his Moll Christian Majesty, Cafar Gabrielde Choiseul, Duke of Prajlin, Peer of France, Knight of the Moll Christian King’s Orders, Lieutenant General of his Forces, Counsellor in all his Councils, and Minister and Secretary of State of his Commands and Finances; and his Catholic Majesty has likewise named and authorized Dom Jerome Grimaldi, Marquis de Grimaldi, Knight of the Moll Christian King’s Orders, Gentleman of the Bedchamber to his Catholic Majesty in Employment, and his Ambassador Extraordinary to his Moll Christian Majesty; who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers in good Form, have agreed on the following Articles.

Article I.

As soon as the Preliminaries shall be signed and ratified, sincere Friend flap shall be re-established between Hb Britannic Majesty and his Moll Christian Majesty, and between His said Britannic Majesty and his Catholic Majesty, Their Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, by Sea and by Land, in all Parts of the World. Orders shall be sent to the Armies and Squadrons, as well as to the Subjects of the Three Powers, to liop all Hollilities, and to live in the most perfect Union, forgetting what has pant'd, of which their Sovereigns give them the Order and Example: And, for the execution of this Article, Sea Passes shall be given on each Side, for the Ships which shall be dispatched to carry the News of it to the respective Possessions of the Three Powers.

Article II.

His Most Christian Majesty renounces all Pretension which he has heretofore formed, or might have formed, to Nova Scotia, or Acadia, in all its Parts, and guaranties the whole of it, with all its Dependencies, to the King of Great Britain: Moreover, his Most Christian

Vol. 29.

Majesty cedes and guaranties to His said Britannic Majesty, in full Right, Canada, with all its Dependencies, as well as the liland of Cap Breton, and all the other Islands in the Gulph and River of Saint Laurence, without Restriction, and without any Liberty to depart from this Cellion and Guaranty, under any Pretence, or to trouble Great Britain in the Possessions above mentioned: His Britannic Majesty, on his Side, agrees to grant to the Inhabitants of Canada the Liberty of the Catholic Religion: He will, in consequence, give the moll ex a ft and the most effectual Orders that his new Homan Catholic Subjects may ptofefs the Worship of their Religion, according to the Rights of the Church, as far as the Laws of Great Britain permit: His Britannic Majesty further agrees, That the French Inhabitants, or others, who would have been Subjects of the Most Christian King in Canada, may retire in all Safety and Freedom wherever they please; and may fell their Estates, provided it be to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, and tranl’port their Effects, as well as their Persons, without being restrained in their Emigration, under any Pretence whatsoever, except Debts or criminal Profeoutions: The Term limited for this Emigration being fixed to the Space of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Day of the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

Article III.

The Subjects of France shall have the Liberty of Fishing and Drying on a Part of the Coasts of the Island of Newfoundland, such as it is specified in the 13th Article of the Treaty of Utrecht, which Article shall be confirmed and renewed by the approaching Definitive Treaty except what regards the Island of Cap Breton, as well as the other Islands in the Mouth and in the Gulph of Saint Laurence: And his Majesty

consents to leave to the Most Christian King’s Subjects the Liberty to filli in the Gulph of Laurence, on Condition that the Subjects of France do not exerci fe the said Fishery but at the Distance of Three Leagues from all the Coasts belonging to Great Britain, as well those of the Continent, as those of the Islands situated in the said Gulph of Saint Laurence; and as to what relates to the Fishery out of the said Gulph, his Most Christian Majesty’s Subjects shall not exercise the Fishery but at the Distance of Fifteen Leagues from the Coasts of the Island of Cap Breton.

Article IV.

The King of Great Britain cedes the Islands of St. Peter and of Miquelon, in full Right, to his Most Christian Majesty, to serve as a Shelter for the French Fishermen; and his said Majesty obliges himself, on hisRoval Word, nottofortify the said Islands, to erectno Buildings there, but merely for the Conveniency of the Fishery, and to . keep there only a Guard of Fifty Men, for the Police.

Article V.

The Town and Port of Dunkirk shall be put into the State fixed by the lall Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, and by former Treaties; the Cunette shall remain as it now is, provided that the English Engineers named by His Britannic Majesty, and received at Dunkirk by Order of his Moll Christian Majesty, verify that this Cunette is only of Use for the Wholesomenefe of the Air, and the Health of the Inhabitants.

Article VI.

In order to re-ellabliili Peace on the most solid and lasting Foundations, and to remove forever every fub-ject of Dispute, with regard to the Limits of the British and French Territories on the Continent jit

is agreed. That, for the future, the Confines between the Dominions of His Britannic Majesty and those of his Most Christian Majesty, in that Part of the World, shall be irrevocably fixed, by a Line drawn along the Middle of the River Misissippi, from its Source, as far as the River Iberville; and from thence, by a Line drawn along the Middle of this River, and of the Lakes Maurepas and Pontcharlrain, to the Sea; and to this Purpose the Most Christian King cedes in full Right,

Article XXVI.

The Ratifications of the present Preliminary Articles shall be expedited in good and due Form, and exchanged in the space of One Month, or sooner, if it can be done, to be computed from the Day of the Signature of the present Articles.

In Witness whereof. We the under-written, Ministers Plenipotentiary of His Britannic Majesty, of his Moll Christian Majesty, and of his Catholic Majesty, in virtue of oUr respectiv'e full Powers, have signed the present Preliminary Articles, and have caused the Seal of Our Arms to be put thereto. Done at Fontainebleau the Third Day of November 1762.

His Moll Christian Majesty declares. That in agreeing to the 13th Article of the Preliminaries, signed this Day, he does not mean to renounce the Right of acquitting his Debts to his Allies; and that the Remittances which may be made on his Part, in order to acquit the Arrears that may be due on the Subsidies of preceding Years, are not to be considered as an Infraction of the said Article.

The King of Great Britain, and the Moll Christian King, animated with the reciprocal Desire to re-establish Union and good Understanding between them, as well for the Good of Mankind in general, as for that of their respective Kingdoms, States, and Subjects, having reflected' soon after the Rupture between Great Britain and Spain, on the State of the Negotiation of last Year, (which unhappily had not the desired Effect) as well as on the Points in dispute between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, their Britannic and Moll Christian Majesties began a Correspondence, to endeavour to find Means to adjull the Differences fulfilling between their said Majesties: At the same time the Moll Christian King having communicated to the King of Spain the-fe happy Dispositions, his Catholic Majesty was animated with the same Zeal for the Good of Mankind, and that of his Subjects, and resolved to extend and multiply the Fruits of Peace by his Concurrence in such laudable Intentions , Their Britannic, Catholic, and Moll Christian Majesties, having, iri Consequence maturely considered all the other Points, as well as the different Events which have happened during the coUrfe of the present Negotiation, have, by mutual Consent, agreed on the following Articles, which shall serve as a Bafts to the future Treaty of Peace. Article XVII.

His Catholic Majesty defills from all Pretension which lie may have formed to the Right of Fishing about the Island of Newfoundland.

Article XVIII.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to Spain all that he has conquered in the llland of Cuba, with the Fortress of the Ilavannah; and that Fortress, as well as all the other Fortresses of the said llland, shall be re-liored in the same Condition they were in when they were conquered by His Britannic Majesty’s Arms. Article XIX.

In consequence of the Rellitution stipulated in the preceding Article, his Catholic Majesty cedes and guaranties, in full Right, to His Britannic Majesty, all that Spain possesses on the Continent of North America, to the East, or to the South-east, of the River Mississippi and His Britannic Majesty agrees to grant to the Inhabit tants of this Country, above ceded, the Liberty of the Catholic Religion: He will, in consequence, give the most exact, and the moli effectual Orders, that His new Roman Catholic Subjects may profess the Worlliip of their Religion, according to the Rites of the Roman Church, as far as the Laws of Great Britain permit. His Britannic Majesty farther agrees, That the Spanish Inhabitants, or others, who would have been Subjects of the Catholic King, in the said Countries, may retire in all Safety and Freedom wherever they please, and may fell their Estates, provided it be to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, and transport their Effects, as well as their Persons, without being restrained in their Emigration, under any Pretence whatsoever, except Debts or Criminal Prosecutions: The Term limited for this Emigration being fixed to the Space of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Day of the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty. It is further stipulated, that. His Catholic Majesty shall have Power to cause all the Efl'cdts that belong to him, either Artillery or others, to be carried away.

Article XX.

The King of Portugal, His Britannic Majesty’s Ally, is expressly included in the present Preliminary Articles, and their Most Christian and Catholic Majesties engage to re-establish the ancient Peace and FriendIhip between them and his most Faithful Majesty: And they promise,

ill. That there shall be a total Cessation of Hostili-tics between the Crowns of Spain and Portugal, and between the Spanish and French Troops on the one Side,

and the Portvguefe Troops, and those of their Allies,

on the other, immediately after the Ratification of these Preliminaries: And that there shall be alike Cessation of Hostilities between the respeiStive Forces of the Most Christian and Catholic Kings on the one Part, and those of the Most Faithful King on the other, in all other Parts of the World, as well by Sea as by Land;

which Cessation shall be fixed on the same Epochs, and under the same Conditions, as that between Great Bri-> tain, France, and Spain, and shall continue till the Con* elusion of the Definitive Treaty betwen Great Britain, France, Spain, and Portugal.

2d. That all his Most Faithful Majesty’s Fortresses and Countries in Euro/)e,which shall have been conquer*

ed by the Spanish and French Armies, shall be rellored

in the same Condition they were in when they werecon-quered: And that, with regard to the Co-

ionics in America, or elsewhere, if any Change shall have happened in them, all Things shall be put again on tho same Footing the y were before the present War: And the Most Faithful King shall be invited to accede to the present Preliminary Articles as soon as shall be polfi-ble.

Article XXI.

All the Countries and Territories which may have been conquered in any Part of the AVorld whatsoever, by the Arms of Their Britannic and Most Faithful Ma-jesties, as well as by those of their Catholic and Molt Christian Majesties, which arc not included in the present Articles, either under the Title of Cessions, or under the Title of Rellitutions, shall he reiiored without Difficulty, and without requiring Compensations.

Article XXII.

As it is necessary to assign a fixed Epoch for the Restitutions and the Evacuations to be made by each of the high contracting Parties, it is agreed. That the and French Troops shall proceed, immediately after the Ratification of the Preliminaries, to the Evacuation of the Countries which they occupy in the Empire, or elsewhere, conformably to the 12th and 13th Articles.

The llland of Belleijle shall be evacuated Six Weeks after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done.

Guadeloupe, Defirade, Marie and

St. Lucia, Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done.

Great Britain shall likewise, at the End of Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be doue, enter into Post'eflion of the River, and of the Port of Mobile; and of all that is to form the Limits of the Territory of Great Britain, on the Side of the River Mi/JiJfippi, as they arc specified in the 6th Article.

The llland of Goree shall be evacuated by Great Britain Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, and the llland of Minorca by France, at the same Epoch, or sooner, if it can be done: And, according to the Conditions of the 4th Article, France shall also enter into Post'eflion of the Islands of Peter and of Miquelon, at the End of Three Months.

The Comptoirs, in the East Indies, shall be rellored Six Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done.

The llland of Cuba, with the Fortress of the Ilavannah,

shall be rellored Three Months after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done: And, at the same time, Great Britain shall enter into Possession of the Country ceded by Spain, according to the 19th Article.

All the Fortresses and Countries of his Most Faithful Majesty, in Europe, shall be rellored immediately after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty; and the Portuguese Colonies, which may have been conquered, shall be rellored in the Space of Three Months in the West Indies, and of Six Months in the East Indies, after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, or sooner, if it can be done.

In consequence whereof, the necessary Orders shall be font by each of the high contra6ling Parties, with reciprocal Passports for the Ships which shall carry them, immediately after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty.

Article XXIV.

The Prisoners made respectively, by the Arms of their Britannic, Catholic, Mod Chridian, and Faithful

Majesties, by Land and by Sea, shall be restored reciprocally, and bona'side, after the Ratification of the Definitive Treaty, without Ransom, payingthe Debts they shall have contracted during their Captivity: And each Crown shall respectively pay the Advances which shall have been made for the Subsidence and Maintenance of their Prisoners, by the Sovereign of the Country where they shall have been detained, according to the Receipts and attested Accounts, and other authentic Titles, "which shall be furnished on each Side.

Article XXV.

In order to prevent all Causes of Complaints and Disputes, which may arise on account of Ships, Merchandizes, and other Effects, which may be taken by Sea, it is reciprocally agreed, that the Ships, Merchandizes, and Eli'eCis, which may be taken in the Channel, and in the North Seas, after the Space of Twelve Days, to be computed from the Ratification of the present Preliminary Articles, shall be reciprocally restored on each Side.

That the Term shall be Six Weeks, for the Prizes taken from the Channel, the Seas, and the North

Seas, as far as the Canary inclusively, either in

the Ocean or in the Mediterranean.

Three Months, from the said Canary Islands, as far as the Equinoctial Line, or Equator.

Lastly, Six Months, beyond the said Equinoctial Line, or Equator, and in all other Parts of the World, without any Exception, or other more particular Dif-tinction of Time and Place.

Article XXVI.

The Ratifications of the present Preliminary Articles shall beexpedited ingood and due Form, and exchanged in the Space of One Month, or sooner, if it can be done, to be computed from the Day of the Signature of the present Articles.

In Witness whereof, We, the under-written, Ministers Plenipotentiary of His Britannic Majesty, of his Catholic Majesty, and of his MoltChrillian Majesty, in virtue of our respective full Powers, have signed the present Preliminary Articles, and havecaufed the Seal of our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Fontainebleau, the Third Day of November 1762.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. John Runnington, Clerk to the Trustees, laid before your Committee an Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Tolls for Eight Years last past, by which it appeared. That, in that Time, there had been receiver! the Sum of £.3,289 os. and dif-

bursed the Sum of £.3,217 19*. 6%d. and also another Account, by which it appeared, that there is now owing upon the Credit of the said Acts the Sum of £.1,700.

Mr. John Bury, Surveyor, said, He had taken a Survey of the said Roads; and that, in order to make the same safe and commodious for Passengers, it is necessary, that Two Bridges should be erected; that several Parts of the Roads want to be widened, and that the Roads in general want to be effectually repaired; and he laid before the Committee an Eliimate of the Expence of the Works necessary to be done upon the Roads, amounting to £.2,291 ior. od.

Mr. John Runnington, and Mr. John Bury, severally said. That the said Roads could not be effectually repaired, widened, and kept in Repair, and the Money now owing be repaid, unless the Term of the Acts was further continued* and some further Provisions were made by Parliament for those Purposes.

Ordered, That the said Accounts and Paper do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

The House being informed that Mr. Owen (from the Office for Affairs of Taxes) attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Order,

An Account of the Total Number of Houses and Cottages in England and Wales, distinguishing the inhabited from the uninhabited, according to the last General Return.

And then he withdrew.

And the Title of the said Account was read.

Ordered, That the said Account do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

The said Account is preserved amongst the other Papers of this Session.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a new Writ for the electing of a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Corse Cqftle, in I he County of Dorfel, in the room of Henry Bankes, Esquire, who, since his Election for the said Borough, hath accepted the Office of One of the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs.

A Motion was made, and the Quession being proposed, That the Preliminary Articles of Peace, signed at Fontainebleau, November 3d, 1762, and Declaration be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Sevennight;

Vol. 29.

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Word "Sevennight," and inserting the Word " Fortnight" instead thereof.

And the Question being put. That the Word " Se-vennight" Hand Part of the Question;

The House divided.

The Yeas went forth.

Tellers for the Yeas 5 The TjCrd 7

1 el/ers for the 1 eas, j Mr Salisbury: j 21

Tellers for the Noes IThe Lord \

1 ellers for the Woes, j Mr Calvert. $ 74-

So it was resolved in the Affirmative.

Ordered, That the Preliminary Articles of Peace, signed at Font aitteblean, November 3d 1762, and Declaration, be taken into Consideration Tomorrow Seven-night.

Ordered, That all the Members of this House, who are in and about the Town, do attend the Service of the House upon Tomorrow Sevennight.

The Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickiti/on took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Tetney. A Petition of several of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Canal. Traders, and others, Inhabitants of the County of Lincoln, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Land Carriage in that Part of the said County which leads from Telney to the Town of Louth, and Parts adjacent, is, for several Miles, through very bad Roads, attended with great Inconvenience, as well as great Expence, and that the making a Canal or navigable Cut from the Humber, at or near Tetney, to the River Ludd, in the Parish of Akoingham, and the making the said River navigable from thence to or near the Town of Ijouth, will be of the ulmost Advantage, not only to the Petitioners, but to the Trade and Commerce of the said County, and the Public in general: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making the said Canal, or navigable Cut, and making the said River Ludd navigable, and such other Works as may be necessary for the convenient Use thereof, under such Regulations, and with such Powers and Provisions as the House shall think necessary and convenient.

H>rbour« -That he is employed in carrying on the Work« at Bye, and that Two Stone tiers, and One Timber Pier, a*e already erected, which extend ,200 Feet from the Harbour into the Sea, and a Groin carried from the Head of the Timber Pier 120 Feet, jn order to flop the Beach from coming down.

And the Witness said. That several Vessels have already been in the new Cut; that there had been 20 in at a Time; and that he believed there were Eight , or Ten there at present:

That it will hold 300 Vessels to ride in Safety at a ‘Time, there being 20 Feet Water in a common Spring Tide; that there has been 22 Feet and a half Water; and in a Neap Tide 14 or 15 Feet Water.

And, being asked what the ufuaf Tides were upon that Coast, he said, That in good Spring Tides they had about 20 Fathom Water, and in Neap Tides, about ': .14 or 15 Fathom::

That in order to fcoixr the said new Cut, and to keep dt clean,.he laid it was propossd to bring the Waters front the Uplands, which was practicable; and that there whs no Doubt, but by that Means the Cut would be kept entirely dean, as there are upwards of 100,000 Acre* of Land from1 whence the M aters might be brought; and the doing this will also open a navigable Communication between the new Cut and the Town ofifytf.

And he laid, That the WharJing of the new Cut is at present in bad Repair for Want of the Water being fanner let in:

Hgh Price A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the Town of of Nottingham, act’embled in their Common Council, Com, &c. was presented to the Iloufo, and read; Taking Notice of the very high Price of all Sorts of Corn and Grain in the Markets of the said Town, and more particularly' in the Northern and North-Western Parts of England, and that the same are likely to advauee, owing to the bad Crops of the last Season; and that the Petitioners are informed, that in the Southern and South-Eastern Counties of this Kingdom, where good Crops were well got, Corn bears a very moderate Price, but that the Inhabitants, encouraged by the Bounty allowed for' Exportation of Corn, will be thereby induced to export their Grain beyond the Seas, rather than suffer the same to be brought to those Northern and North-Western Counties, to the very great Detriment of the Inhabitants thereof in general, and of the working Poor in particular, utdefs restrained by due course of Law: And therefore the Petitioners request the House tb take the Premises into Consideration, and to apply such Remedies for the Prevention of so great a Grievance, by taking off the Bounty for a limited Time, or such other Methods as to the House shall feetn most meet and expedient.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That in Obedience to the Commands of this House of the 9th Day of December last, he had signitied to his Serene Highness Prince Ferdinand of Brunswictheir Thanks for the great and important Services he has performed to this Country, in the several Campaigns during which he has commanded His Majesty’s Army in; and that

he had, on the 1 ith instant, received a Letter; in Answer, from Prince Ferdinand, in the French Language; a Translation of which is as followeth;

Sir,

From Brunfu ick,

27 Dec. 1762.

I have received the Letter which you, Sir, did me the Honour of writ ing to me on the 9th of this Month, to acquaint me with the Resolution which the House of Commons of Great Britain have come to, to give me their Thanks for the Services which I have been able to perform to Great Britain during the Time that I was at the Head of His Majesty’s Army in Germany.

I am infinitely flattered with fodiftiuguished an Honour; And I entreat you, Sir, to express to that illustrious Body my lively Acknowledgments for thisfignal Mark which they have given me of their Approbation.

I am happy to express to you in particular, upon this Occasion, with how much Efieem I am.

Sir,

Your moll humble

and most obedient Servant, Ferdinand,

Due de

et de Lunebourg.

To Sir John Cuji.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had, on the 29th Day of December last, received from Rear-Admiral Rodney the following Letter in return to the Thanks of this House, signified to him by Mr. Speaker, in Obedience to their Commands of the 6th Day of May last.

8th, 1762.

Sir,

I embrace the first Opportunity to acknow ledge the Receipt of your Letter of the 6th of enclosing the Resolution of the Hotife of Commons of the same Date.

Thefavourable Regard with which the House has been pleased to look upon my Services demands my earliell and moll grateful Acknowledgments; but, Sir, I claim no other Merit than having been, in conjunction with Major General Moncklon, the happy Instrument of executing the wife Measures concerted anddirettedbyHis Majesty, to which alone are owing the valuable Acqui-fitions made to His Dominions in this Part of the World.

But I ftitould be insensible indeed, Sir, if I did tiot receive the distinguistied Honour the House of Coirw inons has conferred on me with the most sincere and most respectful Thanks, which I beg you will be pleased to signify to the House in my Behalf; and that it shall ever be my constant Care to retain thedeepell Senseof this Testinionv of their Regard and Approbation.

My particular Thanks, Sir, are due to you for the polite and obliging Manner in which you have been pleased to communicate to me the Resolution of the House; and I take this Opportunity of alluring you,

that I have the Honour to be, with the most sincer* Respect and Esteem,

Sir,

Your most obedient

and most obliged humble Servant,

G. B. Rodney.

Mr. Speaker acquainted the House, That he had, in Obedience to the Commands of this House of the 2d Day of December last, signified to Sir George Pocock, Knight of the most honourable Order of the Bath, their Thanks for the many important Services performed by him during the Course of this War, and particularly in the glorious Expedition against the: And that

he had received the following Answer;

Whitehall, 25 th Mr. Speaker, 1763.

I have received the Honour of your Letter, dated the 2d of December last, inclosing the Resolution of the House of Commons of the same Date, to give me the Thanks of the House for the many important Services performed by me during the Course of this War, and particularly in the glorious Expedition against the Ilavannah: Upon this Occasion, Sir, I cannot sufficiently express my Thanks for the great Honour the House have conferred on me, in taking Notice of the Services I have been so happy to render mv King and Country during the Course of the War against France and Spain.

S I R, January izth, 1763.

The Honour of your Letter, of the Third of lall Month, was not delivered to me till a few Daysfince; the Physicians who attended me in my Illness having forbid any Letters being given to me, in the Situation my Health then was: This, I hope, will plead my Excuse for your not having received an immediate Answer.

Though I cannot. Sir, be vain enough to think any Services I may have done my Country, can have merited so high a Reward as the Thanks of the Honourable House, yet it was with the utmost Satisfaction I reseived them.

I shall beg to look upon them as a Mark of their Ap-

frobation of my Conduct; arising, I hope, from their erfualion of my having always zealously promoted the Service, in which His Majesty has done me the Honour to employ me, and of my having constantly endeavoured, to the best of my Abilities, punctually to execute the wife and able Orders I received.

I mult beg, Sir, that you will, when proper, return the House my moil sincere, and grateful Thanks for this great Honour conferred upon me, which I shall always, with the utmost Gratitude, remember: The belt Return I can make, will be a perpetual Attention to the Interests of my King and Country.

Give me leave. Sir, at the same Time, to return you my particular Thanks for the obliging Manner in which you communicated to me this high Honour; and believe me to be, with the greatest Regard and Respect,

Sir, your most obedient

Humble Servant,

Granby.

Right Honourable Sir John Baronet, Speaker of the honourable House of Commons.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and Over-seers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint Matthew, Bethnal Green, within the Tower Divi-

fion, and County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Poor of the said Parish are become very numerous; and the Cliarge and Expence of their necessary Support is lb considerable, that the annual Rates for their necessary Relief amount to £.1,300 and upwards, one Year with another; and that many hundred Houses within the said Parish are taken on Lease by a few People, who chiefly let them out into Lodgings, or separate Apartments, to Journeymen Weavers and others, which divided Houses do not pay any thing towards the Poors Rates; and the Petitioners have not Power to compel the Landlords or Leaseholders of such divided Houses to pay the Rates.; and alleging, that the Want of a proper Place to maintain their Poor in, with sufficient Powers to compel such of them as are able to work, and to provide a more comfortable Support for such of them as are aged and infirm, is another Caufie why the said Rates are increasing; and that the Petitioners conceive, that if they had Power to erect a Workhouse, or Work-houses, and to pnrehafe Land for that Purpose, or to purchase or hire any Houses, Messuages, or Tenements, and to convert 1 he same into a Workhouse, or Work-houses, and to furnish and regulate the fame, for the better maintaining, employing, and governing the Poor therein; and were enabled to borrow Monies for that Purpose, and to make Rates for the Relief, Maintenance, and Employment of the Poor, and for securing the Repayment, and the Principal and Interest of the Monies so borrowed, and were also enabled to charge the several Landlords and Leaseholders (who so divide their said Houses) with the Payment of such Rates, it would be a Means not only of the Inhabitants of the Parish being more equally taxed, but also of lowering the said Rates, and tend greatly to the Benefit of the Parish, and the Health, Welfare, and Preservation of their Poor: And therefore praying, That Leave maybe given to bring in a Bill for the several Purposes above Hated; or to grant the Petitioners such Relief) as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Cooke, Mr. Byde, Mr Caj-zvall, Mr. Jackson, Mr. GrosvenMr. Hume, Sir Jar-

Mr. OJbaldeston reported from the Committee, to Scarborough

whom the Petition of the several Persons whose Names Harbour, are thereunto subscribed, being Commissioners appointed to put in execution Two Acts, one made in the Fifth, and the other in the Twenty-fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for enlarging the Pier and Harbour of in the County of York, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had di-reded him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the said Acts were read: And,

Mr. RobeJ't Duesbury, being examined, said. That a Pier has been carried on from the old Pier, about 150 Yards; by which an Addition of Five or Six Foot of Water has been made; and that Ships, drawing 16 Foot Water can now go into the Harbour at Neap Tides:

That another Pier is carried on about 30, or 35 Yards; which is proposed to be extended near 200 Yards; in order to make the Bason larger:

That it is the only useful Harbour between the Humber and Shields, for large Ships: And to complete the Pier now erecting will require at least £.25,000, and an annual Expence of Four or Five hundred Pounds, to keep the whole in Repair:

That some Difficulties have arose in putting the Acts in execution, with respect to punishing Persons committing Annoyances in the Harbour:

That the said Harbour cannot be completed, and kept in sufficient Repair, without a Continuance of the Duties granted by the said Acts; Part of which are near expiring.

Mr. Christopher Salletl confirmed the above Evidence.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the Duties, and enlarging the Powers granted by Two Acts made in the Fifth and 2 5th Years of his late Majesty’s Reign, for enlarging the Pier and Harbour of Scarborough, in the County of York: And that Mr. OJbaldeston and Mr. Major do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Persons interolled in, or entitled unto, any Bills payable in Course of the Navy or Victualling Offices, or for Transports, which were made out on or before the 3 ill Day of December lait, who shall, on or before the 25th Day of March next, carry the same (after having had the Interefidue thereupon computed and marked upon the said Bills at the Navy or Victualling Office respectively) to the Treasurer of His Majesty’s Navy, to be marked and certified by him, or his Paymaster and Cadiier, to the Governor and Company of the Bank of England shall be entitled unto, and have, an Annuity trnnsferrable at the Bank of England for the Principal and Interefidue on the said Bills after the Rate of Four Pounds per Cent, per Annum, to commence from the 25th Day of March next, payable half-yearly, in lieu of all other Interest, until redeemed by Parliament; the said Annuities to be charged upon

the Sinking Fund; and the Sums which shall be issued out of the Sinking Fund, for Payment of the said Annuities, to be from Time to Time replaced out of the next Aids to be granted by Parliament.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of the Lords of the Manors of Glentham,

' in the County of Lincoln, and others, whoseNames are thereunto subscribed, beingOwners and Proprietors of Lands, and other Property, within the said Manors of Glentham, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That within the said Manors and Parish of Glentham aforesaid, are several Open and Common Fields, called the East Field, West Field, Ox East Pafiure, and Car Ground, the whole consisting of

about Two thousand Five hundred and Seventy Acres; and alleging, that the Lands of the several Proprietors in the said Fields and Car, lie greatly intermixed, and are in their present Situation incapable of Improve* ment; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that it would be of great Advantage to all Parties concerned, if the same were inclosed, and divided amongst the several Persons having Interest therein, according to their respective Rights, Interests, and Properties: And therefore praying That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for those Purposes, under such Regulations as to this House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Ixave be given to bring in a Bid, pur-fnant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Whiche ot, the Lord Burgh and Lord Broitnlout

Bertie, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. De Grey accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Allegations of the Bill, and found the same to be true* and that the Committee had directed the Rill to be reported to the House, without any Amendment: And be delivered the Bill in at the Clerk's Table.

Sir Robert Long reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Freeholders, and Traders, of the Hundreds of Bradford,

and Whorlfdmn, in the County of Wilts, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read j and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Samuel Plummer, being examined, said. That there is a large Trade in fine Cloth, and other Woollen Manufactures in the said Hundreds, in which many Thousands of People are employed, who are perpetually contracting small Debts, which in the whole amount yearly to a great Sum of Money.

That the Difficulties and Expences that Creditors are put to in filing for small.Debts, is a great Injury to the Traders, and a Discouragement to necessary Credit:

And that a speedy and easy Method of recovering small Debts, within the said Hundreds, would be highly advantageous to the Country.

Upon the Evidence here Hated your Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee. That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

A Petition of the several Attornies and Solicitors reading in the Cities of and and Counties of

Somerset, Wilts, Hants, and Gloucester, and other Cities

and Counties within that Part of Great Britain called England, was presented to the House and read} Reciting, That by an Act made in the Second Year of His late Majesty’s Reign, for the better Regulation of Attornies and Solicitors, it is enacted, That no Person shall be permitted to act as an Attorney, or sue out any Process in any Court of Law, unless such Person shall have been bound by Contract in Writing to serve as a Clerk for Five Years to an Attorney duly sworn and admitted is One of the Courts at r; and such Person, during the said Term, shall have continued in such Service; and also, unless such Person, after the Expiration of the said Five Years, shall be examined, sworn, admitted, and inrolled, as in the said Act is particularly directed; and alleging, that the Petitioners, in Conformity to such Law, were respectively bound by Articles of Clerkship for the Term of Five Years, and considerable Sums of Money were advanced by them to their respective Matters, <as a Consideration for the Education und Instruction they were to receive, and, upon their Admission, paid a Duty of Six Pounds to the Government; and that the Petitioners always apprehend, that the preparing Conveyances of all Sorts has. Time immemorial, been as much the Butt-ness of Attornies and Solicitors, as commencing or defending Suits at Law or in Equity, but that Part of the Petitioners’ Practice hath of late Years been greatly reduced, by the Interference of Schoolmasters, Parish Clerks, and others, not skilled in such Matters; that the Petitioners apprehend, that, by patting the aforesaid Law, the Legislature intended that the Business and Profession of an Attorney and Solicitor should be conduced by Men who had, by their Education, gained Knowledge and Experience therein, and which would prevent the Disorder and Confusion which the Property of Men woidd be subject unto under a contrary Direction; and therefore conceive, that the Mischief in this Particular is equal to any provided against by the aforesaid Act: And therefore praying the House to permit a Bill to be brought in for retraining Personsfrom drawing, writing, or ingrotting, finishing or perfecting, any Deed, Conveyance, Assign-"ment, Mortgage, Lease, Articles of Agreement, A-wards, or any Writing or Instrument whatsoever, to be written or ingrotted on Stamps, who shall not be a Barrister at Law, or an Attorney or Solicitor, legally admitted according to the Act above mentioned, or Persons by them immediately employed, or who shall not be of the Scriveners Company in the City of London, or of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England and South Sea, and other public Companies or Offices, or employed of concerned in Business relative to any Bodies corporate or collegiate.

Ordered, That the said Petition he referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Bethnal Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom Green the Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, and Over-

*>oor* seers of the Poor, and other Inhabitants of the Parish

of Saint Matthew, Bethnal Green, within the Tower Division of Middlesex, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and . had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of the 43d Year of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, An Act for the Relief of the Poor, was read: And,

Mr. George Poller being examined, said, That the said Parish consists of near 1,800 Houses, which are, in a great measure, occupied by Persons concerned in the Silk and Woollen Manufactures, and great Numbers of them by Journeymen, who take Apprentices, whereby

the Poor are become very numerous: And that the Poor’s Rates in the said Parish are much increased of late Years, and amount at present to between 13 and 1,400 I. per Annum.

That about One Third of the Houses in the said Pari fh are let out into Lodgings, or separate Apartments, and pay nothing to the Poor’s Rate, there being no Power to compel the Landlords, or I ^eafeholders of such Houses, to pay it; and that if the Tenants in the divided Houses were to be rated, they would thereby gain Settlements, by which means the Parish would be great Sufferers; and that the rating such Tenants is attended with many other Difficulties.

That the Want of a proper Workhouse within the said Parish, with sufficient Power to compel such Poor to work as are able, and to provide for the Support of the Aged and Infirm, is One Cause why the Poor’s Rates are continually increasing; and is likewise very inconvenient, on account of the Poor being continually loitering and wandering about the Streets:

And that if Power was given to build or purchase a proper Workhouse, and to furnish and regulate the fame, for the better Relief, Maintaining, Employing, and Governing the Poor; and to borrow Money, and make Rates, for those Purposes; and to charge the Landlords and Leaseholders, who let their Houses out in Tenements or ready furnished Lodgings, with the Payment of the Poor’s Rates; thelnhabitants of the said Parish would be more equally taxed, the Rates would be lowered, and many of the Poor would become useful to the Public.

Mr. Paumiere being examined, said. That the Mailer Weavers would be able to furnish Work for such Workhouse, as they give out their Silk to be manufactured.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor within the Parish of Saint Matthno, Bethnal Green, in the County of Middlesex: And that Mr. Cooke, Mr. Nicholson Calvert, Sir William Beauchamp and Mr.

Gascoyne, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Lane reported from the Committee, to whom York the Petition of the Mayor and Commonalty of the Streets, *c* City of York, and of the Gentlemen, Clergy, Merchants, and other principal Inhabitants of the said City of York, and the Suburbs thereof, and the Liberty of Saint Peter's within the said City, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as jt appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr.

John Ward, being examined, said, That he is well acquainted with the said City, Suburbs, and Liberty; that the Streets are at present very ill lighted; that the Pavements and Highways are in very bad Repair* and not sufficiently cleansed; that Passengers in the Streets are much annoyed by Water falling from the Tops of Houses, through Spouts of different Lengths; and that Coachmen, Chairmen, Carmen, and Draymen, working for Hire, are not at present under any Regulation, which often occasions Impositions on the Public:

And he further said, That if Power was given to prevent such Inconveniences and Annoyances, it would be highly advantageous to the Inhabitants of the said City, and all Persons resorting thereto.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Clergy, and principal Inhabitants of the City of Cortnhy, on Behalf of themselves and many other Inhabitants of the said City, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice of

the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same Mas read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the first mentioned Petition, an Act, made in the Forty-third Year of Queen Elizabeth, for the Relief of the Poor, was read: And,

Mr. Edward Hawkins and Mr. Thomas Diming being severally examined, said, That the Poor of the said Parish are very numerous, and of late Years much in-«reased; that at present upwards of f. 2,600 is assessed in One Year for their Maintenance; and that if a proper Workhouse was provided for the Reception of the Poor, and sufficient Power given to oblige the aide Poor to work, they would not only be better provided for and employed, but the Expence of maintaining them would be greatly reduced:

That the Streets and Open Places within the said Parish are at present very ill cleansed and lighted; and the Bill for paving, lighting, and cleansing the Streets,

Ditto.

that if proper Powers were given for cleansing and enlightening the said Parish, and keeping a uell regulated nightly Watch theioin, it would be a great Conveniency and Safety to the Inhabitants; but that these salutary Purposes cannot be obtained without an Act of Parliament.

And to prove the Allegations of the second mentioned Petition;

Mr. Thomas Price, Churchwarden of the said Parish, informed yeur Committee, That a Twelve Months Rate has been.levied for repairing the Church, amounting to £\, 100, which has been found insufficient for that Purpose.

Mr. Edward Haze kins. Surveyor, being examined, said, That the Repairs of the Church w?ere at first estimated at Eight or Nine hundred Pounds, but that since they begun the Works, they found several Defects which could not possibly be discovered before, particularly that the Parapet Walls, and all the principal Timbers, are decayed, and the Galleries in so bad a Condition, that it will be absolutely necessary to rebuild them:

That the Parishioners are desirous to have a Wall built round the Church-yard, which is only inclosed with Pales:

That 15 or £.1,600 has been already expended in repairing the Church, and it will require £. 1,100 to complete the Works:

That an immediate Tax for these Purposes would be a great Hardship on Individuals, especially such as should quit the Parish soon after having paid it, as they w ould be at the Expence, and the Persons who succeeded them would enjoy the Advantage.

Which Evidence was confirmed by Mr. Thomas Langley, the Carpenter employed in repairing the Church.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor within the Parish of Saint Mary, Whitechapel, in the County of Middlesex; for cleansing and lighting the Streets, Lanes, Alleys, Courts, Yards, and other Open Passages and Places, and regulating and keeping a nightly Watch within the said Parish; and to enable the 17

Causeways, Lanes, and Pali'ages in the C ity of try, and its Suburbs; for preventing Annoyances therein; and for better ordering the public Weils and Pumps there; which, the Petitioners allege, if passed into a Law, will not only be greatly prejudicial to the Petitioners, but to many others, the poorer Inhabitants of the said City: And therefore praying, That the Petw tioners may be beard, by themselves or Counsel, against such Parts, and so much of the said Bill, as they conceive may be prejudicial to them; and that they mpy have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard by their Counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

Ordered, That it be an Instruct ion to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same Time, in Favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Your Committee are sensible that in their Inquiry they confined themselves to a few Cafes, and so a few Houses; but to obviate any Conclusion from thence, that Cafes existing are rare, and the Abuse the Milcon-du£> only of particular Persons, they beg Leave to a shire the House, that a Variety of other Instances, arifingin other Houses, offered themselves for Examination, and that Turlington's House was in no Degree a ('elected Cafe; but taken up by the Committee in the course of the Inquiry, and merely as it prefen ted itself upon the Report of the Witnesses, your Committee reltraining themselves out of a Regard to the Peace and Satisfaction of private Families, from the Examination of more Cafes, than they judged to be necessary and sufficient to establish the Reality of the too great Abuses com [darned of in the present State of private Mad-houses; the Force of the Evidence, and the Testimony of the Witnesses, being at the same Time so amply confirmed, and materially (Lengthened, by the Con-sessions of Persons keeping private Madhouses, and by the Authority, Opinions, and Experience of Doctor Battle, and Doctor Monroe.

Whereupon your Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that the present State of Private Madhouses in this Kingdom, requires the Interposition of the Legislature.

The laid Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Questkm put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

It is with the great eft Gratitude that I fee, by the Refutation of the 16th of December of the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament allenibled, that that augu(t Afl’embly condescends to declare their Approbation of my Behaviour during this War.

Although I am not able to express how much I arrt sensible of so high a Distinction, and how much 1 feet the Value of it; I take the Liberty to desire you to lay my most dutiful Thanks before the House, for the Honour they do me: My utmost Desire will always be to merit that respectable Senate’s Approbation, which I consider as an inestimable Reward of my Endeavours* to manifest my zealous and moil respectful Attachment to His Majesty and His Allies.

I beg you will receivemy sincerest Acknowledgements for transmitting to me the Resolution of the House in fa obliging a Manner as you are pleased to do, in the Letter you have honoured me with on that Occasion. I am, with the greatest Regard,

A Petition of the Coal Owners and Coal Fitters of Scarborough the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, harbour, in the County of Durham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on Behalf of themselves and the several other Coal Owners and Coal Fitters of the said River,

Port, and Haven, was presented to the House and read; Setting forth, That in pursuance of several Acts, made in the 3d and 13th Years of the Reign of King George the First, and the 20th and 3id of His late Majesty, very large Sums of Money have been levied upon the Coal Owners and Fitters, and Factors of the Port of Sunderland, for rendering the Port and Haven of Sunderland safe and commodious; and that a Pier and Quay have been erected at or near the Mouth of the said River; the Channel of the said Port hath been much deepened, several considerable and necessary Alterations and Additions made in the said Pier, and divers other Works done for the Improvement and Security of the said Port, Haven, and River, at a very great Expence; and that by the said several Acts the Coal Owners are liable to pay a Sum not exceeding Three Halfpence for every Chalder of Coals and Cinders brought to the said Harbour; and the Coal Fitters and Factors a Sum not exceeding one Halfpenny for every such Chalder; and that by an Act made in the Fifth Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, for enlarging the Pier and Harbour of Scarborough, among other Duties, a Duty of One Halfpenny was laid upon every Chalder of Coals that should be laden on board any Ship, Hoy, or Vessel at Sunderland, for extending and repairing the said Pier and Harbour of Scarborough, and that although the Port of Sunderland is of great public Convenience to all Persons trading the re, and all Persons have equally the Benefit of the Improvements made in the said Port, Haven, and River, yet the Expence thereof has been wholly borne by the Coal Owners and Coal Fitters of that Port only, without any Aid or Contribution either from the Port of Scarborough, or from any other Port whatsoever: And taking Notice of the Bill for continuing the Duties, and enlarging the Powers granted by the several Acts for enlarging the Pier and Harbour of Scarborough; and further alleging, that the further Continuance of the said

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing the Open and Common Fields, Common Meadows, Common Pastures, Common Grounds, and Waste Grounds, in the Manor and Parish of Woodford, in the County of Northampton; without any Amendment.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for rectifying Mistakes in the Names of several of the Commissioners appointed by an Act made in the iaft Session of Parliament, to put in Execution an Act, made in the same Section, intituled, An Act for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to he raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1762; and for appointing other Commissioners, together with those named in the First mentioned Act, to put in Execution an Act of this Session of Parliament, for granting an Aid to His Majesty by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1763; was committed; the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amend* ment, in at the Clerk’s 1 able: Where the Amendment w’as twice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, was, with several Amendments thereunto, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Bill, with the Amendment, be ingrafted.

Laws Sir Robert Ladbroke reported from the Committee, <*nceming to whom the Petition of the Mailer, Wardens, or new making Keepers, and Commonalty of Freemen of the My fiery*

of Coopers, of the City of London, and of the Suburbs of the same City; and also the Petition of the Muller and Keepers, or Wardens, and Commonalty of the My-fiery or Art of Brewers, of the City of London-, were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and her read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, an Act of the 23d Year of King Henry the Eighth w as read, Whereby Brewers are restrained from making Vessels, wherein they shall put Beer or Ale for Sale; and the said Act requires, that all fitch VeflMs shall be made and marked by the common Artificers of Coopers; that SoapmaJkers, who shall fell Soap by the Barrel, or other Vessel, shall cause the same to be made, according to the Rates, Weights, and Assizes* in the said Act mentioned; and authorizes the Wardens of the Mystery of Coopers, within the City of London, when they shall think convenient, taking with them an Officer of the Mayor, to search and gauge all Rich Vessels within the City of London, the Suburbs thereof, and Two Miles Riftance without the fame, and to mark such Vessels, containing their true Contents, for which the said Wardens are to have One Farthing for each Vessel so gauged and marked; and if they shall find any Vessels defective, not bearing their true Contents, the said Wardens are impowered to seize and detain every such Vessel, and cause the same to be amended, according to the true Contents, or may cause the same to be burnt; and the Owner of the Vessel is to forfeit Twelve Pence for every Vessel that is not of the full Contents mentioned in the said Act.

Mrs Benjamin Clempfon being examined, said, That the Coopers used formerly to seal all calks, but that this Custom as been discontinued for about 25 Years.

Mr. John Edifon, Clerk to the Coopers-Comps ny, informed your Committee,'That the Company formerly made Searches every Year; but that they brought an Action against one Mr. Blake, aSoapmaker, about 25 Years ago, for felling Casks that were not sealed, in which they were nonsuited, and it was the Opinion of the Court, that the said Act, so far as it relates to Soap Vessels, is virtually repealed by forae subsequent Laws of Excise:

That the Profits arising from searching, gauging, and marking Vessels, having, in Consequence of such virtual Repeal, been greatly diminished, the said Wardens have aifeontinued making Searches since that Time, as the Benefits have been inadequate to the Expence.

John Chillcot, a public Gauger, being examined said, that great Frauds are committed in making Vessels; and that he has known some fold for 36 Gallon Casks, which contained no more than Thirty-two Gallons.

Mr. Alexander Whitchurch and Mr. Edifon said. That the Brewers Company are defiroiis that some Regulation should be made, in regard to the gauging and sealing of Casks.

And all the Witnesses said, That such Regulation, would be of great Advantage to the Public.

Mr. Clempfon being again examined, said, That it is impossible to know the Contents of a Cask exactly by gauging it, on account of the irregular Thickness of the Staves.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain, amend, and render more effectual, an Act made in the 23d Year of the Reign of King Henry the Eighth, concerning new making of Barrels, Kilderkins, and other Vessels: And that Sir Robert Ladbroke, Sir Richard Glyn, Mr. Alderman Harley, the Lord Mayor of London, Mr. Alderman Dickinson, Mr. Cooke, and Mr. Mawbey, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of JohnIJarrifon of the Parish of Saint George the Martyr, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer (by His Majesty’tf Command) acquainted the House, That His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Reciting, That by an Act of the 12 th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, a Reward of £. 20,000 was enacted for the Discovery of the Longitude at Sea; and alleging, that an Instrument which could keep trueTime at Sea, notwithstanding the Differences of Climates, has been allowed, on all Hands, to be the bell Method of discovering the Longitude for the Use of Navigation; and that the Petitioner has employed himself for Thirty-five Years in the forming of such an Inllru-ment, and has at length succeeded in bringing it to due Perfection, which has proved its Sufficiency by a Trial made of it in a late Voyage to Jamaica, of which the Petitioner is ready to give full Evidence to the House; and that the Petitioner would not, by any Means, decline any further Trial of the Instrument, before the Principles thereof shall be made public; but that his present advanced Age, the Weaknefr of his Sight, and the Danger of the Voyage to the Health and Life of his Son, upon whom alone this Affair will depend, may risk the Loss of this useful Discovery, to the Di fad vantage of the Petitioner, and of the Public; and that at a Meeting of the Commissioners, appointed by Act of Parliament for the Discovery of the Longitude at Sea, on the 26th Day of February last, it was unanimously agreed to recommend 10 the Petitioner to make an Application to Parliament for this Purpose: And therefore praying the House to grant the Petit ioner such a Part of the Reward as shall be thought adequate on the Proof of his Cafe, and that the Remainder may be secured to the Petitioner when the Utility of the Instrument shall be proved to the Satisfaction of the House; and the Petitioner will immediately disclose the Manner and Principles of framing it to such Persons as the House shall appoint, in such Manner as that other Workmen may be able to execute the fame, so that it may in a short Time become l'erviceable to this Kingdom, and to all who use the Sea; and that the House will have Regard to the Security of the Petitioner against any other Claim of the said.Reward for discovering the Longitude at Sea, by Means of any Instrument for keeping Time, until the Merits of this Instrument, invented by the Petitioner, shall be ascertained to the Satisfaction of the House.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine and Rate to the House, the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition:
