To prove the Allegations of the ift mentioned Petition, Sir John Bentley Knight, being examined, fa id. That he has known Gosport 14 or 15 Years; and had lived there 3 Years together; and is a great Resort for Seafaring People; that the Streets are extremely bad and dirty, occasioned by Dungheaps lying the rein, which in a few Days have been spread about; and that he never saw any carried away; that Brewers Carts, Drays, and Timber, lay about the Streets, the Pavements of which are very bad, and make it dangerous for Passengers; and that Sheep and Swine are killed in the Streets; and has heard frequent Complaints of Nuisances, and never knew of any Method taken to prevent the fame; and thinks it cannot be remedied without an Act of Parliament, it not being a Corporation Town, or any Justice of Peace there; that there are many considerable Families, and thinks the promoted Tax will not fall upon the Poor.

Mr. John Pye, being examined, said, That he lives at

Farcham, and has known Gosport 15 or 16 Years, which is a Place of great Resort on Account of the King’s Ships and Merchants Ships coming to Portsmouth, to which it is very near; that the Pavements of the said Town are very bad; that he has always observed Dung-heaps in the Streets when he has gone thither, which has been once or twice a week; that Carts and Drays (land in the Streets; and by Sheep and Swine running about the fame, are become very offensive; that he does not know whether there is any Pound in Gosport, or whether the said Nuisances can' he prevented by the Taws in being.

Captain SherrocJc, being examined, said, That he has known Gosport Forty, and very well for Twelve Years pall, and is a large populous Town; that he lives Two Miles from it; that he has observed many Dungheaps in the Streets; and that when he goes thither he leaves his Horses or Carriage at t he End of the Town, it being dangerous to ride through it at certain Times; that there are many wealthy Inhabitants there, and has heard that a Tax of 6d. in the Pound will be sufficient to cleanse and keep the same in Repair, but that it will be a hard Matter to do it without an Act of Parliament, being 26 Miles from that there

is a weekly Meeting of Justices at Fareham, 5 Miles from Gosport; but that he never knew of an Application to Parliament, on Account of being so far from Justices of Peace; nor does he know of any Application to the Quarter Sessions for a Rate, but has heard there has.

Mr. Thomas Male, being examined, said, That the Pavements of the said Town are very bad, and that

Vol. 29.

there are many Nuisances; Butchers kill Sheep in the Gosport Streets before their Doors; that Dungheaps remain 3 Streets. . or Days, or till such Time as the Farmers come to take it away; that he never served any Office in Gosport, nor does he know whether any Scavenger is appointed, but any body takes away the Dung that Ivill; that he has been occasionally there, and always observed Dung in the high Street, and every Street, which lays more or less Time, as agreed with Farmers to fetch it away.

Being asked if the major Part of the Inhabitants would be able to pay 6d. in the Pound, he said. He could not think it would hurt any more this Way than another; that he did not remember he was ever summoned, or paid for a Man for working on the Highways; but it would tend to the Health of the Inhabitants, if the said Streets were properly cleansed.

Mr. William Bedford being examined, said. That it

has been a Custom to gather a Shilling a Year from each House, of those who would pay it; and that he had paid it annually to the Surveyors of the Highways; but has known several refuse to pay it, and that Difficulties had arose to recover it, it being a p ;ved Town; that if it was a Market Town Scavengers would be appointed, and Qd. in the Pound would be sufficient to keep the Pavement in Repair; but till in proper Repair it will require more, but afterwards apprehends a less Sum will be sufficient; that the Difficulty of applying for Assessments at Winchester, which is 25 Miles off, and when the Rate is confirmed, and the Money demanded, and not paid, the Officers must be obliged to go 5 Miles to a Magistrate, once fora Summons, and another Time for a Warrant of Distress, the Trouble and Difficulty of which has deterred Officers from doing their Duty; that the Witness knew a Rate made on the Inhabitants, about 10 or 12 Years ago, 0fTw0Per.ee in the Pound in Favour of Mr. Charles Child, a Surveyor, who is lately dead, to repay him upwards of Fourscore founds he had laid out as Surveyor of the Highways, which Rate he informed the Witness he could not possibly collect by about half; that this is the only Rate he remembers:

That the Difficulty of attending Justices of the Peace, and the Favour shewn by one Tradesman to another serving the Office of Surveyor, prevents the Laws in Force being put in Execution; that if they were, they might be sufficient to keep the Town in Repair; but the Witness apprehends the Time and Expence of going to Winchester to indH, and another Time to convict an Offender for any Nuisance, prevents it; that the Expence of such Process will eoli about 12 Guineas if there is no Defence, but if defended will coll more.

That the Witness apprehends the proposed Rate will produce above £. 300 a Year at present, and that it will require a Capital of about 900 or £.1000 to pave and cleanse.

That some People will be obliged to pay to this Rate, who do not at present pay to the Poor, though there are but few Houses which do not make such Payments; that the Price of Labour is i8d. a Day, and those People will be Savers by paying 6d. as more Work will be done for 3$. than double that done by the Statute Labour; and that landlords will reap an Advantage by their Houses letting better, and moll of the Principal of them are for the Bill, and the poorer People will pay less than they are now liable to by Law.

To prove the Allegations of the Second mentioned Petition.

Mr. John Pointer, being examined, said, He has known Gosport 72 Years or more, has been Mailer of a Ship, but was never absent from the Place 2 Years at a Time; that the Streets are in good Condition now, though some Parts are better than others, nor never knew any Accidents from the Bad net’s of the Pavements; that he has seen Heaps of Dirt in the Streets, which is generally carried away every Day by anybody that will, who look upon it as their own Property, and fell it to Gardeners and Farmers; that he has seen Timber on the Beach, but it was 30 or 40 Yards from the Town; and that he never knew any infeClion in the Town, occasioned by Annoyances.

Being atked what Rate would be fufiieient to put the Streets in proper Repair, said 6 in the Pound, or less, on the Tenants would do; that he has heard Complaints, that Surveyors have had some trouble in collecting the Rates:

That the Foot-ways are generally in good Repair, though in some Places they are broke, and in Holes; that Persons are obliged to repair before their own Doors, though exclusive of which there is a Parish Rate, but never knew any punished for not doing it; and believes there is no Law in Force to oblige Officers of Men of War to do it; that Beamis's La ue, which is about 9 or 1 o Feet wide, is the greatest Thoroughfare to the Church and Meeting, but is not in so good Repair as it ought, and has seen some Dungh^aps there; that the Streets in general would admit of Foot-paths, besides Room for Carriages:

That he has seen what is called Sweepings of Ships on the Green, which lay in the Middle, and not in the Foot Way, and Blocks of Stone which are sawed there to put into Carriages, to prevent the tearing the Pavements of the Town; that there are many Butchers Gallon’s upon which they hang their Meat, Blocks, and Bulks, in the Streets, but don’t know they are any Obstruction to Foot Passengers:

That there are about 200 Shipwrights live there, who rent Houses from 61. to a Year, and some Gentlemen; and does not think many more would live there, if the Town tvas cleaner; and that the Town has not been put into better Order since the Talk of the present Application to Parliament.

Mr. John Noel being examined, said, He has known Gosport 20, and that he lived there 10 or 12 Years; that the Streets are much as they were since he knew them, and want Repair; that there are some Nuisances by Dungheaps, which in some Places lay Weeks together, and the Farmers come and take it away when convenient to them, but don’t apprehend in the Times of their Harve'l they will leave that to fetch it away; and that Butchers Blocks, Bulks, and Cellars, may be some Obstruction to Foot Passengers:

That he does not know of any Rate for paving the Highways; but the Surveyors have collected a Shilling a Year from each House; but has heard they could not get it from the Poor, and knows of no other Rate; that he looked upon this Shilling to be applied towards mending the Pavements; but that would not remove the Nuisances, there being bo way to do it but by Indictment at the Quarter Sessions; that he paid £. 50. a Year for his House, and paid only a Shilling to the Surveyors of the Highways; and thinks it would be more equitable for the Poor if a Rate was made, than paying a Shilling a House:

In Support of the Allegations of the said Petitions, an Act made in the 26th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Amendment and Preservation of the Public Highways and Turnpike Hoads of this Kingdom, and for the more effectual Execution of the Laws relating thereto; and also an Act made in the 30th Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, intituled, An Act to render more effectual the several Laws now in being, for the Amendment and Preservation of the Public Highways and Turnpike Roads of this Kingdom; were read: And,

Mr. John Dandridge informed your Committee,

That the Farms in the County of Worcester are in general extremely small; that the Farmers are not able to support the Expence of strong Teams, and to furnish themselves with broad Wheel Waggons; that a good broad Wheel Waggon will coll about £.30 and a narrow Wheel One about £.12 or £.13 that the Roads coniift of deep Clay, and Materials lie at a great Distance; that he is a Trustee for repairing the Road leading to and from Worcester, and the Debt upon that Road has increased £.2,000 since the Use of broad Wheels; that the Roads have been greatly tom up by the excessive Weights carried on broad Wheel Wag-Vol. 29.

gons; that the Waggons weigh One Ton and a Half, and they frequently carry Five Ton.

That the Witness is informed there have been Two or Three People who have brought Actions again!! several of the Farmers for making Use of narrow Wheel Waggons, not with an Intent to enforce the Execution of the Law, but to put Money in their Pockets; and that there have been Fifty-six Prosecutions commenced, and never heard of any one of them being prosecuted with Efl'eft; that they appoint a Day of Meeting, and the Farmers compound upon as easy Terms as they can; that they have taken from Two Guineas to Five, in Proportion to the Number of Offences, and sometimes Cotnpositions have been made where no Action has been brought; One Person has been prosecuted for taking Money on false Pretences; that the Farmers are never taken before a Justice of the Peace, nor the Prosecution carried on regularly; and that no Part of the Composition has beenappliedastheAftsdireft; and, notwithstanding the Use of broad Wheels, their Roads are Hill in a ruinous Condition, and in many Places very narrow, and not capable of carrying broad Wheels; and that the Farms in general are under £. 25 per Annum, and incapable of bearing the Expence of broad Wheels; that he thinks the limiting the Weights to be carried on broad Wheels would be of great Service; but, in general, the Roads cannot be made wide enough to receive Two broad Wheel Waggons, as the Income of the Tolls are very inconsiderable, occasioned by the little Travelling on the Roads.

Mr. James While, a Farmer, being examined, said, ’ That the Weight usually carried by Farmers in the Course of their Husbandry, is, from 25 to 30 hundred Weight; Forty Bushels of Wheat is usually called a Load; that they generally carry Three Hogsheads of Cyder or Perry, of 110 Gallons each Hogshead, to every Load; and about a Ton, or 25 hundredweight, of Cheese; that there are not many broad Wheel Waggons; that the Farmers in general are not able to purchase them, as a broad Wheel Waggon generally costs about £.35, and a narrow Wheel Waggon about£.io; that there are Twelve or Fourteen Teams in the Parish of Eckington, and not One of them able to carry One

Ton Weight; that the Roads are so very narrow that they cannot use broad Wheel Waggons if the Horses draw in Pairs, but that broad Wheel Waggons will not hurt the Roads so much as narrow ones, if the Weight to be carried on them was to be limited, and they were allowed to have the Horses draw in Lengths; and that Coaches cannot, without great Difficulty, quarter in the Ruts made by broad Wheel Waggons, as the Horses cannot tread in the Ruts without great Pain.

Mr. James Woolley, a Trader in being

examined, said, That the Roads where broad Wheel Waggons are leall in Use, are in much better Repair than where there are many broad Wheel Waggons; Evesham Roads have suffered much from broad Wheel Waggons; that the Road from Worcester to Upton is a goo«l Road, as there are not any broad Wheel Waggons travel there; if the Weight was to be limited, broad Wheel Waggons would not do so much Mischief, as it chiefly arises from the excessive Weights they carry, and from their Horses drawing in Pairs; that if they were allowed to have their Horses in Lengths it would not be so prejudicial to the Roads: The Witness said. That, by the Use of broad Wheels, travelling on Horseback is rendered much more dangerous than formerly.

Whereupon the Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petitions.

An Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, intituled, "An Act for providing a Public Reward for such Person or Persons as shall discover the u Longitude at Sea," was read: And,

Mr. William Harr if on, Son of Mr. John Harrison, produced toyour Committee a Paper, intituled, " Some " Account of Mr. Harrifos Inventions for determining the Longitude at Sea, and for correcting the Charts of the Coasts;" being a Copy of the Opinion of many great and eminent Astronomers, that the Machine, invented by the Petitioner, will be of great and excellent Use for determining the Longitude at Sea, and for correcting the Charts of the Coasts; which Paper is hereunto annexed, N° 1. Doctor John Bavis being examined, said, That the first Time he saw Mr. s Clock was at Mr.

Graham's, the latter End of the Year 1735, and that Mr. Graham told him, that he had kept it in extreme Heat and Cold, and with a great Swing, and that it always went very well by his Regulator.

Mr. William Harrison being examined, said, That in the Year 1726 his Father fiuithed a Pendulum Clock for the Land, the Performanc e of which greatly ex-

ceeded his Father's Expectation; and that about two Difcdvefy Years after he begun a Machine for the Use of the Sea, of the and has employed himself in that Way ever since, and Longitudes has now completed a Watch, or Instrument, of due Perfection, for discovering the Longitude at Sea.

Being a iked, To what Perfection it is now brought?

He said. To a greater Perfection than required by the Act of Parliament: That the Witness went to Jamaica with this Instrument, by Order of the Commissioners of Longitude; and he produced to your Committee a Letter, sent to his Father by Mr. Stephens, (Secretary to the said Commissioners) acquainting him, that he might cause his Son to proceed to try the Experiment, and also sent a Paper of Instructions, relating to the Method of keeping the Watch, and for making Observations of equal Altitudes at Poand Jamaica, and directing him to return by the first Ship that iliould fail for England-, which Letter and Paper are hereunto annexed, N° 2 and 3.

Mr. William Harrison also produced Four other Papers, containing the Observations made at PortJ'mouth and Jamaica, pursuant to the said Instructions; which Papers are likewise hereunto annexed, N*4,5,6, and 7;

And,

Mr. James Short being examined, said, That he had seen the said Papers of Observations of equal Altitudes, made at PortJ'mouth and Jamaica, and afterwards at PortJ'mouth again:

That, from a Calculation made of those Observations, he finds, That Mr. Harrison's Watch came greatly within the nearest Limit of the Act of Parliament, of the 1 ath of Queen Anne, in the Voyage to Jamaica, the Error amounting only to Five Seconds of Time, bei ng eq u al to a little more than One G eographical M ile:

That the Longitude between Portsmouth and Port Royal in Jamaica was determined by the Transit of Mercury in 1743; all which appears by the Calculation hereunto annexed: N*8.

And being aiked. If he was fully satisfied this Calculation was right?

He said. It was.

And he further said. That he found the whole Error of the Watch, from its leaving Portsmouth, in November, till its Return thither in April following, amounted only to One Minute and Fifty-four Seconds and a Half of Time, which is equal to Twenty Minutes and Thirty-seven Seconds and a Half of a Degree, which is nearly equal to 18 Geographical Miles in the Latitude of Portsmouth.

And the Witness likewise said, That by Observations of Two Eclipses of the Moon, recorded in the Philosophical Transactions, the Difference of Longitude between Port Royal and Portsmouth comes out nearly the same as that determined by the above mentioned Transit of Mercury:

That the Longitude of Places is determined with more Certainty by Transits of Mercury over the Sun, than by the Eclipses of Jupiter's first Sattelite; the utmost Limit of Error observed in the Observations of the Transit of Mercury amounting only to 3® Seconds of Time; whereas the Limit of Error in the Eclipses of Jupiter's first Sattelite (which is the belt for determining Longitude) amounts Sometimes to 3 Minutes Seconds of Time, as appears from corresponding Observations made at Greenwich by Mr. Flamstead, and Mr. Mar aid i at Paris, from the Year 1677 to the Year 1701, recorded in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences: This is likewise confirmed by like Observations made at the Cape of Good Hope, by Monsieur

L'Abbede la Caille, and at Paris by Monsieur Maraldi, in 1751, in which Observations the Limit of Error amounts to 1 Minutes 45 Seconds.

He further said, That the Rojral Astronomers at Greenwich and Paris have not been able to settle the Difference of the respective Longitudes of those Places, by Means of the Eclipses of Jupiter 's Sattelites, not-

Mr. Robert Bishop, a Pilot, sent by the Government to the Fleet in the West Indiessaid, That he failed in the Deptford Man of War with Mr. William Harrison, on the 29th of November 1761; and that on the 9th of December following the y made the Hland of Porto Santo, by the Assistance of Mr. Harrs Watch, which did Ilonourto him, it being much juster than the Ship’s Reckoning; and said, that there were the like Errors in the Ship’s Reckoning in the Voyage from the Madeiras to the Hland of Defeada, which the Watch like-wife corrected; and that they made that Hland a great deal better than they could have done without the Help of the Watch.

Mr. William Harrison being again examined, said, That they took their Departure (in the Deptford) from the Lizard on the 9th of November 1761, and that on making the Hland of Porto Santo, the Error in the Ship’s Reckoning was about a Degree and a Half to the Eastward, but that the Watch was found to be quite right: That on making the Hland of Defeada, the Ship’s Reckoning, and that kept by the Watch, differed about Two Degrees and a Half; and that the Watch was then also found to be right; and that in the Run from Defeada to Hispaniola, the Ship’s Reckoning differed from that of the Watch about a Degree, when the Watch was likewise found to be right; that they were then in Sight of Jamaica, and arrived there on the 19th of January 1762, and afterwards found the

Longitude by the Watch differed from that which was settled by the Transit of Mercury no more than Five Secoqds of Time, which is equal to a Geographical Mile and fth of a Mile.

He further said, That, pursuant to his Inllructions, he failed in the Merlin Sloop on the 28th of January 1762, this being the first Vessel that failed from thence, and that they did not meet with any other Ship till the 23d of March, when the Essex Man of War (poke to them in the Channel before they saw the Land; that the Essex had seen ScillyLights the Evening before, and could not be much out in her Reckoning; that Capt. Scomberg, of the Essex, came on board the Merlin, and compared the Reckonings of both Ships, which very nearly agreed, and that Three Days after the Merlin came to Spithead: That in the Voyage from Jamaica the Officers of the Ship, in a great measure, gave up their own Reckonings, and trusted to the Watch for the Correction of them; that the Weather was very tempestuous during the Passage, and that the Watch was placed in the After-part of the Ship, the Captain thinking that to be the dryefl, but by that Postion it received very violent Shooks, by means of which its Motion was a little retarded, and occasioned it to vary more in coming Home than in going; for in the Voyage Home it loll One Minute 49 Seconds, being about 16 Geographical Miles, whereas in going it loft only Five Seconds, being about One Mile and One Fifth, as was above mentioned.

APPENDIX, NT.

Some Account of Mr. Hars Inventions for de-

termining the Longitude at Sea, and for correcting the Charts of the Coasts;

If Clocks or Watches could be made to keep Time exactly on Ship-board, it is allowed on, by all Hands, they would be the bell Means for determining the Longitude at Sea.

In this the famous Monsieur was so fully

satisfied, that he spent much Time, and thought upon the Improvement of Pendulum Watches for that Purpose, and proceeded so far as to prevent that Irregularity in their Motion which the Agitation of the Ship would otherwise occasion, and accordingly his Watches were found very useful in quick Voyages to correct the Ship’s Reckoning; but being Hill subject to several small Irregularities, which in Time would amount to a considerable Error, they could not lately be trusted 111 veiy long Voyages.

It is well known that the Variation of Heat and Cold, of Moillureand Dryness; of the Friction of Bodies in Motion, and of the Fluidity of Oil, are the Causes of very considerable Irregularities in the Motion of the bell Clocks at Land: Mr. Harrison at first was led, by mere Curiosity, into a Consideration of these Causes; and after various Expedients, happily contrived to remove some, and balance others against one another, he has, in Effect, removed them all, and made a Pendulum Clock that keeps Time so exactly with the Heavens, as not to err above One Second in a Month for Ten Years together; an Invention not only admirable in itself, but of very great Use towards the Improvement of Afironomy and Navigation.

After this M r. Harrison, living near a Sea Port Town, was induced to consider how to alter the Construction of his Clock, so as it might not be subject to any of the said Irregularities even on Ship-board, and did accordingly conllrucl a Machine for keeping Time, which, upon Trial, answered his Expectation; for being put on board of a Ship, after a Voyage to Lisbon and back again, it corrected the Reckoning at the Mouth of the Channel about a Degree and a Half, as appears by Certificate from the Mailer of the Ship.

The Commissioners appointed by Act of Parliament for providing a Public Reward for such Person, or Per-: fons, as shall difeaver the Longitude at Sea, having seen and approved this Machine, were pleased to en- courage Mr. Harrison to make another of the fama Kind, but with several Improvements.

This second Machine was finished about Two Years ago, and a Journal of its Motion compared with that of the Clock above mentioned, has been kept ever since, with little Interruptions, and at sundry Times the Machine has been very much heated by Fire, and suffered to cool again, and has been agitated for many Hours together, with greater Violence than what it could receive even from the Motion of a Ship in a Storm: And the result of all these Experiments is this, that (as far as it can be determined without making a Voyage at Sea) the Motion of the Machine is sufficiently regu- lar and exact for finding the Longitude of a Ship within the neared Limits proposed by Parliament, and probably much nearer.

But, as all Inventions are capable Improvement, Mr. Harrison, by the Knowledge he acquired from Experience

Discoverjf

of tkc Longitude.

T)ifeovery of the Longitude.

548 - 12° Martl

perience of these Two Machines, has been enabled to contrive a Third, still upon the same Principles, but of aConftruclion something different; and has already made Part of this Machine, which, when finished, will have the following Advantages above the former: That being of a smaller Size, it will be more commodious; that being ofa plainer and simpler Construction, it will be less subject to any Disorder, will be easier adjusted, and will serve as a better Model for Workmen to make others by, so that Ships may be furnished with the like Machines at a cheaper Rate.

We therefore, whose Names are underwritten, are of Opinion, That these Machines, even in their present Degree of Exactness, will be of great and excellent Use, as well for determining the Longitude at Sea, as for correcting the Charts of the Coasts; and, as every Step towards further Exactness and Security, in a Matter of such Importance to the Public, is greatly to be valued, we do hereby recommend Mr. Harrison to the Favour of the Commissioners appointed by the said A6i, as a Person highly deserving of such further Encouragement and Assistance as they shall juge proper and sufficient to finish his Third Machine.

M. Polices, Pr. R.S.

A Calculation, shewing the Result of an Experiment made with Mr. Ilarrifon's Time-keeper, In Consequence of the Instructions and Directions of the Commissioners of the Longitude, in a Voyage from PorlJmouth to Port Royal in Jamaica, in order to determine by that Time-keeper the Difference of Longitude between these Two Places; and to find how much the Longitude found by the rime-keeper differs from the Longitude formerly determined by Astronomical Observations.

The Difference of Longitude between Greenwich and Kingston in Jamaica, determined by the Transit of Mercury over the Sun, the 25th of October 1743, O. S. (the Effect of the Parallaxes = 54" being included) is found to

be, as recorded in the Philosophical Transactions.....5b. 6'. 52' \V

Difference of Longitude between Greenwich and Portsmouth *- - - - . - - o 4'. 1 iMt

Therefore the Difference of Longitude between Portsmouth and Kingston is - - - 5b. 2. 41" W

Port Royal is 10" of Time to the West of Kingston..... o 1 o' W

Therefore the Difference of Longitude between Portsmouth and Port Royal is - 5b. 2'. 5,1 W

The Time-keeper was found, by equal Altitudes, taken on the 28th October 1761, to be 3' 21" 1 after than Mean Time at Portsmouth.

The Time-keeper was found, by equal Altitudes, taken on the 6th of November 1761, to be i 57" faster than Mean Time at Portsmouth.

Therefore, by these Observations, the Time-keeper is found to be going at the Rate of losing 2. "66 in One Day.

On the 7th of November 1761, the Time-keeper was set back 3' of Time, at the Desire, 2nd in the Presence, of Commissioner Hughes and others, pursuant to the Orders of the Commissioners of the Longitude, and certified accordingly, as well as the above Observations of equal Altitudes.

Therefore the Time-keeper is flower than Mean Time at Portsmouth, on the 6th of November, by 3".

On the Arrival of the Time-keeper at Port Royal equal Altitudes were taken, on the 26th of Junuary 1762, and the Time-keeper shewed mean Noon to beat -r ----- - 4b. 59' 7, "5

But 3" are to be added to this Time, for the Reason given above: The Difference of Longitude therefore, between Portsmouth and Port Royal, as shewn by the Timekeeper, is-----.....-~4h. 59' I0> "5

But the Difference of Longitude found by Observation, as above, is - 5I1. 2' 51"

Therefore the Difference between the Time-keeper and the Observation is - - 3'. 40"

Which Difference is to be diminished by 3' 35", 4 being the Number of Seconds loft by the Time-keeper from the 6th of November 1761 to the 26th of January 1762, in 81

Days as mentioned above.....- 3' 35

So that the Time-keeper shewed the Difference of Longitude between Portsmouth and Port Royal less than the Longitude found by Astronomical Observations - 3,

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House: And it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty being sensible of the Zeal and Vigour, with which His faithful Subjects in North America have exerted themselves in Defence of His Majesty’s just Rights and Possessions, recommends it to this House to take the same into Consideration, and to enable His Majesty to give them a proper Comperifation, for the Expences incurred by the respective Provinces, in the Levying, Clothing, and Pay of the Troops, raised by the fame, according as the active Vigour, and strenuous Efforts of the respective Provinces ilia.ll justly appear to merit.

G. R.

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Making Act for explaining and amending an Act, made in the Brtad* Thirty-first Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King Scotland’ George the Second, intituled, An Act for the due making of Bread, and to regulate the Price and Assize thereof; and to punish Persons who shall adulterate Meal, Flour, or Bread; so far as the same relates to that Part of Great Britain called Scotland; and for rendering the the said Act more effectual in that Part of the United Kingdom; without any Amendment: And also.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Forty-eight thousand Eight hundred and Ninety-one Pounds Fourteen Shillings and Eleven Pence, be granted to His Majesty, to replace to the Sinking Fund the like Sinn paid out of the same to make good the Deficiency on the 5th Day of 1762, of the several Rates and Duties upon Offices and Pensions, and upon Houses, and upon Windows or Lights, which were made a Fund by an Act 31 ft George the Second, for paying Annuities at the Bank of England in respect of Five Millions borrowed towards the Supply granted for the Service of the Year 1758.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Instrument invented by Mr. John HarriJ'on for keeping true Time at Sea, in various Climates, has been found, by Trial already made, to be of great Utility for discovering the Longitude.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it would be of great Service to the Public, if the Principles and Mauner of making the said Instrument were to be now disclosed and made known, on giving to the said John Harrison Part of the Reward ordered to be paid, by an Act passed in the Twelfth Year of Queen Anne, to the First Discoverer of a proper Method for finding the Longitude, with Security for the Residue, on further Trial and consequent Approbation.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson reported from the Committee appointed to inquire into the Elfefts of an Act made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminsterwith Filli, and to reduce the present exorbitant Price thereof, and to protest and encourage Fishermen; and to consider of proper Methods for the further supplying the said Cities of London and Westminster with Eifli at moderate Rates; and to report their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; That the Committee had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Cities of London and Westminster have, ft nee the Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with Fish, and to reduce the present exorbitant Price thereof, and to protest and encourage Fishermen, been better, and in a much larger Degree, than before the passing the said Act, supplied with Sea Fish by Land Carriage; and that the late exorbitant Price of many Sorts of Sea Fish hath thereby been considerably reduced; and the Cities of Iwndon ana Westminster have been* supplied with many Sorts of Sea Fish, not thentofore usually brought there.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the good Elfefts which the said Act hath produced, have been owing to the laudable and indefatigable Prosecution of the Plan or Scheme concerted by John Blake, Esquire, for the better supplying the Cities of Iwndon and Westminster with Sea Fill), by Land Carriage; and which hath in Part been executed by him, notwithstanding the many Difficulties he met with in such the Execution thereof.

Resolved, I'hat it is the Opinion of this Committee," That some A Alliance ought to be allowed or granted to the said John Blake, to encourage and enable him further, and efl'eftually, to carry into Execution the said Plan or Scheme, concerted by him, for the better flip-plying the Cities of London and Westminster with Sea Fish, at moderate Rates.

An Amendment was, propefed to be made thereunto, by leaving out the Word " thentofore."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Who, after having duly communicated to each other their full Powers, in.good Form, Copies whereof are transcribed at the End of the present Treaty of Peace, have agreed upon, the Articles, the Tenor of which is as follows.

Article I.

There shall be a Christian, universal, and perpetual Peace, as well by Sea as by Land, and a sincere and con ft ant Fritudship shall be re-established between their Britannic, Aloft Christian, Catholic, and Most Faithful Majesties, and between their Heirs and Successors, Kingdoms, Dominions, Provinces, Countries, Subjects* and V afi’als, of what Quality or Condition soever they, be, without Exception of Places, or of Persons: So that the I Iigh Contracting Parties shall give the greateu' Attention to maintain between themfel ves and their said Dominions and Subjects, this reciprocal Friepdship and Coijespondence, without permitting, on either Side, any Kind of Floftilities, by Sea or by Land, to be committed, from henceforth, For any Cause, or under any

Pretence whatsoever, and every Thing shall be care-It has pleated the"Most High to diflufe the Spirit of fully avoided, which might, hereafter, prejudice the

Unioii

577

Uniop happily re-established, applying themselves, on the contrary, on every Occasion, to procure for each other whatever may contribute to their mutual Glory, Interests, and Advantages, without giving any Affill-ance or Protection, directly or indirectly, to those who would cause any Prejudice to either of the High Contracting Parties: There shall be a general Oblivion of every Thing that may have been done or committed before, or fmce, the Commencement of the War, which is just ended.

Article II.

The Treaties of Westphalia of 1648; those of Madrid ‘between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain of 166 7 and 1670} the Treaties of Peace of of 1678

and 1679 j of Ryswick of 1697; those of Peace and of Commerce of Utrecht of 1713; that of Baden of 1714; the Treaty Of the Triple Alliance of the Hague of 1717; that of the Quadruple Alliance of Ijyndon of 1718; the Treaty of Peace of Vienna of 1738; the Definitive Treaty of Aix la Chapelle of 1748; and that of Madrid, between the Crowns of Great Britain and Spain, of 1750; as well as the Treaties between the Crowns of Spain and Portugal, of the 13th February) 1668; of the 6th February) 1715; and of the 12th February 1761; and that of the nth April 1713, ‘between France and Portugal, with the Guaranties of Great Britain-, serve as a Bafts and Foundation to the Peace, and to the presentTreaty: And for this Purpose, they are all renewed and confirmed in the best Form, as well as all the Treaties in general, which subsisted between the High Con trading Parties before the War, as if they were inserted here Word for Word, so that they are to be e.xaCily observed, for the future, in their whole Tenor,'and religiously executed on all Sides, in all their Points.which shall not be derogated from by the present Treaty, notwithstanding all that may have been flrpul.ited to the contrary by any of the High ContFading Parties: And all the said Parties declare. That they will not suffer any Privilege, Favour, or Indulgence, to fnbfift Contrary to the Treaties above confirmed, except what shall have been agreed and stipulated by the present Treaty.

Article III.

All the Prisoners made, on all Sides, as well by t-and, as by Sea, and the Hostages carried away, or given during the War, and to this Day, shall be restored, without Ransom, Six Weeks, at latest, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratification of the present Treaty, each Crown respectively paying the Advances, which shall have been made for the Subsistence and Maintenance of their Prisoners, by the Sovereign of the Country where they shall have been detained, according to the attested Receipts and Estimates, and other authentic Vouchers, which shall be furnished on one Side and the other: And Securities shall be reciprocally given for the Payment of the Debts which the Prisoners shall have contracted in the Countries, where they have been detained, until their intire Liberty. And all the Ships of War and Merchant Vessels, which shall have been taken, flnee the Expiration of the Terms agreed upon for the Cessation of Hostilities by Sea, shall be likewise restored bona with all their Crews, and Cargoes: And the Execution of this Article shall be proceeded upon immediately after the Exchange of the Ratifications of this Treaty.

Article IV.

His Most Christian Majesty renounces all the Preten-fions which he has heretofore formed, or might form, to Nova Scotia, or Acadia, in all its Parts, and guaranties the whole of it, and with all its Dependencies, to the King of Great Britain: Moreover, his Most Christian Majesty cedes, and guaranties to His said Britannic Majesty, in full Right, Canada, with all itsDependeneies, as

well as the Island of Cape Breton, and all the other Islands, and C.oafts, in the Gulph and River St. Laurence, and, in general, every thing that depends on the Vox.. 29.

said Countries, Lands, Islands, and Coasts, with the Sovereignty, Property, Possession, and all Rights acquired-by Treaty or atherwife, which (lie Most Christian King, and the Crown of France, have'had, till now, over the said Countries, Islands, Lands, Places, Coasts, and their-Inhabitants, so that the Molt Christian King cedes and makes over the whole to the said King, and to the Crown of Great Britain, and that in the most ample Manner and Form, without Rellri&ion, and without any Liberty to depart from the said Cession and Guaranty, under any Pretence, or to disturb Great Britain in the Possessions above mentioned. His Britannic Majesty, on His Side, agrees to grant the Liberty of thcCathqlic Religion to the Inhabitants of Canada: He will, consequently, give the most precise and most effectual Orders, that His new Roman Catholic Subjects may profess the Worth ip of their Religion, according to the Rites of the RomtjhChurch, as far as the Laws of Great Britain permit. His Britannic Majesty further agrees, that the French Inhabitants, or others who had

been Subjects of the Most Christian King in,

may Retire, with all Safety and Freedom, wherever they Until think proper, and may fell their Estates, provided it be to Subjects of His Britannic Majesty, and bring away their Effects, as well as their Persons, without being restrained in their Emigration, under any Pretence whatsoever, except that of Debts, or of Criminal Prosecutions: The Term limited for this Emigration shall be fixed to tile Space of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty.

Article V.

The Subjects of France shall have the Liberty of Fishing and Drying, on a Part of the Coasts of the Island of Newfoundland, such as it is specified in the Xlllth Article of the Treaty of Utrecht; whidh Article is renewed and confirmed by the present Treaty, (except what relates to the Island of Cape Breton, as well as to the other Islands and Coasts, in the Moutli and in the Gulph of St. Laurence:) And His Britannic Majesty consents to leave to the Subjects of the Most Christian King the Liberty of fishing in the Gulph of St. Laurence, on Condition that the Subjects of France do not exercise the said Fishery, but at the Distance of Three Leagues.from all the Coasts belonging to Great Britain, as well those of the Continent, as those of the Islands situated in the said Gulph of St. Laurence. And as to what relates to the Fishery on the Coasts of the Islands of Cape Breton out of the said Gulph, the Subr jests of the Most Christian King shall not be permitted to exercise the said Fishery, but at the Distance of Fifteen Leagues from the Coasts of the Island of Cape Breton-, and the Fishery on the Coasts of Scotia or Acadia, and every where else out of the said Gulph, shall remain on the Foot of former Treaties.

Article VI.

The King of Great Britain cedes the Islands of St. Peter and Miquelon, in full Right, to his Most Christian Majesty, to serve as a Shelter to the French Fishermen: And his said Most Christian Majesty engages not to fortify the said Islands; to erect no Buildings upon them, but merely for the Convenience of the Fishery; and to keep upon them a Guard of Fifty Men only for the Police.

In order to re-establish Peace on solid and durable Foundations, and to remove for ever all Subject of Dispute with regard to the Limits of the British and French Territories on the Continent of It is

Article XVI.

The Decision of the Prizes made, in Time of Peace, by the Subjects of Great Britainon the , shall be referred to the Courts of Justice of the Admiralty of Great Britain, conformably to the Rules established among all Nations, so that the Validity of the said Prizes, between the British ami Spanish Nations, shall be decided and judged, according to the Law of Nations, and according to Treaties, in the Courts of Justice of the Nation, who shall have made the Capture.

Article XVII.

His Britannic Majesty shall cause to be demolished all the Fortifications which His Subjects shall have erected in the Bay of Honduras, and other Places of the Territory of Spain in that Part of the World, Four Months after the Ratification of the present Treaty: And his Catholic Majesty shall not permit His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, or their Workmen, to be disturbed, or molested, under any Pretence whatsoever, in the said Places, in their Occupation of cutting, loading, and carrying away Logwood: And for this Purpose, they may build without Hindrance, and occupy without Interruption, tireIloufes and Magazines which are necessary for them, for their Families, and for their Effects: And his Catholic Majesty assures to them, by this Article, the full Enjoyment of those Advantages, and Powers, on the Spanish Coasts and Territories, as above stipulated, immediately after the Ratification of the present Treaty.

Article XVIII.

His Catholic Majesty desists, as well for himself, as for his Successors, from all Pretension, which he may have formed, in favour of the and other

his Subjects, to the Right of Fishing in the Neighbourhood of the Island of Newfoundland.

Article XIX.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to Spain all the Territory which he has conquered in the 1/land of Cuba, with the Fortress of the Havana, and this Fortress, as well as all the other Fortrefies of the said Island, shall be restored in the same Condition they were in when conquered by His Britannic Majesty’s Arms; provided, that His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, who shall have settled in the said Island, restored to Spain by the present Treaty, or those who shall have any Commercial Affairs to settle there, shall have Liberty to fell their Lands, and their Estates, to settle their Affairs, to recover their Debts, and to bring away their Effects, as well ajs their Persons, on board Vessels which they shall be permitted to send to the said Island restored as above, and which shall serve for that Use only, without being restrained on account of their Religion, or under any other Pretence whatsover, except That of Debts, or Criminal Prosecutions: And for this Purpose, the Term of Eighteen Months is allowed to His Britannic Ma-jefiy’s Subjects, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty: But as the Liberty, granted to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, to bring away their Persons, and their Effects, in Vessels of their Nation, may be liable to Abuses, if Precautions were not taken to prevent them; it has been expressly agreed, between His Britannic Majesty and his Catholic Majesty, That the Number of Vessels, which shall have Leave to go to the said Iftitnd restored to-Spain, shall be limited, as well as the Number of Tons of each one; that they shall go in Ballast; shall let Sail at a fixed Time; and shall make One Voyage only; all the Eft efts belonging to the being to be embarked at the same Time: It has been further agreed, That his Catholic Majesty shall cause the necessary Passports to be given to the said Vessels^ that, for the greater Security, it shall be allowed to placeTwo Vox. 29.

Spanish Clerks, or Guards, in each of the fr.id Vessels, which shall be visited in the Landing-places, and Ports of the said Island restored to Spain, and that the Merchandizes, which shall be found therein, shall beeonfifeated.

Article XX.

In consequence of the Restitution stipulated in the preceding Article, his Catholic Majesty cedes and guaranties, in full Right, to His Britatinic Majesty, Florida, with Fort St. Augustin, and the Bay of as well

as all that Spain possesses on the Continent of North America, to the East, or to the South East, of the River Mississippi. And, in general, every thing that depends on the said Countries, and Lands, with the Sovereignty, Property, Possession, and all Rights, acquired by Treaties or otherwise, which the Catholic King, and the Crown of Spain, have had, till now, over the said Countries, Lands, Places, and their Inhabitants; so that the Catholic King cedes and makesover the Whole to the said King, and to the Crown of Great Britain, and that in the most ample Manner and Form. His Britannic Majesty agrees, on His Side, to grant to the Inhabitants of the Countries, above ceded, the Liberty of the Catholic Religion: He will consequently give the most express and the most effectual Orders, that His new Roman Catholic Subjects may profess the Wor/liip

of their Religion, according to the Rites of the Romijk Church, as far as the Law's of Great Britain permit: His Britannic Majesty further agrees, that the Spanish Inhabitants, or others who had been Subjects of the Catholic King in the said Countries, may retire, with all Safety and Freedom, wherever they think proper; and may fell their Estates, provided it be to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, and bring away their Effects, as well as their Persons, without being restrained in their Emigration, under any Pretence whatsoever, except that of Debts, or of Criminal Prosecutions: The Term, limited for this Emigration, being fixed to the Space of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty. It is moreover stipulated, that his Catholic Majesty shall have Power to cause all the Effects, that may belong to him, to be brought away, whether it be Artillery, or other Things.

Spain, and Portugal, before the present War.

Translation of the Declaration of His Most Christian Majesty’s Plenipotentiary, with regard to the Debts due to the Canadians, dated Paris, February 10th, -»763-

DECLARATION.

The King of Great Britain having desired, that the Payment of the Letters of Exchange and Bills, which had been delivered to the Canadians for the Necessaries furnished to the French Troops, should be secured, His Most Christian Majesty, intirely disposed to render to every one that Justice which is legally due to them, has declared, and does declare, that the said Bills, and Letters of Exchange, shall be punctually paid, agreeably to a Liquidation made in a convenient Time, according to the Distance of the Places, and to what shall be possible, taking Care, however, that the Bills and letters of Exchange, which the French Subjects may have at the Time of this Declaration, be not confounded with the Bills and Letters of Exchange, which are in the Possession of the new Subjects of the King of Great Britain.

In Witness whereof, we the underwritten Minister of His Molt Christian Majesty, duly authorized for this Purpose, have signed the present Declaration, andcaufed the Seal of our Arms to be put thereto.

' Done at Paris the 1 oth of February 1763,

Art. I.

There shall be a Christian, univerlaf, and perpetual Peace, as we!! by Sea as by Land, and a sincere and constant Friendlfiip shall be rc-established between their

Britannic, Catholic, Most Christian, and Most Faithful Majesties, and between their Heirs and Successors, Kingdoms; Dominions, Provinces, Countries, Subjects, and Vassals, of what Quality or Condition soever they be, without Exception of Places or of Persons: So that the High Contracting Parties shall give the greatest Attention to maintain between themselves and their Paid Dominions and Sul^jects, this reciprocal Frietidship and Correspondence, without permitting, on either Side, any Kind of Hostilities, by Sea or by Land, to be committed, from henceforth, for any Canfe, or under any Pretence whatsoever, and every thing shall be carefully avoided, which might, hereafter, prejudice the Union happily rc-established, applying themselves, on the contrary, on every Occasion, to procure for each other whatever may contribute to their mutual Glory, Interests, and Advantages, without giving any Abidance or Protection, directly or indirectly, to those who would cause any Prejudice to either of the High Contracting Parties: There shall be a general Oblivion of every Thing that may have been done or committed before, orfince, the Commencement of the War, which is just ended.

I.

Some of the Titles made use of by the Contracting Powers, either in the Full Powers, and other Acts, during the Course of the Negotiation, or in the Preamble of the present Treaty, not being generally acknowledged; it has been agreed, that no Prejudice shall ever refidt therefrom to any of the said Contracting Parties, and-that the Titles, taken or omitted, on either Side, on occasion of the GiidNegoriation, and of the present Treaty, shall not be cited, or quoted as a Precedent.

‘ ’ ’ ' II.

' It has been agreed and determined, that the French Language, made use of in all the Copies of the present Treaty; shall not become an Example, which may lie-alleged, or made a Precedent of, or prejudice, in any Manner, any of the Contracting Powers; and that they shall conform themselves, for the future, to what has been observed, and ought to be observed, with Regard to, and on the Part of the Powers, who are used, and have a Right to give and receive Copies of like Treaties* in another Language than French; the present Treaty having still 'the same Force and Effect, as if the aforesaid Custofn had been therein observed.

Whereas, in order to perfect the Peace between Us and Our good Brother the Most Faithful King, on the one Part, and Our good Brothers the Most Christian and Catholic Kings, on the other, which has been happily begun by the Preliminary Articles already signed at Fontainebleau the 3H of this Month, and to bring the same to the desired End, We have thought proper to invest some fit Perl'on, with full Authority, on Our Part; Know ye, that We, having most intire Confidence in the Fidelity, Judgment, Skill, and Ability in managing Allaire of the greatest Confe-quCliee, of Our Right. Article VIII.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to France the Islands of Guadeloupe, of Marie Gaof Defirade, of Martinico, and of Belleijle-, and the Fortresses o’fthefe Islands shall be restored in the same Condition they were in, when they were conquered by the British Arms; provided that His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, who shall have settled in the said Islands, or those who shall have any Commercial Affairs to settle there, or in the other Places restored to France by the present Treaty, shall have Liberty to fell their Lands and their Estates, to settle their Affairs, to recover their Debts, and to bring away their Effects, as well as their Persons, on board Vessels, which they shall be permitted to send to the said. Islands, and other Places restored as above, and which shall serve for this Use only, without being restrained on Account of their Religion, or under any other Pretence whatsoever, except that of Debts, or of Criminal Prosecutions: And for this Purpose, the Term of Eighteen Months is allowed to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty; but, as the Liberty, granted to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, to bring away their Persons and their Effects, in Vessels of their Nation, may be liable to Abuses, if Precautions were not taken to prevent them; it has been expressly agreed between His Britannic Majesty and his Moll Christian Majesty, that the Number of English Vessels, which shall have Leave to go to the said Islands and Places restored to France, shall be limited, as well as the Number of Tons of each one; that they shall go hi Ballad; shall set Sail at a fixed Time; and shall make One Voyage only, all the Effects belonging to the English, being to be embarked at the same Time. It has been further agreed, that his Moll Christian Majesty shall cause the necessary Passports to be given to the said Vessels; that, for the greater Security, it shall be allowed Two French Clerks, or Guards, in each of the said Vessels, which shall be visited in the Landing Places, and Ports of the said Islands, and Places, restored to France, and that the Merchandize, which shall be found therein, shall be confiscated.

Article IX.

The Moll Christian King cedes and guaranties to His Britannic Majesty, in full Right, the Islands of Grenada, and of the Grenadines, with the same Stipulations in Favour of the Inhabitants of this Colony, inserted in the IVth Article for those of CanadaAnd the Partition of the Islands, called Neutral, is agreed and fixed, so that those of St. Vincent, Dominica, and Tobago, shall remain in full Right to Great Britain, and that That of St. Lucia shall be delivered to France, to enjoy the same likewise in full Right; and the High Contracting Parties guaranty the Partition so stipulated.

Article X.

His Britannic Majesty shall restore to France the llland

176*3.

of Goree, in the Condition it was in when conquered: And his Most Christian Majesty cedes, in full Right, and guaranties to the King of Great Britain, the River Senegal, with the Fortsand Factories of St. Laois, Potior, and Gainin', and with all the Rights and Dependencies of the said River Senegal.

Article XI.

In the East Indies, Great Britain shall restore to France in the Condition they are now in the different Factories, which that Crown possessed, as well on the Coall of Coromandel, and Orix a, as on that of Malabar, as also in Bengal, in the Beginning of the Year 1749. And his Moli Christian Majesty renounces all Pretension to the Acquisitions which he had made on the Coast of Coromandel and Orixa, since the said Beginning of the

Year 1749. His Most Christian Majesty shall restore. on his Side, all that he may have conquered from Great Britain, in the East Indies, during the present War; and

will expressly cause Nattalany Tapanaully, in the llland

of Sumatra, to be restored; he engages further, not to erect Fortifications, or to keep d roops in any Part of the Dominions of the Subah of Bengal. And in order to preserve future Peace on the Coast of Orixa, the English and French shall acknowledge Mahomet Ally Khan for lawful Nabob of the and Salabat sing for lawful Subah of the Decan-, and both Parties shall renounce all Demands and Pretensions of Satisfaction, with which they might charge each other, or their Indian Allies, for the Depredations, or Pillage, committed, on the one Side, or on the other, during the War.

Article XII.

The llland of Minorca shall be restored to His Britannic Majesty, as well as Fort St. Philip, in the same Condition they were in, when conquered by the Arms of the Most Christian King; and with the Artillery which was there, when the said llland and the said Fort were taken.

Article XIII.

The Town and Port of Dunkirk shall be put into the State fixed by the last Treaty of Aix la Chapelle, and by former Treaties. The Cunette shall be destroyed immediately after t he Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty, as well as the Forts and Butteries which defend the Entrance on the Side of the Sea; and Provision shall be made, at the same Time, for the Wholesomeness of the Air, and for the Health of the Inhabitants, by some other Means, to the Satisfaction of the King of Great Britain.

Article XlYth.

France shall restore all the Countries belonging to the Electorate of Hanover, to the Landgrave of Ileje, to the Duke of Brunjioick, and to the Count of La Buckeboitrg, which are, or shall be occupied by his Most Christian Majesty’s Arms: The Fortresses of these different Countries shall be restored in the same Condition they were in, when conquered by the French Arms; and the Pieces of Artillery, which shall have been carried elsewhere, shall be replaced by the same Number, of the same Bore, Weight, and Metal.

Article XV’.

In case the Stipulations, contained in the Xlllth Article of the Preliminaries, should not he compleated at the Time of the Signature of the present Treaty, as well with regard to the Evacuations to be made by the Armies of France of the Fortresses of Cleves, Guelders, and of all the Countries belonging to the King of Prussia, as with regard to the Evacuations to be made by the British and French Armies of the Countries u'hich they occupy in Westphalia, Lower Saxony, on the Lower

Rhine, the Upper Rhine, and in all the Empire, ami to the Retreat of the Troops into the Dominions of their respectiveSovercigns;Their Britannic, and Most Christian Majesties promise to proceed, bona < with all the Dispatch the same will permit of, to the said Evacuations, the intire Completion whereof they ltipulate before the

15th of March next, or sooner if it can be done; and Their Britannic and Most Christian Majesties further engage, and promise to each other, not tofurnith any Succours, of any Kind, to their respective Allies, who shall continue engaged in the War in

Article XVr.

The Decision of the Prizes made, in Time of Peace, by the Subjects of Great Britain, on the Spaniards, shall be referred to the Courts of Justice of the Admiralty of Great Britain, conformably to the Rules established among all Nations, fu that the Validity of the said Prizes, between the British and Nations,

shall be decided and judged, according to the Law of Nations, and according to Treaties, in the Courts of Justice of the Nation, who ihalJ have made the Capture.

Article XVII.

His Britannic Majesty shall cause to bedemolished all the Fortifications which His Subjects shall have erected in the Bay of Honduras, and other Places of the Territory of Spain in that Part of the World, Four Months after the Ratification of the present Treaty: And his Catholic Majesty shall net permit His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, or their Workmen, to be disturbed, or molested, under any Pretence whatsoever, in the said Places, in their Occupation of Cutting, Loading, and Carrying away Logwood: And for this Purpose, they may build without Hindrance, and occupy without Interruption, the Houses and Magazines which are necessary for them, for their Families, and for their Effects: And his Catholic Majesty assures to them, by this Article, the full Enjoyment of those Advantages and Powers, on the Spani/hCoafts and Territories, as above

stipulated, immediately after the Ratification of the present Treaty.

Article XVIII.

His Catholic Majesty desists, as well for himself, as for his Successors, from all Pretension, which he may have formed, in favour of the Guipufcoans, and other his Subjects, to the Right of Fishing in the Neighbourhood of the Island of Nciufoundland.

Article XIX.

The King of Great Britain shall restore to Spain all the Territory which he has conquered in the Island of Cuba, with the Fortress of the Havana, and this Fortress, as well as all the other Fortresses of the said Island, shall be restored in the same Condition they were in when conquered by His Britannic Majesty’s Arms; provided, that His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, who shall have settled in the said Island, restored to Spain by the present Treaty, or those who shall have any Commercial Affairs to settle there, shall have Liberty to fell their Lands, and their Estates, to settle their Affairs, to recover their Debts, and to bring away their Effects, as well as their Persons, on board Vessels which they shall be permitted to send to the said Island restored as above, and which shall serve for that Use only, without being restrained on account of their Religion, or under any other Pretence whatsoever, except that of Debts, or of Criminal Prosecutions: And for this Purpose, the Term of Eighteen Months is allowed to His tannic Majesty’s Subjects, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty: But as the Liberty, granted to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, to bring away their Persons, and their Effects, in Vessels of their Nation, may be liable toAbufes, if Precautions were not taken to prevent them; it has been expressly agreed, between His Britannic Majesty and his Catholic Majesty, That the Number of English Vessels, which shall have Leave to

go to the said Island restored to Spain, shall be limited, as well as the Number of Tons of each One; that they shall go in Ballast; shall set Sail at a fixed Time; and shall make One Voyage only; all the Effects belonging to the English being to be embarked at the same Time:

It has been further agreed, That his Catholic Majesty shall cause the necessary Passports to be given to the said Vessels; that, for the greater Security, it shall be Vol 29.

allowed to place Two Span Clerks, or Guards; iri each of the said Vessels, which shall be visited in the Landing-places, and Ports of the said Island restored to Spain, and that the Merchandize; which shall be found therein, shall be confiscated.

Article XX.

In consequence of the Rellitution ftipuiateci in the preceding Article, his Catholic Majesty cedes and guaranties, in full Right, to His Britannic Majesty. Florida, with Fort St. Augustin, and the Bay of as

well as all that Spain possesses on the Continent of North America, to the East, or to the South East, of the River Mi/Ji/jippi.And, in general, every thing that

depends upon the said Countries, and Lands, with the Sovereignty, Property, Possession, and all Rights, acquired by Treaties or otherwise, which the Catholic King, and the Crown of Spainhave had, till now, over the said Countries, Lands, Places, and their Inhabitants; so that the Catholic King cedes and makes over the Whole to the said King, and to the Crown of Great Britain, and that in the most ample Manner and Form. His Britannic Majesty agrees, on HiS Side, to grant to the Inhabitants of the Countries, above ceded, the Liberty of the Catholic Religion: He tVill consequently give the most express and the most effectifal Orders, that His new- Roman Catholic Subjects may profeis the Worth ip of their Religion, according to the Rites of the Romifii Church, as far as the Laws of Great Britain

permit: His Britannic Majesty further agrees, that the* Spanish Inhabitants, or others who had been Subjects of the Catholic King in the said Countries, may retire, with all Safety and Freedom, wherever they tli nk proper; and may fell their Estates, provided it be to His Britannic Majesty’s Subjects, and bring away their Effects, as well as their Persons, without being restrained in their Emigration, under any Pretence whatsoever, except that of Debts, or of Criminal Prosecutions: The Term, limited for this Emigration, being fixed to the Space of Eighteen Months, to be computed from the Day of the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty. It is moreover stipulated, that his Catholic Majesty shall have Power to cause all the Effects, that may belong to him; to be brought away, whether it be Artillery, or other Things.

Article XXI.

The French and Spanish Troops shall evacuate all the Territories, Lands, Towns, Places, and Castles, of his Most Faithful Majesty, in Europe, without any Reserve, which shall have been conquered by the Armies of France and Spain, and shall restore them in the same Condition they were in when conquered, with the same Artillery, and Ammunition, which were found there: And with regard to the Colonies in

America, Africa, or in the East Indies, if any Change shall have happened there, all Filings shall be restored on the same Footing the y were in, and conformably to the preceding Treaties which fubfiiled between the Courts of France, Spain, and Portugal, before the present War.

Article XXII.

All the Papers, Letters, Documents, and Archives, which were found in the Countries, Territories,'I owns, and Places, that are restored, and those belonging to the Countries ceded, shall be, respectively and bona fide, delivered, or furnished at the same Time, if possible, that Possession is taken, or, at latest. Four Months after the Exchange of the Ratifications of the present Treaty, in whatever Places the said Papers or Documents may be found.

Article XXIII.

All the Countries and Territories, which tnay have been conquered, in whatsoever Part of the World, by the Anns of Their Britannic and Most Faithful Majesties, as well as by those of their Most Christian and Catholic Majesties, which are not included in the present Treaty, either under the Title of Cefiions, or under the Title of Restitutions, shall be restored without Difficulty, and without requiring any Compensation.

Article XXV.

His Britannic Majesty, as Elector of Lvnen-

bourg, as well for Himself, as for His Heirs and Successors, and all the Dominions and Possessions of His said Majesty in Germam), are included and guarantied by the present Treaty of Peace.

Article XXVI.

Their Sacred, Britannic, Most Christian, Catholic, and Moll Faithful Majesties, promise to observe, sincerely and bona fide, all the Articles contained and settled in the present Treaty; and they will not fufler the same to be infringed, directly or indirectly, by their respective Subjects; And the said High Contracting Parties, generally and reciprocally, guaranty to each other all the Stipulations of the present Treaty.

Article XXVII.

The solemn Ratifications of the present Treaty, expedited in good and due Form, shall be exchanged in the City of Paris, between the High Contracting Parties, in the Space of a Month, or sooner if possible, to be computed from the Day of the Signature of the present Treaty.

Separate Articles.

I.

Some of the Titles made use of by the Contracting Powers, either in the full Powers, and other Acts, during the Course of the Negotiation, or in the Preamble of the present Treaty, not being generally acknowledged; it has been agreed, that no Prejudice shall ever result therefrom to any of the said Contracting Parties, and that the Titles, taken or omitted, on either side, on occasion of the said Negotiation, and of the present Treaty, shall not be cited, or quoted as a Precedent.

II.

It has been agreed and determined, that the French Language, made ulb of in all the Copies of the present Treaty, shall not become an Example, which may be alleged, or made a Precedent of, or prejudice, many Manner, any of the Contracting Powers; and that they shall conform themselves, for the future, to what has been observed, and ought to be observed, with Regard to, and on the Part of the Powers, who are used, and have a Right, to give and receive Copies of like Treaties in another Language than French; the present Treaty having still the same Force and Effect, as if the aforesaid Custom had been therein observed.

III.

Though the King of Portugal has not signed the present Definitive Treaty, Their Britannic, Most Christian, and Catholic Majesties, acknowledge, nevertheless, that his Most Faithful Majesty is formally included therein as a Contracting Party, and as if he had expressly signed the said Treaty: Consequently, Their

Britannic, Most Christian, and Catholic Majesties, respectively and conjointly, promise to his Moil Faithful Majesty, in the most express and most binding Manner, the Execution of all and every the Clauses, contained in the said Treaty, on his Act of Accefllon.

The present Separate Articles shall have the same Force as if they were inserted in the 'Treaty.

In Witness whereof, we the underwritten Ambafla-dors Extraordinary, arid Ministers Plenipotentiary of Their Britannic, Most Christian, and Catholic Majesties, have signed the present Separate Articles, and have caused the Seal of our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Paris, the roth of February 1763.

DECLARATION.

Whereas on the Conclusion of the Negotiation of the Definitive Treaty, signed at Paris this Day, 10th February, a Difficulty arofeas to the Order of Signing, which might have retarded the Conclusion of the said Treaty, We the underwritten, Ambafl'adorand Minister Plenipotentiary of His Most Faithful Majesty, declare, that the Alternative observed, on the Part of the King of Great Britain, and the Most Christian King, with the Moll Faithful King, in the Act of Accession of the Court of Portugal, was granted by their Britannic and Moll Christian Majestics, solely with a View to accelerate the Conclusion of the Definitive Treaty, and by that Means, the more speedily to consolidate so important and so fulutary a Work; and that this Complai-fance of Their Britannic and Most Christian Majesties shall not be made any Precedent of for the future; the Court of Portugal shall not allege it as an Example in their Favour; shall derive therefrom no Right, Title, or Pretension, for any Cause, or under any Pretence whatsoever.

In Witness whereof, We, AmbafTador and Minister Plenipotentiary of His Most Faithful Majesty, duly authorized for this Purpose, have signed the present Declaration, and have caused the Seal of Our Arms to be put thereto.

Done at Paris, the 10th February 1763.

The House being informed that One of the Sheriffs Supply Bill; of the City of London attended at the Door; he was w!ne*°a called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then he withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth.That the Petitioners have observed by the Votes of the House, that a B ill is now depending for granting to His Majesty an additional Duty onWine, Cyder, and Perry; which Bill the Petitioners have been informed, subjects the Makers of Cyder and Perry to the Laws of Excise; and alleging, that the Petitioners, with the deepest Concern, cannot help considering this unexpected Proceeding as preparatory to a general Extension of those grievous Laws; for when new Orders of Men, by Situation and Profession distinct from Traders, are rendered ObjeCis of the Excise Laws, the Precedent is formidable, not to Commerce only, but hath a fatal Tendency which the Petitioners tremble to think of; and that as every Attempt to enlarge the Dominion of the Excise must awaken the Petitioners Fears it' will also jullifv their dutiful Representations to the House, the Guardians of Liberty, that after all the Burthens so chearfully borne, all the I Iardships so patiently endured, and all the Blood so freely spilt in Support of the late just, glorious, and successful War, the Petitioners hope that the meritorious Subjects of this Country may not feel the Extension of Excise Laws among the First Fruits of Peace:

And therefore praying. That so much of the said Bill as subjects the Makers of Cyder and Perry to the Powers of Excise, may not pass into a Law.

The House was moved. That the Journal of the House, of the 19th Day of March 1756, of the Pn>» ceedings of the House upon the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons of the City of London, in Common Council assembled, might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the said Petition, now presented, do lie upon the Table.

Indico is raised, there is less Rice; but. he believes that little Indico will be made in that Province for the future, as we have now other Countries whose Soil and Climate are litter for the Cultivation of that Plant; that he thinks the Province will be much benelitted by allowing Rice to be carried to the Islands, and to the

Spanish Main; that considerable Quantities are already smuggled in there; and that, if a Trade was opened, it would not only be for the Advantage of the Colony, but that the Revenue of the Crown would be inoreased to the Amount of/. 1,500 or/. a Year, by the Payment of the Half Subsidy DutyattheCulloro-houses of South Carolina and Georgia.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Unit granting Liberty to carry Rice directly from South Carolina to the Madeira and other African Islands will greatly tend to increase the Culture and Commerce of the said Province.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That granting Liberty to export Rice directly from the said Province to the American Islands and Settlements will greatly tend to increase the Culture and Commerce of the said Province,

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Tomorrow Morning.

Importation The Lord Strange reported from the Committee, to of Buuer. whom the Petition of the several Merchants, Traders, and others, employed in the manufacturing, buying, , and vending of Woollen Cloth, in and near the several Market Towns of Rochdale and Bury, in the County ' Palatine of Lancaster, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House -, and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the feme was read; and is as (blloweth; viz....

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Richard, Gore and Mr. Geo. Walmsley being severally examined, laid, That they are Mauurafturers of Bays at Rochdale, which Trade is very oonsiderable, and empJoys the Inhabitants of a Trad of Twelve or Thirteen Miles fauare, which is very populous. — That the chief of this Manufactory is exported to Spain, Portugal, Germany, and other Parts. — That it has incre&fed very considerably. — That Wool cannot be manufactured without Grease^ and that Grease or stale Butter is the properefl for the Purpose. — That there is a Species of Wool called Crake, or Slink Lamb Wool, which can’t be manufactured with any Ingredient but Grease or stale Butter. — That great Quantities of such Wool, to the Amount of 2,000 Packs, is manufactured in that Country in a Year. — That die Quantity of such Grease or stale Butter, now to be had, is not a Quarter of the Quantity necessary in the Manufactory j and that the 'Scarcity is chiefly owing to the great Increase of the Manufactory, and the late bad Seasons, whereby the

Price is become double to what it used to be.

And both the Witnesses added, That, in their Apprehension, the permitting the Importation from Ireland of such Grease or stale and dirty Butter, would lx; a Means of supplying the Manufactory with a sufficient Quantity thereof, and thereby greatly extend and improve the said Manufactory.

Upon the wfioley the Committee came to the following llesolution*.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Manufactory of Broad and Narrow Bays, in and about Rockdale and Bury, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, is large, extensive, and increasing; and that great Quantities thereof are exported to Portugal, German}), and other Parts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committees That, for want of a sufficient Quantity of stale and dirty Butter, not fit for eating, commonly called Grease Butter, which is used in the said Manufactory, the Manufacturers are greatly (liftrelied; and the Manufacture is is danger of being reduced, and the Exportation of such Goods greatly lelfoned.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the permitting the Importation, from Ireland, into the Port of Liverpool, of stale and dirty Butter, not fit for eating, commonly called Grease Butter, will-be advantageous to the Manufacturer, and of great public Utility.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second

Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the Lord Strange have Leave to make a Motion, it being near Five of the Clock.

And he moved the House accordingly.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for permitting the Importation from Ireland, into the Port-of Liverpool^ of stale and dirty Butter,: not fit far eating, commonly called Grease Butter: And that the Lord Strange, Mr. Skuttleworth, Sir Ellis and

Mr. Fuller^ do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.
