Mr. Fuller accordingly reported from the said Committee the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Bill, with the Amendments, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

The other Order of the Day being read;

The House resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for the further Improvement of His Majesty’s Revenue of Customs, and for the Encouragement of Officers making Seizures, and for the Prevention of the Clandestine Running of Goods into any Part of His Majesty’s Dominions.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Fuller took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Fuller reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Sevennight, the x ith Day of April next.

Ordered, That Leave be given to move the House upon Monday Sevennight, that any private Business may be entered upon in the House that Day, after Two of the Clock.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Sevennight, the 1 ith Day of April next, Nine of the Clock in the Morning.

Expenditure of the Public Mons y; Ordnance.

My Lord, and honourable Gentlemen,

I think it my Duty, both in respect to the Trull re-posed in me, and to the essential Good of the Service, to lay before your Lordship and the Board, a State of the Artillery Horses, as they have been during the Course of the last Campaign in Germany: In doing this I ilia.ll express many Inconveniences which arose, to the great Detriment of the Service, and which have been attended with infinite Expence.

I will go so lar back as the beginning of our taking the Field in 1759, when the Proportion of Horses being so insufficient, and tho Horses themselves in bad Condition, made even our first Marches with the Artillery an Affair of great Difficulty. Lord George had, through Captain Brome, settled a Contract with a Man in Holland, to purchase Horses at a certain Price;

and after the Train of Horses were quite complete, 20 were to be brought to the Army at the beginning of every Month; but as our first setting out was attended with the Deaths of many Horse^ and many

638 18° Aprilis. A, 1763.

IxpemHttire more rendered unserviceable, the Artillery became un-rawi^Moneys comP^ete> and without a Possibility of Assistance; for Ordnance. the Contractor living in it w'as lirft necessary

to send to him, and even then some Time was to be allowed ere he could bring Horses to the Army. In this State we marched every Day, and in fitch bad Situation we were in, that Count La has several Times sent

the Horses from other Trains to aflilt us, and who had been arrived many Hours, when we were dill prosecuting a March with extreme Fatigue and Danger.

At the Camp at OfnabH. S. H. the Duke, on being informed of our Diffrcfs, ordered 127 Horses to be furnished by the Country. With this lucky Assistance we marched towards Mint the Desertion, from Time to Time, of these prelfed Horses, and the Deaths of others, made us again more incomplete, and without a Possibility of getting Horses, for, as our Army had evacuated WrJ/phalitt, the Road to was be-

come useless to us, and our Contract of no Effect. The Loss wesustained at the Buttle of joined to our

other Losses, made us waut 200 Horses. Lord George then gave me Orders to send to every Part of Germany to buy Horses for the Service. I accordingly sent to Hanover, and elsewhere, by Express, but -with no Success; for the Contractors for other Trains had already bought all up, and the Communication with Holland being fiopt, wc remained without a Power of Relief: To tins, there was no Horses to be pressed, as we marched through a Country quite ruined by the Enemy. J11 this Situation an accidental good Fortune relieved us:

Some Baggage I lories being taken from the Enemy, ll S. II. the Duke ordered them to be sent to us to purchase.

Our Waut of Drivers, during the Course of the Campaign, has also been of very ill Consequence, the Number sent from Englanddecreasing almost daily by Deaths and Sickness; and having no certain Method of procuring them in Germany, and other Trains having the ir

Contractors at every Place ready to furnish themselves, left us unable to hire any. By this Means it has happened that One Driver has had the Charge of Nine, Ten, and Eleven Horses, too great a Number for One Man to take proper Care of From this Scarcity of Drivers, Numbers of Horses have been neglected and loft.

I did all I could to remedy this Evil, by appointing a certain Number of my own Men to look after the Horses; but as we grew sickly, and the Duty became more and more severe, I was soon obliged to withdraw this Assistance, and we were never able to perfectly complete ourselves, during the whole Campaign.

Thus have I given your Lordship and the Board a true State of the Condition we have been in, during the Time of a long Campaign: I have not enumerated on the extreme Fatigue, Danger, and constant Feayf of being left behind on Marches; these being over are felt only in Remembrance.

I have to beg of your Lordship, and the Board, to take my Letter into Consideration, and hope you will settle the Artillery on some certain Footing, whereby the Service may be neither retarded nor endangered.

I shall take all imaginable Care to make myself worthy of your Confidence in this and every other Trull your Lordship and the Board may repose in me. I have the Honour to be, with greatest Respect,

My Lord, and honourable Gentlemen, Your most obedient Servant,

London, William Phillips.

It is impoflihle to

But Fortune favoured us that Day; fir the " French not caring to attack us, gave Captain " an Opportunity to come over, and he has engaged " for some Horses; so that we shall be able to get " forwards by marching 1 lalf One Day; the Horses " and Oxen returning for the other Half the next " Day."

I imagine this Difirefs must have arofc from an Impracticability of procuring Horses on the Spot, and the Distance being too great to find immediate Relief from Holland.

Your Committee then examined Col. Joseph , who w'as Aid de Camp to Lord and af-

terwards to Lord G ranby, who ftiid, he purchased Horses for the Government in the Years 1758 and 1759, in Holland, and met with a good deal of Difficulty to get them to the Army in the Middle of the Campaign of the Year 1759, bHt could have got them as readily as the Contractors, if he had had Authority to buy them in other Places; and thinks the Horses he purchased were better than the Contractors: Says, that about December 1759, he wrote a letter to Lord Granby, then in Germany, inclosing a Scheme for furnishing Horses, but which was not produced to your Committee; and he said, that allowing Two Sets for the Year, in 1,200 Horses, £. 14,000 at leall would have been saved: That,

had his Scheme been appro\ed, he should have had Time to have got all the Horses wanted: That Ixird Granby approved it so much, that he sent it to Lord I.igonicr in England: Colonel Brome was sent over with his Accounts, and understood Lord Granby recommended his Scheme to Lord Ligonier.

lie said further, that in the Year 1760, the Train of Artillery was attended with less Difficulties, becuufe the Number of Horses was increaTed.

EXTRACT of ? Letter from Lord Granby to Lord JLigonier, dated Rotheim, 1 January 1760.

Inclosed I transmit to your Lordship an Estimate for the Furnifiiing of Horses for the Train of Artillery, during the next Campaign, with Captain ifrwne’s letter to me on that Subject; by which it appears, that there is a considerable Diflference, and a much greater Arb vantage to the Service, by the Board of Ordnance purchasing those Ilorfes, than in having them supplied by Contract: But as your Lordship has more Experience and mud know much more of this Matter than I can possibly pretend to, I submit it to your Lordship’s Opinion, which I lliduld be glad to have as soon as possible. — In the mean while, I have sent to the Man who purchased Horses Iafi Year for the Train, in order to commission him to buy up 600 as soon as possible. 'This, I hope, your Lordship will approve of, as our taking the Field early may be requisite; and should it be your Opinion that the Supply by Contract was the most eligible Method, whoever the Contractor may be, will certainly be glad to take them at the Price they may be bought at.

Office of Ordnance, 15th January 1760. My Lord,

We have the Honour to acquaint your Lordship, that we had agreed to contract with Messrs. Ofzoald and Mill, for Horses, Condu#ors, and Drivers for the Artillery in Germany, before the Receipt of your Lordship’s Letter, to the Mailer General; a Copy of which Agreement was transmitted to Mr. Ofzvald, by last Friday’s Poll: But since the Mailer General received your Letter, Mr. Mill has reduced his Prices, and we have now ordered a Contract to be prepared, on the Conditions mentioned in the inclosed Copy of the Agreement, which, we hope, will be for the Good of His Majesty’s Service, and meet with your Lordship’s Approbation.

As the Post for Germany goes out this Night, Time will not permit us to add more at present; but we will take the first Opportunity to be more explicit. — We «re, with the greatest Respe#,

Your Committee, upon looking into the Rules, Orders, and Indru#ions for the Government of the Board, observing, that no Gratuity or other Reward whatsoever was to be taken by any Officer, Clerk, or Minider, belonging to the Office of Ordnance, by Reason of any Bill, Debenture, Contracts, Bargains, or Payment of Monies thereupon, or on any other Consideration or Pretence whatsoever, judged it proper to inquire into the Pra#ice of the Office as to that Matter; and found, upon Examination, that it had been the frequent Pra#ice for Tradesmen and Contractors to give Gratuities to the Clerks upon taking out their Debentures; which Gratuities are voluntary and uncertain; but in several Indanees which have been pro--duced to your Committee, have amounted to abolit One per Cent. Butthat no Part of the same appear to have been given for the Use of any of the principal Officers.

Your Committee, not having Time to examine these Articles minutely, or to see the Vouchers that were offered them in Support of each, were obliged to content themselves with a particular Account of the Salaries mentioned among the other Articles in the Estimate; and they find that, in every Reign, a Warrant, is granted to the Mailer General, the Contents of which are as follow:

GEORGE R.

Right trusty and well beloved Cousin and Counsellor, We greet you well. Whereas, by the great Increase of our Navy and Army, since the Commencement of the War (compared with what they were in the Days of Our Royal Predecessors) the Fortifications and Defences of Our Garrisons, Forts, and Cattles, as also Our Magazines and Stores, have been greatly augmented, thereby occasioning more Engineers, Storekeepers, Clerks/Labourers, and other necessary Instruments and Ministers, than formerly, to be emyloyed in attending Our Trains of Artillery on Expeditions and Services at home and abroad. And for the better ordering, securing, and due keeping and rendering unto you an exact and just Account of Our said Magazines and Stores, for which reasonable Subfilience, Salaries and Wages ought to be, and have been, constantly allowed and paid to them respectively: And for as much as in some Cafes Officers, their Clerks, and others belonging to Attendants on, and employed in, OurOllice

14

of Ordnance have, and ought to have, some Reward or Gratuity made to them for extraordinary Services by themdonc unto Us in the promoting and assisting in the Dispatch of the Business tending to our Service; and Likewise, for and in Consideration of any Charge, Loss or Damage, incurred or fitllained by them, or any of them, in Our Service, Our Will and Pleasure is, and We do hereby require and authorize you, that from Time to Time, youdo cause such Subfilience, Salaries, and Wages, to be allowed, made, and paid upon the Quarter Books, of Our laid Ollice, or otherwise, unto all and every the said Engineers, Storekeepers, Clerks, labourers, and other Instruments and Ministers, or others, as have been, now are, or which hereafter shall or may be, employed by you in Our said Trains of Artillery on Expeditions, in reforming Our Fortifications, or other Services; also in Our Magazines, Stores, or otherwise, in the promoting and ready Dispatch of Matters relating to Our laid Service, as to you shall iecin just and reasonable. And Likewise such Rewards, and Allowances to be given, made, and paid unto any of Our Officers, Storekeepers, Clerks, Labourers, or other Attendants on, and employed in Our said Service for extraordinary Services by them already done, or hereafter to be done, unto Us, or in Consideration of any Charge, I.ofs, or Damage fuliained by them, or any of them, in Onr said Service, as has been formerly accustomed, and to you shall feemjttft and reasonable; hereby approving, ratifying, and confirming what you have hitherto done in the Premises for Our Service; and for lb doing, this shall be, us well to you as to the Auditors of Onr Im-

prefts, and all other Our Officers and Ministers concerned in allowing and paving the said Engineers, Storekeepers, Clerks, Ministers, and other Attendants, their respective Pays, Salaries, and Wages upon the Quarter Books of Our said Office, or otherwise, and for so long Time as We shall judge necessary, a full and sufficient War rent. Given at our Court at St. James's, the Ninth Day of March 1761, in the First Year of Our Reign.

By His Majesty’s Command,

Yonr Committee then called for an Account of the Salaries, paid by Debenture, and distinct from the Establishment in the Quarter Books, for the Years 1757 and 1762; and, on comparing them together, the Salaries in the First amounted to £.4,934 i8r. 6d. and in the last to £.8,735 17 s.9rf.; which Accounts are annexed to their Report N° V. and VI.

Your Committee would gladly have extended their Inquiry to the State of the Stores, and the Method of Receipts and Deliveries in that important Branch; and a Variety of other Matter hath occurred, which would have rendered their Report much more satisfactory, if they had been less confined in Time. But your Committee beg leave to observe, that, if the Practice of employing the same Tradesmen by the Master General’s Signification had been less frequent, if the Method of regulating the Prices of Commodities by a low Standard In an Office Book, and afterwards relieving the Trades-men by an Allowance of Money upon the Report of inferior Officers, had been altogether laid aside, and more open Bargains for Contracts had been made, agreeably to His Majesty’s Instructions, all engrossing would have been prevented, due Encouragement given to new Proposals, the Board would have been better served, and considerable Sums fared to the Public.

I am persuaded that the short Time you have been in this Country, you have seen enough to convince you, that performing this Service by Coin raft will be greatly to the Advantage of the Public; and it ascertains the Expence, which at present is not known. I beg to have your Answer as soon as possible, that I may know what Preparations to make, in case you agree to this Propofol.

I am, SCc.

Signed Laws Dundas,

Each Driver at 1 s. per Day.

Each Conductor at per Day.

The Committee -think proper to observe, That although they have taken the Gross Sums of the Revenue and Expence, yet the feverat Particulars, of which the same are composed, are specified in the Papers to this Report annexed.

Upon a Consideration of the Inquiry made into the Management of the above Trusts, the Committee have come to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in most of the Turnpikes the Money has not been so properly managed as it might have been.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Trustees of the several Trusts have not given due Attendance at the public Meetings.

Ordered, That the Collectors do give Security in the Sum of Fifty Pounds:

That the said Bonds, when executed, be delivered to the Clerk for the Time being, and that they remain in his Hands, in Trust for the Trustees:

That no Person be employed hereafter, as a Collector, but such as can read and write:

That a little blank Paper Book be given to each of the Collectors to keep their Accounts in; and that they take Care to enter the several Sums that they shall daily collect at the several Turnpike Gates, in order to account, on Oath, for all Sums they tlia.ll receive:

That for all Droves of Cattle passing through the Turnpike Gates, the Tickets that shall be delivered on shall be

in Force till Monday Noon following, and the Tickets that shall be delivered for Droves of Cattle every other Day, besides Saturday, shall be in Force till the Day following at Noon.

That no Collector shall leave his Duty on account of Sickness, or other Inability, without fending to the Treasurer or Supervisor for another Person to discharge that Duty; which Person shall account, on Oath, in the same Manucr as the rest of the Collectors do*.

That upon Reviews, Ilorfe Races, and other 1 ublic Occasions, there shall 1 Hi Two or more additional Persons employed at Hay Hill and Knifing!on Gates, betides the present Collectors, to atlirt in taking the 'loll, under the Direction of the Super- vil'or, Surveyor, or either of them, who are likewise to attend at the said Gates; that is, One of them at each Gate, on such extraordinary Occasions, and take the Money immediately as collected from the Collectors:

79 23 That I.he Treasurer, or his Clerk, do

give Receipts to each Collector for the several Sums he shall receive of them, and that the Collectors do deliver Inch Receipts to the Secretary, in order to charge the Treasurer with the Money received for Toll:

24 That the Secretary compare such Receipts, with their Accounts, to which they are monthly sworn:

That no Collet-for do presume to go off Duty till properly relieved by the other Collector in Turn:

That no Collector do presume to employ any Person to collect in his Stead, nor any Supernumerary Collet-for to go upon I)a‘y, and collect Money, at any Turnpike Gate, without a particular Order from the Tiea-fuier or Supervisor for that Purpose; and that no Collet-for’s Wife or Child do, upon any Pretence whatsoever, receive or collect Toll Money at the Gates, nor be allowed to continue in any Turnpike House, but 011I v to bring her Husband Necessaries when on Duty:

26c 5 That no Collector shall discover to any

other Collector the Amount of his Day’s or Week’s Collection; and in case they presume so to do, they will be dilmiiTed the Service of this Trust:

12 That the Supervisor do, at all future Meetings, report what Supernumeraries, from Time to Time, have been employed, in whose Places, and at what Gates:

13 That all Supernumeraries as shall be put upon Duty, do, at the next Board, attend, in order to swear to their Accounts; and that the Secretary take care they have Notice accordingly:

389 14 That in appointing any Supernumerary

to do Duty for a Rationed Collector, particular Regard be had to Precedency; and that they be put on Duty in Turn, according as they Hand in Priority, upon the Lift settled for that Purpose:

That, for the future, at such Gates where Two Collectors are on Duty at the same Time, that One of the Collectors do alternately take and receive all the Toll collected within the Space of Twenty-four Hours, being the Time they continue on Duty; and that if, for the Sake of Dispatch, it becomes necessary for the other Collector to receive any Part of the Toll that he do immediately deliver the fa ne over to the Collector, whole Turn it shall oe to rece.vc* the Collection of the Day* and that the Supervisor do take partial tlle Order be duly

That each Collector on Duty do mark with Ink the Number of every Hackney Coach as shall pass through the Turnpike Gate, on the Back of the Ticket, which shall be delivered, in order to prevent Frauds from the Sale or Delivery of Tickets by the Hackney Coachmen, and in same of his neglecting so to do, he shall be dismissed.

That Collectors of this Toll do carefully observe and take Notice of all Annoyances that may pass through the Turnpike Gates, or be cast on the Road, and use their utmost Endeavours to discover the Offenders, and give immediate Notice thereof to the Supervisor, that the Board may be acquainted, from Time to Time, of the fame.

That no Collector, under this Trust, do presume to suffer any Person or Persons, under any Pretence whatsoever, to abide, loiter, or remain in any of the Turnpike Houses, but that they do refuse Admittance to any Person or Persons who shall attempt to enter the fame; and that any Collector who shall neglect to put in Force this Resolution, shall incur the severest Censure of this Board.

Complaint being made, that the Collectors had demanded Money of the Passengers in Hackney Coaches which had paid Toll, and for which a Ticket of the Day was produced by the Coachman, with a fraudulent Design;

That if any Collector, for the future, flndl commit, or be any ways concerned in such a Fraud, by demanding Money of the Passengers, in such same such Collector shall, upon Proof thereof, be discharged from his said Office; and that Notice hereof be given to each Collector.

That, for the future, the several Collectors be relieved from Duty at the Hour of Eight o’clock in the Morning, from ift November to ift February, annually; and at the Hour of Seven in the Morning, for the Residue of the Year.

11 That no Collector do absent himself from

Duty, under Pretence of going to Dinner, or otherwise, during the Time appointed for his Attendance at the Gate, by Day or Night, but that every Collector do take Care to provide himself with all Necessaries of which he may be in Want during the Time of his Continuance on Duty.

31 That Two Collectors constantly attend,

and appear on Duty at Hyde Park and singlon Gates, by Night as well as by Day; and that in same of any Neglect herein, such Collector, who shall absent himself in the Night Season, shall be forthwith discharged; and that this Order be fixed up in each of the said Turnpike Htfufes, and that the Supervisor do take especial Care that the above Order be duly observed.

15 That the Boxes in which the Tickets are

That the Number of the Supernumerary Collectors do not, for the future, exceed Twenty-four Persons; and that such Gentlemen of this Trust, who have a Right to nominate new Trustees, shall be intitled to appoint a Supernumerary upon a Vacancy, in the Order, and according to the Precedency in which each shall (land on the Alphabetical List of Trustees for the Time being, intituled to such Nominations, and not otherwise; and that each Supernumerary, who shall for the future be named, do, at the Time of such Nomination, or at the next Board, appear at the Board, and, if approved, his Deputation shall be immediately made out.

That no Person who shall be discharged for a Breach of Trust from the Service of this Trust, shall be admitted into any Employment under it for the future.

That if any Collector, for the future, shall, upon any Pretence whatsoever, absent himself from his Duty at the Gate, where stationed, either by Day or Night, without proper Leave, that he be suspended immediately, and reported at the next Board; and in case of Leave, not till the Person who is to succeed attends.

That if any such Neglect shall happen at a Gate where there are Two Collectors stationed, the Collector not absenting himself do forthwith acquaint the proper Officer, by Notice under* his Hand, therewith; and whether any, and which Supernumerary attends; and where there is but One Collector stationed at a Time, that the other Collector shall fend such Notice as soon as such Absence shall come to his Knowledge.

That the Supernumerary who shall, unauthor i fed, do Duty for such absent Collector, be, for such Offence, struck out of his proper Place in the Supernumerary Lift, and put Two Turns or Removes lower thereon, and from that Day lose his Rank accordingly; but if he be the last Supernumerary, or the lad but one, that he be then struck off the said Lift.

That a List of the Supernumerary Collectors be stuck up at all the Turnpike Houses, and be continued and filled up, from Time to Time, with the Names of such new ones as may be hereafter appointed.

Resolved, That in case any Supernumerary Collector shall be called upon Duty in Turn, and refuse to come, without a reasonable Excuse, to be allowed by the next Board, that he be put by the Supervisor at the Bottom of the Supernumerary Lift; and that when the Supervisor calls such a Supernumerary on Duty, he shall acquaint him with-this Resolution, and that a Copy hereof be forthwith fixed up in the Turnpike Houses.

Committees.

Ordered, That in any Committee hereafter to be appointed, all Trustees that think fit to attend, have Voices.

That, upon a View or Notice of any Encroachment, or Annoyance, that may happen upon the Road during the Times of the Adjournment of this Trust, That the Secretary or Surveyor do apply to the Chairman of the last preceding General Meeting for his Directions thereupon, and in case of the Absence of such Chairman, that he, or they, do immediately cause to be summoned Twelve of the Trustees, residing near the Place where such Encroachment or Annoyance shall happen; which said Trustees (whereof Three to be a Quorum) are desired to meet, and view the fame, and are hereby impowered to give such Orders thereupon for remedying and removing the fame, as shall appear to be immediately necessary; and that they do report their Proceedings to the next Board.

That the Clerk write to the several Proprietors of Bills of Credit to be paid off, to acquaint them with the Time and Place of Payment, and the Numbers ordered to be paid off.

Trustees to be nominated.

That all Vacancies of Trustees shall be filled up by such Persons as shall be nominated by the Trustees next in Turn on the Alphabetical List; and that no new Alphabetical List be made till all the Trustees whose Names are therein specified, have had their Turn of proposing or nominating a ngw Trustee, for the Approbation of the Board; and that every Trustee be proposed at One Board, and ballotted for at the Board following.

That no Trustee shall have a Right to propose a new Trustee, to fill up any Vacancy, although his Name flia.ll stand inserted in the Alphabetical List, unless such Trustee shall have attended some General Meeting of the Board, within the Space of One Year preceding such Vacancy.

That in case any Trustee, whose Turn it shall be, according to the Alphabetical List, to nominate a new Trustee upon any Vacancy, shall neglect to make such Nomination at the First or Second General Meeting of the Board, after Notice given him for that Purpose, such Trustee shall forfeit his Right of Nomination for that Turn, which shall go over to the next Trustee upon the Lift.

That the Secretary do give Notice at every General Meeting of such Vacancies in this Trust as shall happen to come to his Knowledge, in order to his receiving the Di-regions of the Board about notifying the fame.

That, notwithstanding the foregoing Ke-solutions. Two Vacancies be always kept open, and left to be supplied by the General Board of Trustees.

After which His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot put an End to this Session of Parliament, ,$

without expressing My Thanks for the signal Zeal and Speech.8

8 F Dispatch

Parliament

prorogued.

666 \fAprilis — ifjunii — 6°SeptemiiaOBobris.A.i-]6T).

Di(patch which you have manifested in your Proceed ings, and which make it minecessary for Vie to continue it any longer.

I informed you, at your first Meeting, that Preliminary Articles were signed by My Minister, and those of France and Spain.I ordered them to be laid beforeyou; and the Satisfaction which I felt at the approaching He* establishment of Peace, upon Conditions so honourable to My Crown, and so beneficial to My People, was 'highly increased by My receiving from both Houses of Parliament the strongest and most grateful Expressions of their intire Approbation: These Articles have been established, and even rendered still more advantageous to My Subjects, by the Definitive Treaty; and My Expectations have been fully answered by the happy Effects which the several Allies of My Crown have derived from this salutary Measure: The Powers at War with My good Brother the King of have been

induced to agree to such Terms of Accomodation, as that great Prince has approved; and the Success which has attended My Negotiation has necessarily, and immediately, difi'uled the Blessmgs of Peace through every Part of Europe.

I acquainted you with My firm Resolution to form Mv Government on a Plan of ftrid (Economy: The Reductions necessary for this Purpose shall be completed with ail possible Expedition; and although the Army, maintained in these Kingdoms, will be inferior in Number to that usually kept, up in former Times of Peace, yet Itrufi that the Force proposed, with the Establish-roent of the national Militia, (whose Services I have experienced, and cannot too much commend) will prove a sufficient Security for the future.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have seen, with the highest Concern, the great Anticipations of the Revenue, and the heavy Debts unprovided for, during the late War, which have reduced you to the unhappy Necessity of imposing further Burthens upon My People: Under these Circumstances it is My earnest Willi to contribute, by every Means, to their Relief: The utmost Frugality shall be observed in the Disposition of the Supplies which you have granted; and when the Accounts of the Money arising from the Sale of such Prizes as are vested in the Crown shall be closed, it is My Intention to direct that the Produce shall be applied to the Public Service.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Extension of the Commerce of My Subjects, the Improvement of the Advantages we have obtained, and the Increase of the Public Revenue, are the proper Works of Peace: To these important, and necessary Objects, My Attention shall be directed: I depend upon your constant Care to promote in your several Counties that Spirit of Concord, and that Obedience to Law, which is efl'ential to good Order, and to the Happiness of My faithful Subjects: It is your Part to discourage every Attempt of a contrary Tendency; it shall be mine firmly to maintain the Honour of My Crown, and to protect the Rights of My People.

After which the Lord Chancellor by His Majesty’s Command, said.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the 23d Day of June next, to be then here held; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thursday the 23d Day of June next.

The King’s Mr. Speaker reported, That the House attended His Speech Majesty, Yesterday, in the House of Poors; where His reported. Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent MMakes, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

The Re-establishment of the pubJicTranquillity, upon Terms of Honour, and of Advantage to My Kingdoms, was the first great Object of My Reign: That faJutary Measure has received the Approbation of My Parliament; and has since been happily completed, and carried into Execution by the Definitive Treaty. It has been, and shall be, My Endeavour to insure the Continuance of the Peace, by a faithful and steady Adherence to the Conditions upon which it was concluded; and I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that the several Powers of Europe, who were engaged against Us in the late War, have given Me the Itrongeft Affu-Vol. 29.

ranees of the same good Disposition. Our principal Care ought now to be employed to improve the valuable Acquifttions which We have made, and to cultivate the Arts of Peace in such a Manner, as may most effectually contribute to extend the Commerce, and to augment the Happiness of My Kingdoms.

For these great Purposes 1 have called you together.

It will ever be My earned Willi and Endeavour to demonstrate to My People, by My Actions, the Love which I bear them; and I doubt not of receiving from them the grateful and just Returns of Duty and Affection.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I will order the proper Estimates for the Service of the Year to be laid before you. The heavy Debts contracted in the course of the late War, for many of which no Provision is yet made, call for Our utmost Attention, and theftriCleft Frugality. I mull, however, earnestly recommend to you the Support of My Fleet, to which Our pall Succofies have been so much owing, and upon which the future Welfare and Importance of Great Britain do most essentially depend. To ease My People of some Part of these Burthens, I have directed, as I promilbd at the end of the last Session of Parliament, that the Money arising from the Sale of the Prizes vested in the Crown should he applied to the public Service. It is my Intention to reserve, for the same Use, whatever Sums shall be produced by the Sale of any of the Lands belonging to Me in the jftands of the West Indies, which were ceded to Us by the late Treaty.

The Improvement of the Public Revenue, by such Regulations as shall be judged most expedient for that Purpose, deserves your serious Consideration. This will be the surest Means of reducing the National Debt, and of relieving My Subjects from those Burthens, which the Expences of the late War have brought upon them; and will, at the same Time, establish the public Credit upon the most solid Foundation.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

As the Interests and Prosperity of My People are the foie Objects of My Care, I have only to desire that you will pursue such Measures as are conducive to those Ends, with Dispatch and Unanimity. Dom^ftic Union will be essentially necessary to remedy those Evils which are the Consequences of War; to enable us to reap the most permanent Advantages from the Con-elusion of the Peace; and to discourage that licentious Spirit which is repugnant to the true Principles of Liberty, and of this happy Constirution. In this Opinion, I trnlt that My Subjects will be confirmed by your Example; and that they will be taught by your Proceedings, to unite their utmost Endeavours to sup-. port Inch Measure* as may equally tend to the Honour and Dignity of My Crown, and to their own Security and Happiness.

And the said Petition was read; taking Notice of the Act of lad SdTion, for granting to His Majesty several additional Duties uponWines imported into this Kingdom*, and certain Duties upon all Cyder and Perry; and for raising the Sum of Three Millions, Five Hundred Thousand Pounds, byway of Annuities and Lot-

teries, to be charged on the said Duties: And representing to the House, that such of the Rates and Duties by the said Act granted as are charged upon Cyder and Perry, are appointed to be under the Receipt and Management of the Commissioners and Officers of His Majesty’s Revenue of Excise; and ti?e Makers of Cyder and Perry are, by the said Act, made liable to the Search, Survey, and Control of the Officers of Excise, and to divers Forfeitures and Penalties to be infiifted and recovered without the Intervention of a Jury, by summary Methods of Proceeding unknown to the Common Law; and that the Petitioners have been informed that that Mode of collecting the said Duties is an intolerable Burthen to the Farmers, and other Occupiers of Orchard Ground, who, as the Makers of Cyder and Perry, are immediately affected by it; and alleging. That the Petitioners, though not immediately affected by it in its present Operation, are deeply interested therein, as it is a Precedent of an Extension of Excise Laws, which, under any Circum-stancas, bear so hard upon the Liberty of the Subject, as scarcely to be deemed less burthensome, grievous, and prejudicial to the Kingdom, than the Tenures which they abolished; and as this Precedent appears to the Petitioners to have a very general, dangerous, and alarming Tendency, they have therefore thought it their Duty (having regard to the Rank they bear amongst His Majesty's Subjects) to be the earliell in their humble Application to this House, to obtain a Repeal of so much of the said Act as subjects the Makers of Cyder and Perry to the Excise Laws, in the fullcft Confidence that the House will listen to the Petition of any of His Majesty’s Subjects, in a same where they think themselves, or any of their Fellow Subjects, aggrieved, and more efpeeiaWy where their Liberties are concerned: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration, and to grant such Relief therein as so the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, that he had a Message from His Majesty to this* House, signed by His Majesty: And he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker, all the Members of the House being uncovered; and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGER.

His Majesty having received Proposals for a Marriage between her Ubyai Highness the Princess Augvfta, and his Serene Highness the Hereditary Prince of Brunswic and Lunenburg-, and having been pleased favourably to accept and agree to the fame: has thought it proper to communicate His Intentions to this House: And as His Majesty cannot doubt but that this Alliance with so considerable and distinguished a Protestant Family will be to the general Satisfaction of all His Subjects, He promises himself the Concurrence and Assistance of this House, in enabling Him to give such a Portion to His eldest Sifter, as may be suitable to the Honour and Dignity of the Crown.

/ R.

Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That an humble

Address be presented to His Majesty, to return His Majesty the Thanks of this House for His most gracious Communication of the intended Marriage between her Royal Highness the Princess His Majesty’s eldest Sifter, and his most Serene Highness the Hereditary Prince o i Bruns and Lunenburg.

'Fo express the intire Satisfaction of this House at the Prospectof this Alliance with so illustrious a Pro-toliant Family, which has so signally distinguished itself in the Defence of the Liberties of Europe-, and to af-sure His Majesty that this House will enter into the immediate Consideration of this important Affair, in such a Manner as shall demonllrate the Zeal, Duty, and Affection of this House to His Majesty, a just Sense of the eminent Virtues and Merit of her RoyalHighness, and a due Regard to the Honour and Dignity of His Majesty’s Family.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw up an Address, to be presented to His Majesty, upon the said Resolution:

And a Committee was appointed of The Marquis of Granby, Sir James Loivtlier, Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Townshend, Mr. Legge, Mr. Pelham, Lord North, Mr. Hunter, Mr. Mr. Peter

Burrell, Mr. Whichcot, Mr. General

head, Mr. Thomas Townshend, Junior, Lord Garlics, Mr. Jenkinson, Lord George Mr. Nugent,

The Marquis of Granby reported from the Committee appointed this Day to draw up an Address to be presented to His Majesty, that the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s -Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz. (

May it please Your Majesty,

We, Your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return Your Majesty the Thatnks of this House, for Your most gracious Communication of the intended Marriage between her Royal Highness the Princess Augvfta, Your Majesty’s eldest Sifter, and his most Serene Highness the Hereditary Prince ;of Brunswic and Lunenburg.

Permit us to express our intire Satisfaction at the Prospect of this Alliance with so illustrious a Protestant Family; which has so signally distinguished itself in the Defence of the Liberties of Europe-, and to allure Your Majesty that we will enter into the immediate Consideration of this important Affair, in such Manner as shall demonllrate our Zeal, Duty, and Affection to Your Majesty, a just Sense of the eminent Virtues and Merit of her Royal Highness, and a due Regard to the Honour and Dignity of Your Majesty’s Family.

The said Address being read a Second Time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente. That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Address to be presented to His Majesty.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by the whole House.

Ordered, That such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council do humbly know his Majesty’s Pleasure when he will be attended by this House.

Ordered, That His Majesty’s most gracious'Message, of this DaV, be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House. to whom it is referred to consider of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Thursday Morning next. Nine of the Clock.

Lord Bitncnlmo Bertie presented to the House, according to Order, a Bill for dividing and inclosing the Open Common Fields, Common Meadows, and other Commonable Linds, in the Parish of , in the County of Lincoln: And the same was received} and read the First Time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second Time.

A IVtitisn of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint at Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; Setting for:It, That the Inhabitants of the said Parish. from its Situation in the Neighbourhood of London, are greatly exposed to Burglaries and Outrages; and that if the said Parish was lighted, and a well regulated Watch kept therein, it would, in a great Moa-sure, prevent the said Evils; and that the Poor of the said Parish are very numerous, and might be better managed, and regulated, if fullicieut Powers were given for that Purpose; and that, if the Petitioners were impowered to make Hates for defraying the Expences of lighting and watching the said Parish, and for the Relief and Employment of the said Poor, it would greatly tend to the Safety and Advantage of the Petitioners, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid, under such Regulations as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Conluleration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the I louse:

The Lortli North reported, that the Managers had met the Lords at the Conference; which was to acquaint this House, That the Lords have taken into ConiideKAtion the printed Paper, intituled, " The North Briton, N° 45," delivered by the Commons on Friday last at the Conference; as also the Three Resolutions of the House of Commons thereupon, communicated at the same Conference; which Resolutions the Lords have agreed to, by filling up the Blanks with " Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and"

Ditto. Resolved, That the printed Paper, intituled, " The North Briton, N° 45," winch was communicated to the Lords at the last Conference, be burnt by the Hands of the Common Hangman at the Royal Exchange, in London, upon Saturday next, at One of the Clock; and that the Sheriffs of London do then attend, and cause the same to be burnt there accordingly.

Ordered, That the Concurrence of the Lords be desired to the said Resolution.

D;«o. Resolved, Nemine Contradicente, That an humble Ad-

dress be presented to His Majesty, to acquaint His Majesty, that, having taken into our Consideration a late false, scandalous, and seditious Libel, intituled, ic The North Briton, N' 45," we think it our indilr penfable Duty to express our Surprise and Indignation at finding, that neither the Public nor Private Vir-

tues, which so eminently entitle His Majesty to the higlieft Veneration, as well as to the most grateful and local Attachment of all His Subjects; nor the gracious Expressions of His tender Care and Affection for His People, in His Majesty’s Speech from 'he Fhro.ie, at the End of the Iail Session of Parliament, which Ins been thus infamously traduced; should have been fufti-eient to feciire His Majesty f.’oin so insolent, and unexampled an Indignity: That such, indee I, has been His Majesty’s uniform Adherence to the Principles of our happy Cunstitution; and Inch the uninterrupted Harmony and good Correspondence between His Majesty ami His Parliament; that it is no wonder to fee, that the same audacious Hand, which hath dared thus grossly to affront His Majesty, should, at the same Time, violate the other say.od Regards prescribed by the Laws and Constitution of this Country; alperfing and calumniating every Branch of the Legislature; and endeavouring to excite, amongst all Ranks, of His Majesty’s Subjects, such a Spirit of Discord and Disobedience, as could end in nothing but the total Subverlion of all lawful Government.

'Fo express also to His Majesty, our firm Persuasion and just Confidence, that this moll extravagant and' outrageous Attempt will prove as impotent as it js wicked; that, instead of answering the Purposes for which it appears to have been calculated, it will, on the contrary, lerve to excite, in His faithful Subjects, the Abhorrence of such dangerous Practices; to unite them more firmly in their zealous Attachment to His Majesty’s Person and Government, and in a due Reverence for the Authority of the Legislature; and laiily, that, in Consequence of His Majesty’s Directions to prosecute the Authors of this infamous Libel, it will bring such Punishment upon those who shall be found guilty of so atrocious a Crime, as the Laws of their Country have prescribed, and as the public Justice and Safety shall demand.

Ordered, That a Committee be appointed to draw* up an Address, to be presented to His Majesty, upon the said Resolution.

Ordered, That the Managers who managed the last Conference, be the said Committee.

And they are to withdraw immediately into the Speaker’s Chamber.

Mr. Speaker reported, that both Houses had attended His Majesty with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give tins most gracious Answer:

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The very affectionate Zeal which you express for the Vindication of My Honour, and your declared Refo-Jution to support the Authority of Parliament, cannot fail of being extremely grateful to Me: It has been hitherto, and it always shall be. My Care, to regulate My Conduct according to the Principles of the Coniti-tution: I will not therefore be wanting in carrying the Laws into Execution, against all who shall presume to violate any of those Principles; and, in this Resolution, I doubt not of receiving the hearty Concurrence and Support, both of My Parliament and My People.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to considerof the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as folio weth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Sum of Eighty thou fund Pounds be granted to His Majesty, for the Marriage Portion of her Royal Highness the Prineefs Augusta, His Majesty’s eldest Sifter.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Sixteen thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Sixty-four, including Four thousand Two hundred Eighty-seven Marines.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per Month, be allowed for maintaining the said Sixteen thousand Men, for Thirteen Months, including Ordnance for Sea Service.

The first Resolution of the Committee being read a second Time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth

agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the Sum of Eighty thousand Pounds be granted to His Majesty, for the Marriage Portion of Her Royal Highness the Prineefs Augusta, His Majesty’s eldest Sifter.

The subsequent Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That the proper Officer do lay before this House, an Account of the Number of Gallons of Brandies and Rum imported, from Midsummer 1761, to Midsummer 1762; and from Midsummer 1762, to Midsummer 1763; distinguishing each Article, and each Year.

Ordered, That the proper Officer do lay before this House, an Account of the Nett Receipt of the Customs, from Midsummer 1761, to Midsummer 1762; and from Midsummer 1762, to Midsummer 1763; distinguishing each Article, mid each Year.

A Motion was made, and the Question being proposed, that the proper Officers do lay before this House, an Account of all such of His Majesty’s Ships and Vessels, as are now employed in the Smuggling

Service, inserting their particular Stations, their Built, Burthen, Draught of Water, when complete for Service, Complements of Men, and the particular Orders and Instructions they have received; as also an Account of all such Ships or Vessels as are now building, either in His Majesty’s Yards, or by Contract, and defined for the said Smuggling Service; together with an Estimate of the Expence of building and fitting out each separate Vessel so employed, or designed to be employed, on that Service;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " inserting their " particular Stations."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put. thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " and the particular Orders and Infiructions they have received."

And the said Amendment was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Then the main Question, thus amended, was, by Leave of the House, withdrawn.

Mr. Cooke reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and principal Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint John at Hackney, in the County of Middlesex, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he reiul the Report in his Place j and afterwards delivered it in at the ..Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

In support of the Allegations of the said Petition, Lcivis Jones, Esquire, being examined, said, that the Parish of Hackney is large and populous, and greatly exposed to Robberies, and Outrages; which would in a great measure be prevented, if the said Parish was lighted, and a regular Watch established.

That the Poor of the said Parish are very numerous^ and might be put under much better Regulations than they are at present, with Respect both to their Relief and Employment; but that the Inhabitants are unable to defray the Expences necessary for the Relief and Employment of the Poor, and of lighting and watching the said Parish, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

Mr. Dann confirmed the above Evidence in every Particular.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for maintaining, regulating, and employing the Poor within the Parish of Saint John at Hackney, in the County of Middlesex; and for lighting the said Parish, and establishing a regular nightly Watch therein: And that Mr. Cooke and Sir William Beauchamp Proctor do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, the Gentlemen, Clergy, and other the principal Inhabitants, of the City and County of the City of Exeter, met at the Guildhall of the said City the 12th . Day of November t 763, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners being, by their Situation in the Heart of one of the principal Cyder Counties, Eye Witnesses of the great Distress already brought on that County by the new Duty of Excise laid on Cyder and Perry, by an Act pafl'ed in the laliSelfion of Parliament, beg Leave to represent, that its Continuance mull inevitably be attended with the , moll ruinous Consequences, in which the Petitioners . the.nselves will also be deeply involved; and that the Amount, of the said new Duty will, taking one Year with another, be at least equal to the whole Rent of those Lands, on the Product of which it is laid; and that, inch the largest Proportion of the Amount of the said Duty, falls on the ordinary kind of Cyder, consumed by the Land Occupier, his Family, and La-. bourers, and by the poorer Sort of People; and that it must therefore of Necessity affett very injuriously the whole Agriculture of that Part of the Kingdom, already much inure expensive than that of almost any other Part of it, from the Dearness of Manure, and the peculiar Manner of Cultivation, which the Nature of the Soil, and the Circumstances of the Lands absolutely require; that the Price of that Cyder, when it can be fold, foaree ever exceeds the double Amount of - the Duty, and in very plentiful Years is less than even the Duty itself, and that it is therefore utterly incapable of bearing this very heavy Burthen; the unavoida-. ble Coulcquence of which will be* the reducing the . Land Occupier to the Necessity of abandoning for the future that Part of his Cultivation, and of substituting in its Place a Malt Liquor of such Quality, as will be much cheaper to him; and the Land Owner, to that of submitting to such an Abatement in his Kent, as will leave such Orchards on the same Foot, in yearly Value, as other Lands; and that the Cyder made for Sale usually bears a Price considerably higher than such Malt Liquor, as would fully an liver the same Purposes; and therefore can near no additional Burthen by any Duty whatever, since the whole of such Burthen must ne-cellarily fall as a Dead Loss upon the Grower, who will of Course lav bold of the first Opportunity of throwing it upon the Land Owner; and that, as the Rents of the Land Owner will be thereby funk, at least, Ten per Cent, at a Medium, though fti'l charged with the same Land Tax, and public Assessments of every kind as before, he will* in his Turn, find it his Interest to get rid of the great and now useless Expence of supporting his Orchards; and will therefore cither immediately eradicate them, or at least suffer them gradually to decay; and thus tl»e Product, both of the Orchards ami the Duty, will in a few Years be equally annihilated, and the Lands employed to some other Culture; and that the present Duty on Cyder, is considerably higher than double the Duty paid on Malt and Hops for the same Quantity of Malt Liquor, of nearly the same Quality, and applicable to the same Lies; and that the laying a Duty upon Plantations, already made at an immoderate Expence, and which appear to be intitled in common Justice to the same Exemption from being taxed, as a Stock of Goods of any kind, laid in by the Trader, especially where there cannot be the least hope of a Reimbursement, seems contrary to that Spirit of Equity, by which our Laws have been hitherto distinguished, and must prove an effectual Bar to every future attempt towards further Improvements; and that this moil extraordinary Extension of the grievous Hardships and Rigours of the Excite Laws, to the Houses and Property of the Nobility, Gentry, Clergy, Freeholder's, Farmers, and even of many of the Cottagers, not only deprives at once a very considerable Part of His Majesty’s faithful Subjects of the most valuable Privileges derived to them /H>m our excellent Constitution, but must equally alarm the whole Kingdom, by establishing an unanswerable Precedent for ev°ry future Extension of those Laws, which may be projected till that Extension becomes universal: And therefore praying the House to take the Preitvfes into their fei ious Consideration; and to grant the Petitioners such Relief therein, as to the House shall seem meet.

Refoked, Nemine Contradicente, That the Sheriffs of TheSW

London and Middlesexhave conducted themselves with of LwW proper Spirit and Vigour in the Execution of the Orders of both Houses of Parliament, for burning "the North Briton, N° 45," on Saturday last: And that Mr. Speaker do return them the Thanks of this House for their good Behaviour therein.

And Mr. Alderman Harley, a Member of this House,

One of the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex, being in the House, Mr. Speaker acquainted him with the said Resolution; and gave him the Thanks of the House, accordingly, as followeth; viz.

Mr. Sheriff Harley,

Upon the Inquiry which this House has made, into a very high Insult lately offered to the Authority of Parliament, and the Laws of the Land, they could not pass by unnoticed, the zealous Endeavours of yourself and your worthy Colleague in Support of both: But, as I cannot better express the Sense, which this House has of your Conduct, on this Occasion, than in their own Words, I will read to you. Sir, the Resolution to which they have just now agreed.

Refoked, Nemine Contradicente, That the Sheriffs of London and Middlesex have conducted themselves with proper Spirit and Vigour, in the Execution of the Orders of both Houses of Parliament, for burning "the North Briton, N* 45," on Saturday last: And that Mr. Speaker do return them the Thanks of this House for their good Behaviour therein.

That

’> *$'

W;

Geo. III. 8* — o° Dece. 099

That Spirit of Licentiousness, which so unhappily prevails at present, however it may be disguisetl under the specious Name of Liberty, is diametrically opposite to, and fubvcrfive of, it; and unless a feasonable Check is put to this Spirit, it cannot fail of ending in Anarchy, the sure Forerunner of the rankest Tyranny and Def-potism.

True Liberty confifis in that Security, which the Laws and our happy Constitution give us, for our Persons, our Lives, and our Property; nor can this valuable Bleifing be preferred without a due Veneration for the legislative Authority of the Kingdom, and a perfect Obedience to the Law. Thefewill be kept up, if the civil Magistrates (especially those who fill that high and important Station, to which you have been called by your Fellow Citizens) faithfully discharge the Trull repo fed in them.

How great therefore, Sir, must your Merit be, who, in defence of Parliament and the Law, have, with a truly becoming Fortitude and Resolution, exposed your Person to the greatest Danger, from the Fury and Resentment of a lawless Mob. Such Merit is intitled to the highest Reward: You cannot receive a greater and more honourable one (and I am persuaded. Sir, you are of that Opinion) than the Approbation of live ' Commons of Great Britain.

The Commands of this House will be always obeyed by me with the greatest Pleasure, but I think myself particularly happy to receive them upon the prefect Occasion; I could only have wished I had not been so suddenly called upon, that I might have endeavoured at least, to have performed this Duty in a manner more suitable to the House as well as to yourself: However, in tl»e bell Manner I am able, upon so short a Recollection, I do, in Obedience to those Orders, return you, Sir, the unanimous Thanks of this House, for the Spirit and Vigour, with which you conduced yourself in the Execution of the Orders of b rth Houses of Parliament, for burning the North N* 4^, on

Saturday last.

Upon which Mr. Alderman Harley said,

Mr. Speaker,

It is with the greatest Difficulty I now rife, toexprefs a due Sense of the high Honour which the House has now conferred upon me, by signifying their Approbation of my Conduct on Saturday last; I cannot help thinking, that the House has greatly overvalued my Services on that Occasion, and lamenting that it was not in my Power to put that Order in Execution, in a Manner more suitable to the Honour and Dignity of Parliament. The only Return that I can make for this lignal Mark of Favour, is, to afiilre the House, that so long as I continue in the high Office which I now bear in the City of London, I shall firmly, vigorously, and a&ively, fee the Laws carried into Execution, which are so essentially necessary for the good Order and Government of this Kingdom.

Give me Leave, Sir, to return you my sincere Thanks, for the very obliging Manner in which you have expressed yourself on this Occasion; and to assure you, that I shall ever retain a grateful Sense of it, and make it the Pride and Glory of my Life to deserve it.

A Petition of the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Mercers of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting, That by an Act passed in the 21st Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the Relief of the Annuitants of the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Mercers of the City of London, it is enacted, That the Duty of

Six-pence a Chaldron upon Coals, which by an Act of the Fifth and Sixth Years of King William and Queen Mary, for the Relief of the Orphans of the City of London, was granted to the City of London for a Term of Fifty Years to commence from the 29 th of September 1700, should be continued for the further Term of Thirty-five Years; and the Monies arising thereby he paid into the Receipt of the Chamber of London, and that the yearly Sum of £. 3000, out of the Produce of the said Duty, should, during the said additional Term, be paid, by the Chamberlain of London, to the Petitioners, by half yearly Payments, to be applied by them towards the Payment of their Annuitants, and other Creditors: and to that Purpose the Petitioners were directed, within One Month after Mich 1

to make out a general Account, in Manner in the Petition described, of all Sums that should be then due and in Arrear to the Petitioners Annuitants, and their Representatives; which Sums were thereby declared to be principal Sums, and to carry an Interest at Three per Cent, until the same should be paid and difehirged; and that after Michaelmas 1750, the Petitioners should apply the said yearly Sum of£. 3/100, in the First Place, towards Payment of so much of the Annuities which should from thenceforth become payable, by virtue of the Deeds of Settlement made for the Benefit of the Annuitants, as the Estates of the Petitioners in Set-

tlement would not be sufficient to satisfy; and that when the said yearly Sum of Three Thousand Pounds, together with the Rents and Profits of the Estates in Settlement, should be more than sufficient to pay the said Annuities, that then, as any Surplus should arise, and be sufficient to pay half a Year’s Interest, the Petitioners were required to apply such Surplus, as the same should come in, in the first Place, towards discharging the Interest, which, after Michaelmas 1750, shall grow due on the Sums of Money, which, at that Time, were due for the Arrears of the said Annuities before directed to be considered as Principal, until such Interest should be all paid, and after Payment thereof, and of the growing Interest thereon, such Surplus should, so often as the same would be sufficient to payTen Pounds per Cent.on the Principal, be applied to reduce and pay off the principal Sums, in an equal Proportion, until the w?hole should be fully paid and discharged; and that when the said yearly Sum of £.3,000, together with the Rents and Profits of the Estates in Settlement, should have paid and discharged all the Arrears of the said Annuities, and the Interest thereof, and should be more than sufficient annually to pay the respective Annuities, the Petitioners were required to reserve the Surplus arising from the said yearly Sum of£.3,000, to be applied to the Payment of such other Creditors of the Petitioners as should be deemed proper Objects of Relief, and in such Manner as should be directed by any future Act or Acts of Parliament; and alleging, that the Petitioners, by the Bounty of Parliament, wdiich they acknowledge with the greateftThankfulness, together with the Rents and Profits of their Estates in Settlement, have been enabled not only to discharge all the Arrears of the Annuities, with the Interest thereof, but have also duly and punctually paid their respective Annuities, and that there is at present a Surplus of 4000 reserved in the Hands of the Petitioners, arising from the said yearly Sum o {£.3000, to be applied by Parliament to the Payment of such other Creditors of the Petitioners as shall be deemed proper Objects of Relief; and representing to the House, that the said Surplus will annually inercafe; but the Petitioners cannot apply the same to the discharging of Debts due to any other of their Creditors, without the Authority of Parliament; and further representing, that the Petitioners are indebted in very considerable Sums of Money, for Charities, or Money Legacies, Bond Debts, and Ample Contraft Debts, which they have no other Way of satisfying than out of the Surplus resulting from their Estates in Settlement, which is very insufficient to discharge the fame; and therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant such Relief therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the feme, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of several of the Holders of the Navy and Victualling ^Bilfs, not subscribed into per Cent. Annuities, agreeable to tho'Directions of an Act passed in the Iaft Session of Parliament for that Purpose, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read: Taking Notice, That by the said Act it is ordered, that all Persons possessed of or interested in Navy or Victualling Bills, made out on or before 31 December

1762, carrying them to the proper Oflices at any Time on or before the 31st of March 1763, the Sums, with the Interest due thereon, should be made into Annuities, to bear Interest from the said 45th of

1763, at the Rate of per Cent, but that having omitted to subscribe their Bills as aforesaid, which they are willing to do, and to be put upon the same Footing with those already subscribed; therefore praying the House will take their same into Consideration and grant such Relief as the House shall think proper.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That there be laid before this House, an Account of Navy, Victualling, and Transport Bills, which were made out on or before the 31st Day of December 1762, and have not been converted into Annuities af7 ter the Rate of £. 4 per Centum, per Annum, pursuant to an Act made in the Iaft Session of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Order be discharged.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Complaint be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Monday the 13th Day of February next.

be lawfully resumed, or not; And that ‘many of the Truliees appointed by the said Act are now dead, and moll of those who are living, and qualified to act, have declined acting, alleging the Doubts, Uncertainties, and Ditficulties aforesaid; so that no Meeting of the said Trustees for putting the said A 6tin Execution hath beeu had since the Month

Fitzgerald’s \ Petition of Gerald Fitzgerald, of Rathrone, in the

Elutes. County of Meath, and Kingdom of Ireland, Esquire, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, gives His Consent that the House may do therein as they shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That King Charles the Second, by Letters Patent, dated 12th December, in the 36th Year of his Reign, granted unto Gerald Fitzgerald, the Petitioner’s Great Uncle, and to his Heirs and Assigns forever, the Town and Lands of Rathrone, and several other Lands' and Tenements in the Counties of Meath, Westmeath, Kildare, and Cavan, in the Kingdom of Ireland, subject to certain yearly Quit Rents; and that by a Family Settlement made in 1685, the said Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, so granted to the said Gerald Fitzgerald, were granted to Trustees, and their Heirs, to the Use of the said Gerald Fitzgerald for Life; Remainder, as to the Lands of Rathrone, to Mary his Wife, for her Jointure; Remainder, as to all the Lands therein comprised, to the First and other Sons of the said Gerald Fitzgerald in Tail Male; Remainder to Henry Fitzgerald, the Brother of the said Gerald Fitzgerald, for Life; Remainder to his First and other Sons in Tail Male, with several Remainders over to others of the Family; Reversion to the right Heirs of the said Gerald Fitzgerald; and that the said Henry Fitzgerald was outlawed for High Treason, on Account of the Rebellion which happened in Ireland in 1688, and his said

Estate in Remainder in the said Lands, his Brother the said Gerald Fitzgerald being the n, and for many Years after, living, became vested in the Trustees appointed by the Act of the nth and 12th of King William the Third, for the Sale of the forfeited Estates in Ireland j and that Gerald Fitzgerald the younger, and Edward Fitzgerald, the Sons of the said Henry Fitzgerald, being Minors, by William Fitzgerald their next Friend, on the 9th August 1700, did make and tender their Claim to the said Trustees, and proved the said Settlement of 1685 5 and the said Claim was heard, and determined by the said Trustees, on the 23d Day of March in 1701; and the said Trustees thereupon declared the said Gerald Fitzgerald the younger, and Edward Fitzgerald, respectively, to be intitled to an Estate in Tail Male, in the Lands and Premisses comprised in the said Settlement, expectant upon the Death of the said Gerald Fitzgerald the elder, and Henry Fitzgerald, who were both then living; and that the said Gerald Fitzgerald the elder, and Mary his Wife, and the said Henry Fitzgerald, died many Years ago, and the said Gerald Fitzgerald the elder died without KTue, and upon their Death, the said Gerald Fitzgerald the younger, who was the eldell Son of the said IIany Fitzgerald, and was also the Nephew and Heir at Law of the said Gerald Fitzgerald the elder, entered into, and became seised of an Estate in Tail Male of and in the f.tid Lands and Premisses, and levied several Fines, and fullered several common Recoveries of the said Lands and Premisses; and that by Deeds of Lease and Release, bearing Date, respectively, the 7th and 8th Days of April 1725, the said Gerald Fitzgerald the younger mortgaged great Part of the said Lands and Premisses to Elizabeth O'Farrell, the Widow of Major General O'Farrell, and her Heirs, for securing the Sum of £. 2,700, with Interest," and otherwise considerably incumbered the said Estate; and that the said Gerald Fitzgerald the younger died in 1729, leaving his eldell Son, the Petitioner his Second Son, and Christopher his Third Son; and the said John died without Jfiue soon after the Death of his Father; and thereupon the Petitioner became seised of and intitled to the said Lands and Premiires, subject to several Incumbrancs; and that the Petitioner is Grand Nephew and Heir at Law of the said Gerald Fitzgerald the elder, the Patentee; and the Petitioner hath levied several Fines, and fullered common Recoveries of several of the said Lands, and hath become personally liable for several of the Debts of the Petitioner’s Father, and also for Debts contrafted by the Petitioner; and alleging, that it hath been lately discovered, that the Reversion iu Fee of and in the said Lands and Premisses, expectant upon the Determination of the Estate in Tail Male veiled as aforesaid in the Sons of the said Heniy Fitzgerald, became vested in the said Trustees, and is now veiled, by the Act of the First and Second Year of Queen Anne, in the Crown, subject to the Orders of Parliament; and that the Petitioner has no other Fund or Expedient for Payment of his Father’s or his own Debts, or for securing the Petitioner’s Liberty, but by Sale or Mortgage of Part of the said Lands and Premisses; but no Person will deal with the Petitioner for the fame, until the Reversion in Fee thereof shall be divelled out of the Crown, and vested in the Petitioner, which cannot be done without the Aid of Parliament; and that it has been frequent in such Cases to shew Favour to Protestant Purchasers and Creditors: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for divesting the Reveifion in Fee of and in the said Lands and Premisses out of His Majesty, and for veiling the same in the Petitioner.

C.King.Esq. and Hejtcr Maria Salusbury, Administrators of the Estate and Effects of Cotton King, Esquire, deceased, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That Thomas King, late of Combermere, in the County Palatine of Chester, and then of Easthidc, in the County of Bedford, Esquire, did, in his Life-time, duly make and publish his Last Will and Testament, bearing Date the 1 ith Day of August 1733; and did (amongst other Things) devise and bequeath unto his Son Keating King, and the Issue Male of his Body in Tail Male successively, all his Lands, Tenements, and Hereditaments, and real Estate whatsoever, in the Kingdom of Ireland; and in his said Will did direct, that in case his said Son Keating King should die without such Issue Male of his Body as aforesaid living at his Death, then he gave and devised all his said real Estate in Ireland to his Son Richard King, and the Issue Male of his Body, successively, in Tail Male; and on Failure and Want of such Issue living at his Death, he gave and devised the same to his Son Cotton King, and the Issue Male of his Body, successively, in Tail Male; and for want of such Issue, he gave and devised the same to his own right Heirs for ever; and alleging, that the said Thomas King died, without having revoked his said Will, and that the said Keating King, Richard King, ami Colton King, are all dead, without Issue; and the said Cotton King dying without making any Will,

the Petitioners took opt Letters of Administration of the Estate and Effects of tj)e said Cotton King; and that the said Will hath beeh proved in the High Court of Chancery in Great Britain; and the Petitioners may have frequeut Occasion to produce or give the same in Evidence, as well in Great Britain as in Ireland; and the said Will cannot, as Occasion may from Time to Time require, be carried from one Kingdom to the other, fu as to be made use of at any Trial at Law, without great Hazard; nor can the Witnesses, who are able to prove the due Execution of the said Will, be compelled, by any Process, to attend in the said Kingdom of Ireland, to give their Testimony at any Trial at Law to be had there: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for making the Exemplification of the Last Will and Testament 01 the said Thomas King Evidence in all Courts of Law and Equity in Great Britain and Ireland.

A Petition of the Guardians of the Poor within the Hundreds of Colneis and Carlfo in the County of Suffolk, in their General Quarterly Meeting assembled, the 26th Day of December 1763, was presented to the House, and real; Set ting forth, That the Petitioners were incorporated by an Acr passed in the 29th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poorin the 1 lundredsofCo/wmand Carl-ford, in the County of Su folk; and that they have put the said Act, and the Powers thereby vested in them, as Guardians of the said Poor, in Execution, and have experienced the good Effects of it; but the Petitioners are subject to One considerable Expence, to which they apprehend it was not the Intention of the Motife to make them liable, viz they are required by the said

Act to lay their Accounts, and also the Rates made by them in pursuance of the said Act, every Quarter, before the Court of Quarter Sessions, for the Examination, Approbation, and Allowance of that Court; and the Court have obliged the Petitioners to apply, from Tim- to Time, by a Counsellor and Solicitor; and this Expence, added to the other Fees of the Court, at the Midsummer Sessions 1778, amounted to Five Guineas; and though the Clerk of the Peace hath since agreed to moderate his Fees, the Expence of having the Accounts and Rates allowed at the Quarter Sessions since Lady Day 1758, to this Michaelmas Sessions 1763, inclusive, amounts to £.73, and upwards; and therefore the Petitioners hope that they may be relieved from this Expence by the Authority of Parliament, in such Manner as to the House shall seem meet; and Hating to the House several other Powers which, the Petitioners perceive, are wanting for the due Government of the said Poor; and taking Notice that the Petitioners are informed, that the Inhabitants of Bofrnere and Claydon, in the said County, intend to apply to

Parliament, that they likewise may be incorporated for the like Purposes: the Petitioners therefore hope, that some Clause or Clauses may be added to the said Act for incorporating the said Hundred of Bofrnere and Claydon, for relieving the Petitioners as well from the Handing Expence as from the several Inconveniences mentioned in the Petition; and likewise for extending the fame, and the like Privileges, Power, and Authority, to the Petitioners and their Success'ors, in the Hundreds of Colneis and Carlford, as in or by the said Act is or shall be granted to the Directors and acting Guardians of the Poor in the said Hundred of Bofrnere and Claydon.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee to whom the laH preceding Petition is referred: And that they do examine the Matter of this Petition; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.
