To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, Mr. Henry Negus was examined; who said, that he

knows the several Hundreds of and Mutford,

and Lothingland-, that the Poor within the said Hundreds are of late Years considerably increased, and the Rates higher than formerly, as appears by the several Rates for several Years lad pait, which he had examined.

That the incorporating the Gentlemen of a certain Qualification, and appointing them Governors of the Poor within the said Hundreds, and giving them proper Powers for providing a proper Place for the Reception and Employment of the Poor, would be an effectual Means of reducing the Rates, as has been shewn by Experience in a neighbouring Hundred, where the same Scheme was adopted some Years ago; and that now great Part of the Debt of the said Hundred is paid off, and the Poor maintain themselves by their Labour.

A Petition of the Commissioners and Trustees named and appointed by and in pursuance of an Act of Parliament, made in the 10th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for making more effectual an Act made' in the 9th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, in-"tituled, An Act for completing the Repairs of the Harbour o f Dover, in the County of Kent; and for restoring

the Harbour of Rye, in the County of r, to its ancient Goodncl’s, so far as the same relates to the Harbour of Rye-, was presented to the House, and read; Reciting That by several Acts of Parliament made in the 11 tli and 12th Years of King William the Third, a certain Duty was laid and continued upon all Ships and Vessels therein described, for the Repair of Dover Harbour; and that the said several Acts were, by an Act made in the 9th of King George the First, for completing the Repairs of the Harbour of Dover, in the County of Kent-, and for restoring the Harbour of in the County of Sujjfex, to its ancient Goodness; continued until the First Day of May 1744; and the said Duty was directed to be appropriated, divided, and paid, for

V01. 29.

the Benefit of the said Harbours of Dover and Rye respectively, in Manner therein mentioned; and that by the said Act of the Tenth of King George the First, the Commissioners and Trustees are impowered to erect or order all Matters and Things necessary for opening a new Cut or Channel from Winchelsea Wall to the Sea, and to do all other Works necessary for effecting the Purposes of the said Act; and that by an Act made in the Eleventh Year of King George the Second, the said Duty was further continued until the First Day of May 1765, Old Style; and that by an Act made in the 31st of King George the Second, it was enacted.That after the Expiration of the Term granted by the said Act of the 1 ith of his said Majesty, One Moiety of the Rates and Duties granted and continued by the said former Acts should be continued for a further Term of Twenty-one Years, and be applied for the Benefit and Support of the Harbourof Dover: And alleging, That in pursuance of the said Act of the 10th of King George the First, the Petitioners have made a new Cut or Channel from a Wall called Winchelsea Wall, which divides the said new Cut from the said Channel of Winchelsea and Breade, right out to the Sea; and Stone Piers and other Works have been erected at the End of the said new Cut next the Sea, and a navigable Sluice has been built at the Difiance of 150 Rods from the said Piers, and the Walls of the said new Cut have been wharfed, and are, as well as the said Winchelsea Wall, of sufficient Height and Breadth, according to the Directions of the said Act; and in pursuance of an Act made in the Second Year of his present Majesty, the Sea and Tides have lately been let into the said new Cut or Channel, as far as the said Winchelsea Wall only, and that without any Danger to the Lands lying near thereto, or to the said Channel of Winchelsea and; and that since

the Sea and Tides have been let into the said new Cut or Channel, many Vessels have come into the fame, and have lain there in great Security; and that Ships and Vessels, to the Number of 300, may safely ride and lay at Anchor in the said new Cut or Channel; and that the repairing and heightening the Walls of the said Channel of Winchelsea and Breade, from the said new Cut or Channel to the Town of Winchelsea, and from the said new Cut or Channel to the Town of Rye, and the letting the Sea and Tides into the said Channel, through the said hew Cut or Channel, and the issuing the Land Waters of near 100,000 Acres through the same into the Sea, will be the Means of keeping the said new Cut or Channel clean and open, and prevent the lilting thereof, and will make a navigable Communication between the same and the Town of Rye; and that the Wharfing and other \forks in the said new Cut, for want of letting in the Sea and Tides sooner to the fame, have run greatly to Decay, which the Petitioners are unabe to do, and to repair and to heighten the Walls of the find Channel of Winchelsea and Breade, and to perform such other Works as may be found ne-celfary to be done for restoring the Harbour to its ancient Goodness, and to keep the whole in proper Repair, unless the Terms for which the said Rates and Duties are granted by the said former Acts be enlarged, or some other Provision be made in that Behalf; And therefore praying, That a Bill may be brought in for continuing One Moiety of the said Rates and Duties granted by the said Act of the 1 ith and 12th Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty King William the Third, to be paid and applied pursuant to the Directions of the said Acts of Parliament, of the 9th and iolh Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty King George the First, so far as the same relates to the said Harbour of Rye, for such further and longer Time as the House shall think fit; Navy A Petition of the Chaplains of the Royal Navy, '-Chaplains. being offered to be presented the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s 1 Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty

- having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; i Setting forth. That after the Peace of Utrecht, a Bounty

was granted by the House of Commons to the Chaplains dismissed from the Royal Navy; and that, in 1754, the House voted a Subsistence of Two Shillings and Vot. 29.

Sixpence a Day to the Twenty senior Chaplains of His Majesty’s Fleet, and Two Shillings a Day to the next Twenty, provided they had personally served Five Year*, and enjoyed no Ecclesiastical Preferment of the annual Value of Fifty Pounds; and that Hostilities commencing in the following Year, that Vote, in favour of the Petitioners, was not renewed; and now, that the Blelfing of Peace isreftored to the Nation, and an annual Relief is allotted to every other Rank of Officers discharged from His Majesty’s Service, it has so fallen out, that the Petitioners are-alone excluded from so general a Bounty; that the Situation of the Petitioners seems in some Degree to merit the Companion of the House, as the greater Part of them forsook their Friends, and the Means of their Support, to embrace His Majesty’s Service, on the first Equipment of the Fleet, and continued in the Royal Navy whilst their respective Ships -remained in Commission, having the comfortable View before them of a moderate Subsistence, in common with the dismissed Chaplains of the Army, when Times of Tranquility should arrive; and that, by their long Absence in remote Parts of the World, many of the Petitioners are become, as it were.

Strangers in their owu Country, and shall be reduced to a State of evident Distress, should this Memorial foil of meeting with a favourable Reception; and that the Petitioners humbly beg Leave to represent, that should a suitabie Encouragement be granted to the Chaplains in Time of Peace, it would not only do Honour to their Profession, but would induce Clergymen of Character and Ability, on future Occasions, chearfully to engage themselves in His Majesty’s Naval Service: And therefore praying, That the Petitioners may have such a Provision, as to the House the Petitioners Circumstances may appear to deserve.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to Account* j His Majesty, that He will be graciously pleased to give Directions, that there be laid before this House, a List of P*8** the Chaplains who have served in His Majesty’s Fleet during the late War; distinguishing the Time of their respective Services.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to His Majesty by such Members of this House as are of His Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

The House being informed, that Mr. Julliott, from the Exchequer, attended at the Door; he was called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, pursuant to their Order,

A Petition of the several Persons resident in the Cities of London and Westminster, in the Borough of South-

wark and Parts adjacent, employed in making and vending Beaver Hats, and Hats rhixed with Beaver, Rabbets Fur, and other Materials whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves and others, concerned in the said Manufacture in Great tain, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Act of making Mats chiefly coniposed of Beaver Wool, hath been carried to such Perfection in this Kingdom, that great Quantities of such Hats have heretofore been exported to foreign Parts; and that Beaver Skins, though greatly different in Size, Weight, and Value, are all rated at the same Duties inwards, which are Seven Pence, Three Twentieths and Five Eighths per Skin; and do all draw back Four Pence, Six Twentieths and Thirteen Sixteenths per Skin, upon Exportation: And as Two Cub Skins hardly weigh so much as One Skin which is full grown, those Cub Skins are principally bought for Exportation, and of late Years large Quantities of Beaver Skins have been exported, and considerable Sums of Money have been paid as Drawbacks thereupon; and that, owing to the French Policy in preventing the Exportation of Beaver Wood, and Beaver Skins, the Beaver Wool in France, has been principally, if not wholly, worked up into Hats; and as Labour is considerably cheaper in France than in England, this, with the Drawback upon Beaver Skins, which the French receive from hence, enables them to manufacture Beaver Hats, and Hats mixed with Beaver, and other Wool, much cheaper than the Subjects of Great Britain can do, and to fend large Quantities of such Hats to and Portugal,

where there are great Demands for them, and where the Manufacturers of this Kingdom, who ttfed principally to supply those Countries, afe so much undersold, as to he driven out of them and most other European Markets; ‘!.ourrh the Petitioners had conceived Hopes, that up< > the Acquisition of Canada, they should have been enabled <u regain to this Kingdom the Hat Trade to foreign Part*, they find it utterly impracticable without the Aid of Parliament: And that the Portuguese (who never uA-d to make any other than Felt, or Wool Hats) have lately ei'rabished a Manufacture for making fine Hats, which meets with great Encouragement; and that as His Map tty is become possess’ed of most if not all the Countries from whence Beaver is imported, it may now denominoted a Staple Commodity of the British Dominions; and the Petitioners apprehend, that it is renugnant to the true Interest of this Country, (whose Riches arise chiefly from the Labour of its Inhabit ms) to allow a Bounty to our Rivals in Trade, upon the Exportation of any Article that is raw, which tends to throw a valuable Branch of Manufacture into the Hands of other Countries, to the Disadvantage of His Majesty’s Revenue, to the Discon-ragement of the British Manufacturers, who Work up Beaver with the full Duty upon it, and to the very great Loss of the Nation, which otherwise would receive the Benefit arising from the Extension -of the Hat Manufacture; and that the Petitioners apprehend, if Relief were given in the Article of Beaver, in Favour of the Manufacturers of Great Britain, it would enable them to regain the tine Hat Trade, and to export Beaver Woul worked into Hats, to Spain, Portugal, Italy, and to other foreign Parts, with the Labour of great Numbers of Workmen charged upon it, who are now wholly out of Employ, and destitute of the Means of supporting themselves and Families; and who, the Petitioners have great reason t o apprehend, unless relieved, will be under the Necessity of seeking . Employment in foreign Countries: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant

Vol. 29.

such Relief and Encouragement to the said Manufacture, as the Credit and Importance thereof deserve, and as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Journeymen in the Beaver Hat Trade, redding in and about London, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves and the rest of the Journeymen of the same Trade, Was also presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That there are many Thousands of Journeymen living in the City of London, and Suburbs thereof, who have served regular Apprenticeflnps, to the said Trade, and who depend wholly thereupon for the Support of themselves and their Families: and alleging, that upwards of 1,600 Journeymen of the same Trade are now wholly out of Employ, and many more are daily expeCling to bedif-tnified from the Service of their Matters, owing, as the Petitioners are well allured, to the general Debay of the Trade of all the Master Hatmakers in and

that many of the Journeymen of the said Trade, have lately been induced to quit this Kingdom with their Families, arid more are preparing to follow them, in order to gaiii a Livelihood in those Countries where they can find Employment; and that the Petitioners have great Reason to believe, that this Decay of their Trade arises from the large Quantities of Hats which the French feiid to those foreign Nations, which used to be chiefly suppl ied with Hats by the English Hatmakers, who, by the Dearness of the Materials, are hot able to fell their Hats at such low Rates as the French Hats are now sold at; and that the greatest Part of the Petitioners and their Families must be ruined, if the said Trade should continue to decay as it has lately done: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to grant such Relief to the Petitioners as is most suitable to their Cafe.

A Petition of several Persons resident in the Town cAManchester, in the County of and in Parts

Roads.

A Petition of the several Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Trustees appointed to put in Execution an Act of Parliament madie in the 26th Year of the Reign VOL. 29.

bf his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act to continue and render more effectual, Thi;ee Acts of Parliament, passed in the 1 ith Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, and in the Third and 2 2d Years of the Reign of His present Majesty, for Repairing the Road from Sherbrooke Hill, near Buxton and Chapel in the Frith, in the County of Derby through the Town of,

in the County of Chester, to Manchester, in the County of Lancaster-, and other Roads in the said Acts mentioned; and for repairing the Road from the School House in Didsbury to the Bridge in Wilmjlmo, in the said County of Chester; and for erecting a Bridge over the River Mersey-, and also of the several Gentlemen, Land Owners, and other Inhabitants, whose Names are also thereunto subscribed, living near the said Roads; was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Tolls collected on the said Roads, together with several Sums of Money, to the Amount of Three thousand Two hundred Pounds, borrowed upon the Credit thereof, have been duly applied in repairing the said several Roads, and the same are greatly improved; but the Road from Whaley Bridge to a Place called Sparrow Pit Gate, upon the said Turnpike Road, in the said County of Derby, (being Four computed Miles, or upwards) is so very mountainous, steep, and difficult to pass in many Parts of it, that the same is greatly incommodious and dangerous to Travellers; and that, by diverting and turning the said Road from Whaley Bridge, over Hotridge Common, and from thence through some inclosed Lands lying at or near Chapel Tunfead, to Chq-pel in the Frith aforesaid, and from thence through certain Parts of the inclosed Lands lying betwixt Chapel in the Frith aforesaid, and the present Turnpike Road at Sparrow Pit Gale aforesaid, would be of great Convenience, not only to the adjacent Parts of the said Counties of Derby and Chester, but to all Passengers in general, and an Advantage to Trade and Commerce; and that the present Tolls at the several Turnpikes at Whaley and Midway, by reason of the large Debt owing bn the Credit thereof, and the great Extent of Road to be repaired thereby, are not sufficient of themselves so defray the Charge and Expence of making the said new intended Road; but the Petitioners apprehend, that if a Bar be erected across the fame, and One or more Side Bar, or Side Bars thereto, and a small Toll granted at such Bar, or Bars, with such Exemptions as may be thought reasonable, such new Road will soon be completed, and the Charge and Expence thereof, with the Aid and Assistance of such Tolls, in a few Years, be reimbursed, when the same Bars are intended to bg thrown down, and discontinued; and that the Road from Whaley Bridge, in the County of Chester, to the Extent of One computed Mile, or upwards, toward* the Wellerly End of a Common, or Parcel of Waste Ground, called the Longside Common, upon the same Turnpike Road, by reason of the quick Rife and Af-ceut of the same is very incommodious and dangerous to Passengers, as well on Horseback as with Carriages; and that, to divert or turn that Road over and through the adjoining Lands, would be of great Convenience to the adjacent Parts, and to all Travellers, and the Public in general: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Amending the said last mentioned Act, in the several Instances before mentioned; and for erecting a Bar across the new intended Road from Whaley Bridge to Chapel in the Frith aforesaid, with One or more Side Bar, or Side Bars, to the fame; and for diverting the Road from Whaley Bridge, over and through the adjacent Lands, to the Westerly End of Longside Common aforesaid, in the said County of Chester.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Con-fuleration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame,*as it shall appear to them, to the House.

By the said Act made in the 10th Year of King George the First, for making the last mentioned Act more effectual, so far as the same related to the Harbour of Rye, Power was given to make a new Cut, from Winchelsea Water to the Sea, and to heighten the Walls of the Channel of Winchelsea and Breade in Manner

therein mentioned.

By the said Act made in the i ith Year of his late Majesty King George the Second, the said Duties were further continued for the Term of 21 Years.

And the said Act made in the 31st Year of his said late Majesty directs, that, from the Expiration of the Term granted by the last mentioned Act, which will happen upon the 12th Day of May 1765, Old Stile, One Half Part of the said Duties shall be continued, for the further Term of 21 Years, and be applied for the Benefit and Support of the Harbour of Dover.

And by the lait of the said Acts, of the 2d Year of His present Majesty, Power was given to let the Sea and Tides into the said new Cut, as far as Winchelsea Wall 011I3’:. Then,

Mr. Robert Cooper, Engineer, being examined, said. That he has been employed in carrying on the Works at Rye, for upwards of Six Years pafl; and that a new Cut or Channel has been made from a Wall called Winchelsea Wall, which divides the said new Cut from the Channel of Winchelsea and Breade, right out to the Sea; and Stone Piers and other Works have been erected at the End of the said Cut next the Sea.

That the new Cut has been wharfed, and is, as well as the said Winchelsea Wall, of a proper Height and Breadth; and that the Water is let into the said new Cut, pursuant to the Directions of the said Act of the Second Year of His present Majesty.

And he further said, That several Vessels have already been in the new Cut; and that it will hold 300 Vessels, from 100 to 300 Tons Burthen, to ride in Safety at a Time; there being, in common Spring Titles, from 17 to 20 Feet Water, and at Neap Tides from 11 to 16 Feet Water.

That the new Cut is 300 Rods in Length, and 150 Feet wide, upon an Average; and that the repairing and heightening the Walls of the Channel o( Winchelsea and Breade, from the new Cut to the Town of Winchelsea, and from the said new Cut to the Town of Rye, and the letting the Sea and Tides into the said Channel, through the said new Cut, and the ilfuing the Land Waters of near 100,000 Acres through the same into the Sea, will be a means of keeping the said new Cut clean and open, and will make a navigable Communication between the same and the Town of Rye.

And he said. That the wharfing of the new Cut is at present in bad Repair, for want of the Water being sooner let in.

That there are several other Matters wanting to be done, and the Works will want a constant Repair, for which a Fund will be necessary.

----- Stuffold, Captain of a Coasting Vessel, and

Mr. John Beadle, an Officer belonging to His Majesty’s Customs, confirmed the Evidence of Mr. Cooper.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners produced to your Committee, an Account of the Works which Mr. Smeaton, an Engineer, who has lately surveyed the said Harbour, apprehends necessary to be performed for iinithing and completing the said Harbour; whereby it will, in his Opinion, be a safe, useful, and commodious Harbour: Which Account is hereunto annexed.

And Mr. Cooper further said, That he was present at taking the said Survey, and had read and considered the said Account; and is of Opinion, that the Method proposed by Mr. Smeaton, for finishing the said Harbour,' is mosteligible, and that it cannot be finished in a more proper Manner.

Manner how the Harbour is to be finished and completed; subject to Alterations, as mentioned in the

Act.

The Channel of Winchelsea, from the North End of the new Canal to the Junction of Tillingham Channel, near the Town of Rye, to lie widened, deepened and straitened, so as to be, at a Medium, 50 Feet wide in the Bottom; each Side to batter at the Rate of Two Feet horizontal, te One Foot in Depth; the Bottom to be so disposed as to make a Part of a Plane, regularly inclined, from the lowest Sell of Scotch Flatt Sluice upon the Rothsr, as it was in the Month of February 1763, to the Sell of the great Sluice upon the new Harbour; the Banks, or Walls, to be set at lead 40 Feet, at a Medium, from the Brink, and to be raised to 25 Feet at the Least, above the Sell of the great Sluice; to beat Least Six Feet Top, to batter Two and One Half to One towards the Canal, and One and One Half to One to Landward.

To widen, deepen andftraiten the Tillingham Channel, in the same Manner and Proportion as the preceding, from the Point aforesaid, so far upward as shall be necessary to come at a proper Place of Departure into a new Canal, next hereafter mentioned.

To make a new Cut, or Canal, to the North of the Town of Rye, from some convenient Part of the 77/-lingham Channel, as aforesaid, to some convenient Point of the River Rother , the Cut to be 40 Feet Bottom, to agree with the inclined Plane aforesaid; its Sides to have the same Batters as the former; its Banks, or Walls, to be raised to the same Height; to have the same Dimensions at Top, the same Batters and Distance, as before described, as far as the crossing of the present Turnpike Road, which leads from Rye towards London: But if any Part of the Ground shall not be sufficient to allow of the Batters, Slopes, and Distance of the Banks before specified, then the Sides of the Canal and Banks to be wharfed up, or otherwise supported, so as to preserve the Bottom of the Canal of the Width before specified, and the Banks to be made sufficiently strong, to hold in the Water to the same Height as before assigned.

A Bridge to be built upon the said Turnpike Road, for crossing the Canal, to consist of Three Arches; One of 13 Feet 6 Inches wide; the others of 12 Feet each; the large Opening to be furnished with Two Pair of Gates, pointing to Seaward, so as to form a navigable Lock, and one Pair of Gates pointed to Landward; the other Two Arches to be furnished each with One Pair of folding or falling Gates to Seaward, and Draw-Gates to Landward; the Sells of those Gates to be laid even with the proposed Bottom of the Canalat this Place.

To fix a Dam acrol’s the River Rother, near below the Point where its Course shall be diverted, as aforesaid; and to erect a Sea Wall, or Bank, from the said Dam, to some convenient Point Eastward, upon the present Sea Wall of the adjoining Marshes; and to carry another Sea Wall from the said Dam Westward, to abut upon the aforesaid Turnpike Road; the said Dam and Walls to be raised to an equal Height with the adjoining Wall against the said Marshes, to be Six Feet at l of, and to batter both Ways, as Two- and One Half to One.

A navigable Sluice to be fixed across the Tillingham Channel, at l’ome convenient Place within Half a Mile of the Bridge at the Ferry near Rye, of 13 Feet 6 Inches in the Clear, with a Pair of Gates pointing to Seaward, and another Pair to Landward, with Draw Shuttles, or Slakers, in the latter; and the Walls, or Banks, of the Tillingham Channel, from the said Sluice downwards, to its Junction with the Canal before described, to be heightened, in such Manner and Proportion as is described for the main Channel from the newCanalto Rye.

Mr. Burton reported froip the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Governor and Company of the Bank of England, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place: and afterwards delivered it iu at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read , and is as followeih;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Nathaniel Hammond, Accountant to the Bank, and 14

Mr. Benjamin Sabbarton, one of the Cashiers, being ex* a mined, said, 'Flint the Edifice erected in Street, by the said Governor and Company, is finer Trade and Credit, together with the Parliamentary Funds transferrable there, arc so greatly increased, become too confined for the proper Dispatch of Bu fine is, and to admit of sufficient Air for the Health of the Number of Clerks and Officers, and Persons attending the re; that there are Two kinds of Stock in One Office, which is much too small for the proper Transacting the Uufincfs: And Mr. Sabbarton said. That great Inconveniences arise from the Want of more Room in the Hall, for the proper placing of their Books, in order to have recourse thereto.

Mr. Gate Morris, and Mr. John Guitton, Stock Brokers, being examined, said, 1 bat from the Number of Persons retort ing to the different Offices, which are so small and confined, as to make them very offensive, it is very difficult for them to perform their Business therein.

Mr. Hammond and Mr. Sabbarton further said, That from the Number of Persons retorting to the Bank, and the Avenues leading thereto being so very narrow, the same are become very dangerous to Passengers; and, from the Contiguity of several Houses, most of which are Public I loufes, that in same of Fire, the Bank, together with the Papers and Property belonging to the said Governor and Company, would be in great Danger of being destroyed.

Mr. Robert Taylor, Surveyor, being examined, said,

That most of the Houses round the Bank are either Taverns, Coffee Houses, or other Public Houses, some of which ad join to the fame, and are very old and rotten; that in same of Fire, the Old and New 3 per Cent. Offices mud inevitably be burnt, and the whole Fabrick be in imminent Danger; that the said Inconveniences would in a great n tea fit re be removed, if the said Governor and Company wore enabled to open a Way for Carriages from Cornhillto the Bank, and to purchase the Ground, Houses, and Buildings, on the North Side of 77 treadncalle Street, from the Bank East-ward, quite through to Bartholomew' Lane; and also the Ground, Houses, and Buildings, on the Well Side of BarlholomexvLane, from the South End of the said

Lane, Northwards, to the House in the Possession of Mr. Holden, for the Purposes of lay ing so much of the said Ground into the public Highway in

Street, as will range in a Line from the Bank, to the South Weli Angle of Saint Bartholomew's Church, and for the Purpose of enlarging the Buildings of the Bank on the Residue of the said Ground.

And Mr. Taylor further said, That the said Governor and Company have purchased some of the said Houses, have contracted, and are in Treaty for several others; hut some Difficulties have arose, with respect to some of the Estates being entailed, others in Infants, and for Want of proper Titles being made to others; and that the said public Improvements cannot be carried into Execution, without the Aid of Parliament.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Thomas Wildman, being examined, said, That in the Town of Kirkby in Kendal, there is a Court of Record held once in Three Weeks* by the Mayor, Recorder, and Two Senior Aldermen, lor the Trial of Actions under the Value of Forty Pounds; that the Proceedings of the said Court are very tedious and expfcnfive; the Exjrence in a common Action, will sometimes come to Four or Five Pounds; whereby many Persons, who are often obliged to give Credit for small Sums bf Money, aredifabled, or intimidated from applying for Relief in the said Court; that a Cause cannot be brought to Ill’ue in the said Court in less than Nine Weeks* and is frequently Half a Year before it is. determined.

Mr. James Wiljbn confirmed the aforegoing Evidence.

To prove die Allegations of the said Petition, an Act made in the 28th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, for repairing and widening the Road from Rochdale to BurtdeyK in the County of Lancaster, tvas read: And,

A. 1754.

Mr. Alexander Fothergill being examined, said, That in pursuance of the said Act, a competent Number of the Trustees met, and proceeded to put the said Act in Execution; and borrowed £.500 of Mr. Joftas upon the Credit of the 1'olls; which Sum, together With Interest for Five Years, still remains due to the said Mr. Mor ley.

That the Witness saw the Deed for the Security of the said Money executed by the Parties, and that there is no Power given to the said Mr. Morley to enter upon the Turnpikes or Toll-houses.

And being asked how the said Money had been applied

He said, That £. 400, together with the Tolls collected, have been applied in repairing Part of the said Road, and in paying Officers’ Salaries.

And he further said. That there were, before the passing of the said Act, several parallel Roads leading from Rochdale to Burnley, one of which Roads is described by the said Act as being Part of the Road from Burnley to Halifax; but the Trustees apprehending that the Act did not determine the Identity of the Road, fixed upon another Road, upon which a loll Bar was erected, and Duties collected, at the Time of borrowing the said £.500; since which, several Doubts have arisen, with Respect to the Course and Identity of the said Road. Then,

Mr. Laurence Lloyd, Clerk to the Trustees, being examined, foid, That a Meeting of the Trustees was appointed for the 12th Day of June 1760; but a Efficient Number not appearing, he gave Notice, as required by the said Act, for the Trustees to meet on a subsequent Day; but no Trustees meeting on that Day, he appointed another Meeting; at which likewise no one appeared; and that there has been no Meeting of the Trustees ever since.

Then the Witness produced to your Committee a Book, Containing the Minutes of the Proceedings of the Trustees; by which it appeared, that the above Meeting was to have been on the 12th Day of June 1760, and not on the 20th, as mentioned in the Petition by' Mistake.

And the Witness further foid. That he never attempted afterwards to give any further Notice; the Turnpikes being pulled down, he knew not where to put up the Notice of Meeting.

And both the Witnesses said, That some of the Trustees are dead, and others, upon Account of the Doubts and Difficulties attending the putting iii Execution the said ACT, have declined acting; and, That that Part of the Road upon which no Money has been laid out, is dill in a ruinous Condition.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing and enlarging the Term and Powers of an Act made in the 28th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for repairing and widening the Road from Rochdale to Burnley, in the County of Lancaster. And that the Lord Strange and Sir George Savile do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Cornczvall, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of such Alterations and Amendments, as may be proper to be made in such Part of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for granting to His Majesty several addi-tidnal Duties upon Wines imported into this Kingdom; and certain Duties upon all Cyder and Perry; and for raising the Sum of Three millions Five hundred thousand Pounds, by Way of Annuities and Lotteries, to be charged on the said Duties; as lays a new Duty of Excile on Cyder and Perry, to be paid by the Maker thereof; the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; vis.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 5th Day of July 1764, instead of the Composition authorized to be made by the Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, for the Duty thereby granted uponCyder and Perry confirmed in the Private Families of the Makers thereof, a Composition be allowed after the Rate of Two Shillings per Annum lor each Person, of or above the Age of Eight Years, in such Families respectively.

Resolved', That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Time for the Payment of the Duties charged on Cyder and Perry, limited by the said Act to the Space of Six Weeks, be prolonged to the Space of Six Months.

Ordered, That the further Consideration of the said Report be adjourned till Friday Morning next.

Newton, Sitcomb, and Abots Bickington, in the County of Devon, in Behalf of themselves and others. Occupiers of Land aforesaid, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners are informed, a Petition from the Mayor, Recorder, and Inhabitants of the Town of Bit!-‘ford, in the County of Devon, hath been presented to this House, foraTurn-pike Road from the West End of the said Town of Bideford, through Buckland Brew to Thornhill Head, and from thence to Woodford Bridge, and from the said West.End of Bideford, through Monkleigh to theljioke Stone, there to branch off one Road to tree Common, through Marland Town, to Sheepwash, which is about Nine Miles from Fritheljioke Stone, the other Road to Stebross, through Slarifi Moor, to Buck-land Filleigh Cross, and to Sheepwufi, which, from theljioke Stone, is about Twelve Miles, and the I'wo Roads run parallel, and not above Two Miles afuuder; and alleging, that the Petitioners are at a great Expence in procuring Lime, being the only Manure in that Country to improve their Lands; that there are three Lime Kilns in the Parishes of Monkleigh and Loner afs, and lay on the River Terudge, known by the Names of Lancrafs, Annerie, and the nearest of which is between Three and Four Miles from Bideford, and no Connexion with the Town of Bideford, to which Kilns the Petitioners are obliged to resort for their Lime; and that the Petitioners are informed that a Toll Gate is intended to be erected at Town,

by Means of which the Petitioners will be deprived of the Benefit of going to the said Lime Kilns, without paying the Toll, though they will not travel above a Quarter of a Mile on the said Turnpike Road, which will be a great Detriment to the Improvement of Lands, and a very great Expence to the Petitioners; and that the Petitioners Servants frequently let out one Day, and are obliged to tarry all Night at the Kilns, and return the next Day, sometimes without their Lime; therefore, if the said Petition passes into a Law, and Toll Gates are erected at Monkleigh, or any other Part of the Road through which Horses or Carriages that go for Lime are obliged to pay the Toll, it will increase a greater Expence on the Manure than the Petitioners can afford: And therefore praying that all Horses or Carriages going to the said Lime Kilns of Lancrafs, Annerie, and Rid, may be exempt and freed from paying any Toll at the said Gate intended to be erected at Monkleigh, or any other Gate to be erected through which the Petitioners must pass to go to the said Lime Kilns; and for such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. John Aujlin, Vestry CJerk of the said Parish, being examined, said, That since the passing of the said Act, the said Parish is become very populous; that the said Act directs but Six Constables for the said Parish, which are not sufficient to do the Duty; and that several Complaints have been made of that Defeat in the Act; which is also Defective with respect to the Number of Lamps; the Money they are enabled to collect for that Service not being sufficient to provide a sufficient Number of Lamps; that the Rate for the Lamps is made at Michaelmas, and every Inhabitant who intends to put up his own Lamp, is to give Notice to the Vestry Clerk of such Intent; but that very few People give Notice, in Consequence of which every Person is rated, which amounts to a great Sum, and when the Collector goes to col left the Rates,

he cannot get the Money:----- That there are many

vacant Spaces of Ground which are not lighted, as the Committee apprehend they have no Power to set up Lamps there.

That it would bean Advantage of £.50 and upwards, to the Parish, if the Poors, and other Rates, were consolidated; and that, if a select Vestry was established, as in many other Parishes, particularly the Parish of Saint George Hanover Square, the Wit-uefs thinks the Parish would be better and more regularly managed.

That there was not any Account passed from the Commencement of the Act till the 8th of April 1760; and that no Account has been passed according to the Directions of the said Act, since that Time.

And that, if the Collector had made good Collections, the Treasurer mull have had large Sums of Money in his Hands.

That several Persons, who are of the Committee, serve the Poor House with Necessaries, which is contrary to the Directions of the Act:--That the Witness has frequently complained to the Committeeof such Practices; but they have ftjll continued to do the fame.

Mr. William Knight, Beadle and Watchhouse Keeper,

said. That he thinks Six Constables are not sufficient to

do the Duty of the Parish:----- That imee the passing

of the Militia Act, they have had a great deal of additional Trouble, and that the Night Duty comes upon them too often. The Constables have frequently complained to the Witness of these Inconveniences; that they are all Tradestnen; and the Parish Duty being so great, prevents them in a great Measure from following their own Business.

Mr. Henry Hollis, Mailer of the Workhouse, said. That the Poor have sufficient Meat and Drink, but are sometimes in want of Clothing: That the Witness has made Application to the Committee; but they have not given Directions for furnishing the Poor, as they sometimes have wanted necessary Clothing, and they have frequently been full of Vermin, which was owing to the want of Linen.

To prove the Allegations of the second mentioned Petition, Mr. Joseph Brockkurjl, being examined, said, That he had served the Office of Overseer of the said Parish; that a Committee of 20 Persons are chosen annually, who, with the Churchwardens and Overseers of the Poor, transact the Business of the said Parish; that they are moltly People of Fortune, and Tradesmen, who are acquainted with Parochial Business; that the Persons who compose the present Committee, have more Property in the Parish than the Petitioners, for the Bill, except the Duke of Portland; and that the Majority of the Parish are very well satisfied with the present Management.

Then the Minutes of Vestry, of the 23d of January last, were read.

those Minutes are not agreeable to the Ord’r of Vestry.

Mo Ciifi reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Mercers of the City of London, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Stephen llarveyj, Esquire, Agent for the Petitioners, produced an Act of Parliament, passed in the 21st Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, whereby it is enacted, that a Duty of Sixpence a Chaldron upon Coals, which, by an Act of the Fifth and Sixth Years of King William and Queen Mary, for the Relief of the Orphans of the City of I^ondon, was granted to the City of London, for a Term of Fifty Years, to commence from the 29th of September 1700, should be continued, from the Expiration of that Term, for the further Term of Thirty-five Years; and that the Monies arising thereby should be paid into the Receiptof the Chamber of London, and the yearly Sum of 3000, out of the Produce of the said Duty, should, during the said Term of Thirty-five Years, be paid by the Chamberlain of London to the Petitioners, by Half-yearly Payments, to be applied by them towards the Payment of their Annuitants, and other Creditors; and to that Purpose the Petitioners were directed, within One Month after Michaelmas 17 50, to make out a General Account of all Sums that should be then due and in Arrear to their Annuitants and their Representatives; and to enter the same in One or more Book or Books to be kept for that Purpose; and a Note, or Certificate, in Writing, containing the Sum due and in Arrear to each Annuitant at Michaelmas 1750, was to be delivered to them and their Representatives; all which Sums are thereby declared to be Principal Sums, and to carry an Interest at Three per Cent, until the same shall be paid and discharged.

That after Michaelmas 1750, the said Wardens and Commonalty should apply the said yearly Sum of £. 3000, as the same should come in and be received, in the First Place, towards Payment and Satisfaction of so much of the Annuities which should from thenceforth become due and payable by virtue of the Deeds of Settlement made for the Benefit of the Annuitants,

as the Estates of the said Wardens and Commonalty, in

Settlement, would not be sufficient to pay and satisfy.

That when the said yearly Sum of £. 3000, together with the Rents and Profits of the Estates in Settlement, should be more than sufficient to pay and tlif-charge the said Annuities, that then, as any Surplus should arise, and be sufficient to pay Half a Year*s Interest, the Petitioners were required to apply such Surplus, as the same should come in and be received, in the First Place, towards paying and discharging the Interest which, after Michaelmas 1750, should grow due on the Sums of Money which at that Time were due for the Arrears of the said Annuities, and which were before directed to be considered as Principal Sums, until such Interest should be all paid; and after Payment thereof, and of the growing Interest thereon, such Surplus should, so often as the same would be sufficient to pay Ten Pounds per Cent, on the Principal, be applied to reduce and pay off the Principal Sums, in an equal Proportion, until the whole should be fully paid and discharged.

_ That so soon as the said yearly Sum of £. 3000, together with the Rents and Profits of the Estates in Settlement, should have paid and discharged all the Arrears of the said Annuities, and the Interest thereof, and should be more than sufficient annually to pay and satisfy the respective Annuities, the Petitioners are thereby required to reserve the Surplus arising from the said yearly Sum of £. 3000, to be applied to the Payment of such other of their Creditors as should be deemed proper Objects of Relief, and in such Manner as should be directed by any future Act or Acts of Parliament.

Mr. William Cawne, Clerk to the Mercers Company, produced to your Committee an Account, shewing the Payment of Arrears due to the Annuitants of the Company, together with a Rental of the Company’s Estates in Settlement; and also an Account of the Receipt and Application of the said £. 3060 per;

and also a List of the Names of the Company’s Annuitants in Possession at Michaelmas 1763, and of those in Expedancy at the same Time; which Accounts and Lifts are hereunto annexed, N* 1,2, 3, 4, 5; by which Papers it appears, that the said Company had discharged all the Arrears of the Annuities for which Certificates were given, in pursuance.of the Directions of the said Act, with the Interest thereof, and had also punctually paid their respective Annuities; and that there is at present a Surplus of £.4640. 1 is. 9 in the Hands of the said Company, arising from the said yearly Sum of £.3000,to be applied by Parliament to the Payment of ;such other Creditors of the said Company as shall be deemed proper Objects of Relief.

And he informed your Committee, That the said Surplus will annually increase; but that the Company cannot apply the same to the discharging of Debts due to any other of their Creditors, without the Authority of Parliament.

He also produced several Accounts, by which it appeared, that the said Company are indebted in very considerable Sums of Money, for Charities or Money legacies. Bond Debts, and Simple Contract Debts; which Accounts are also hereunto annexed, N# 6, 7, and 8. And he informed your Committee, That the said Company have no other way of satisfying such Debts but out of the Surplus of their Estates in Settle ment; which appears by the said Accounts to be very insufficient to discharge the fame.

Expiring

Law*.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to impower the Wardens and Commonalty of the Mystery of Mercers, of the Cit£ of Londonto apply-certain Sums of Money now in their Hands, or due to them of Arrears of Rent; and also all Monies which may hereafter arise from their annual Income and Estates, after Payment of their several Annuities, and other Sums charged and to be charged thereon, towards Payment of the other Creditors of the said Wardens and Commonalty, in Manner in the Bill to be mentioned: And that Mr. Cust, Mr. Glover, and Mr. Chauncy Townshend, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Mr. Fuller reported from the Committee, appointed to inquire what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived or continued; That the Committee had inquired accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s fable: Where the same was read; and the Resolutions of the Committee are as followed 1;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, An Act for the better regulating of Pilots for the conducting of Ships and Vessels from Dover, Deal, and the Isle of Thanet, up the

Rivers of Thames and Medway, which was to continue in force for Seven Years, from the Firi't Day of Avgujl 1717, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and also a Clause in an Act of the Seventh Year of his said Majesty’s Reign, for further regulating the Pilots of , and the Isle

of Thanet, which was to continue in Force during the

Continuance of the said Act of the Third Year of his said Majesty’s Reign; which said Act, together with the said Clause, were, by several subsequent Arts of the 10th Year of the Reign of his said Majesty, and of the 8 th and 23d Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, further continued until the 25th Day of March 1764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 15th and 16th Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act to impower the Importers or Proprietors of Rum or Spirits of the Sugar Plantations, to

land the same before Payment of the Duties of Excise charged thereon, and to lodge the same in Warehouses, at their own Expence; and for the Relief of Raljh Barrow, in respect to the Duty on some Rock Salt loft by the overflowing of the Rivers Weaver and Dane, which was to continue in Force from the 29th Day of September 1742, to the 29th Day of September 1749, and 14 from

4 Geo. III. 90 Februatii. 825

from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts of the 23d and 3ill Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Rejotced, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act made in the 19th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for the further Punishment of Persons going armed or disguised, in Defiance of the Laws of Customs or Excise, and for indemnifying Offenders against those Laws, upon the Terms in this Act mentioned; and for the Relief of Officers of the Customs in Informations upon Seizures; which was to continue in Force for Seven Years, from the 24th Day of July 1746, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts of the 26th and 32d Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day of September x 764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in (he Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George tl»e Second, intituled, An Act for further encouraging and regulating the Manufacture of British Sail Cloth, and for the more effectual

securing the Duties now payable on foreign Sail Cloth imported into this Kingdom, which was to continue in Force for Five Years, from the 24th Day of June 1736, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts of the 13th, 24th, and 31st Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 4th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for granting an Allowance upon the Exportation of British made Gunpowder, which was to continue in Force for Five Years, from the 24th Day of June 1731, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts of the 10th, 16th, 24th, and 3 ill Years of the Reign of his said late Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 6th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for the better Securing and Encouraging the Trade of his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in which was to

continue in Force for Five Years, from the 25th Day of December 1733, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts of the nth, 19th, 26th, 29th, and 31st Years of his said late Majesty’s Reign, and of the First Year of His present Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1763, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the 12th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act for granting a Liberty to carry Sugars of the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of any of his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America, from the said Colonies directly tp foreign Parts, in Ships built in Great Britain, and navigated according to Law, which was to continue in Force for Five Years, from the 29th Day of September 1739, and from thence to the End of the then next vox,. 29.

Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts made in the 17th, 24th, and 31st Years of his said late Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1764, and from thence to "the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Rejilived, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, . That an Act, made in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, An Act to prevent the committing of Frauds by Bankrupts, which was to continue in Force for Three Years, from the 24th Day of June 1732, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by several subsequent Acts made in the 9th and 16th Years of his said late Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1750; and which, by another Act made in the 24th Year of his said late Majesty was amended, and further continued to the First Day of September 1757, and from thence to the End of

the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by another Act made in the 3 ill Year of his said late Majesty, was further continued until the 29th Day

tember 1764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliamet; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee That so much of an Act, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of King George the First, intituled, An Act for giving further Encouragement for the Importation of Naval Stores, and for other Purposes therein mentioned, as relates to the Importation of Wood and Timber, and of the Goods commonly called Lumber, therein particularly enumerated, from any of his Majesty’s British Plantations or Colonies in America, free from all Customs and Impositions whatsoever, which was to be in Force for Twenty-one Years, from the 24th of June 1722; anu which, by several subsequent Acts made in the 16th, 24th, and 31st Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, was further continued until the 29th Day of September 1764, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

The First, Second, and Third Resolutions of the Committee being Severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question Severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fourth, Fifth, and Sixth Resolutions of the Committee being Severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question Severally put thereupon, postponed.

The Seventh and Eight Resolutions of the Committee being Severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

To the honourable the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled.

The Governor and Company of the Bank of England humbly propose.

That they advance the Sum of £. 1,000,000 for the public Service, on Exchequer Bills, to be made forth by virtue of an Act to be passed in this Session of Parliament, bearing Interest at the Rate or Premium of £.3 per Gent, per Ann. the said Interest to be paid quarterly, and the said Exchequer Bills to be charged and chargeable upon, and repaid by and out of, the first Aids or Supplies which shall be granted by Parliament for the Service of the Year 1766; and in case sufficient A ids or Supplies should not be granted for that Purpose before the 5 Day of April 1766, the same to be charged and chargeable upon, and be repaid out of, the Sinking Fund: And also, that they pay into His Majesty’s Exchequer the Sum of^. 110,000, to be disposed of by Parliament, without any Repayment of the Principal, or Allowance of Interest for the fame.

And they humbly further propose, that they be continued a Corporation, with the foie Power of Banking, for the Term of 21 Years, from the First 17(15, with all the Grants, Privileges, and Immunities they now enjoy, by virtue, or in pursuance of their Charter, or of any Act or Acts of Parliament, redeemable afterwards on a Year’s Notice; and the repayment of all the Principal Money; and also the Payment of all the Interest Money which shall be then due and owing to them upon all such Tallies, Exchequer Orders, Exchequer Bills, or Parliamentary Funds, which they shall hate remaining in their Hands, or be intituled <0 at the Time of such Notice to be given as aforesaid, (Inch Funds for the Redemption whereof Provision is already made in any Act or Acts of Parliament now in Force always and only excepted) they continuing a Corporation, with an exclusive Power of Banking, not-wit'hstanding such Notice given, till all the Money due 'to the Bank as aforesaid shall he paid them.

Robert Secretary.

House to take the PremiIts into Cdnsideration; and to give such Preference over Foreigners in what Beaver remains to be worked up in Great Britain, Us the Importance thereof deserves, and as to the House shall (eem meet.

AS* The Lord Warkworth reported from the Committee, r»spe£iing w}j0ni the petition of the Directors of the 1 land in *££ Hand Fire Office, and of the Directors of several other Offices within the Cities of London and Westminster Insuring Houses and Goods against Fire, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, An Act made in the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, for preventing Mischiefs by Fire, was read; whereby it appears, that so much of the said Act as relates to Party Walls, is confined to Cafes, where one of the adjoining Houses is to be new built: And,

Mr. John Pratt, Bricklayer, being examined, said. That some Regulations are wanting, where Party Walls are out of Repair, though neither of the adjoining Houses require rebuilding.

That the Surveyors appointed by the said Act, being Four in Number, are frequently equally divided in their Opinions, which makes it impossible to carry some Provisions in the said Act into Execution.

That Party Walls ought to be built with Stone, or well burnt Bricks.

That they should be Two Bricks and an Half thick . in the Cellar Story; Two Bricks from thence to the , Garret Floor, and One Brick and an Half from thence upwards; and that all Party Walls should be carried . Eighteen Inches, at the Jeaft, above the Roof and adjoining Gutters.

That it would tend greatly to prevent the communicating of Fii'e, if Builders were prevented from laying any Timbers into Party Walls, except the Girders and Templets, and the Purloins and Kirbs, or Cirbs, of the Roofs; and also, if they were restrained from laying the Ends of Girders, or other Timbers, opposite to one another.

That no Inconvenience will arise from these Regulations, but that Houses may be built this Way as cheap as any other, and will be as llrong or stronger.

That if Houses were to be built with Stone or Brick, both forward and backward, from the Breflummer up-' wards, and the Breflummer to be put no higher than the First Floor, it would frequently prevent, the spreading of Fire.

And he informed your Committee, that the said Act is, in many other respects, defective.

Sir Thomas Robinson, Baronet, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Pratt.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating of Buildings to prevent Mischiefs that may happen by Fire within the Weekly Bills of Mortality, and other Places therein to be mentioned: And that the Lord War Mr. Sandys, and Sir William Beauchamp P,do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Lord Strange reported the Conference: And that it was to acquaint this House, That the Lords having taken into Consideration a Book, intituled, le Roy, or a Digejl of the Rights and Prerogatives of the Imperial Crown of Great Britain, had come to the following Resolutions:

" Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal

" in Parliament assembled,

" That the Book, intituled, Droit le Roy, or a Digejl " of the Rights and Prerogatives of the Imperial Crown

" of Great Britain, is a false, malicious, and traiterous

" Libel, inconfilieut with the Principles of the Revo*

lution, to which we owe the present happy Establishment; and an audacious Insult upon His Majesty, " whose paternal Care has been so early, and so effect* " nally shewn to the Religion, Law's, and Liberties of " His People; tending to subvert the Fundamental " Laws and Liberties of these Kingdoms, and to " introduce an illegal and arbitrary Power."

" Resolved, By the Lords Spiritual and Temporal *' in Parliament assembled,

" That one of the said printed Books, be burnt by the " Hands of the Common Hangman, In the New Palace " Yard, Westminster, on Saturday the 25thDay of this " instant February, atOueof the Clock in the After-

" noon; and that another of the said printed Books " be burnt by the Hands of the Common Hangman, " before the Royal Exchange, in London, on Monday " the 27th Day of this instant February, at the same " Hour; and that the Sheriffs of London and

" do attend at the said Times and Places reflectively, " and cause the same to be burnt there accordingly." To which Resolutions their Lordships desire the Concurrence of this House; and that the Conference, also, was to communicate to this House, the said Book.

A Message from the Lords, I>y Mr. Browning and Mr. Anguish:

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for dividing and inclosing certain Open Common Fields and Grounds in the Manor and Parish of Stainton in the Hole, in the County of Lincoln, without any Amendment: And also,

A Petition of John Blake, Esquire, being offered to be presented to the IIouf<»;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioner drew up a Plan for the better supplying this Metropolis with plenty offifli by Land Carriage; and accordingly an Act passed in 1762 for the better supplying the Cities of London and Westminster with Fish, and to reduce the present exorbitant Price thereof, and to protest and encourage Fishermen; and that several of the Nobility, Gentry, and others, associated for the Encouragement of Arts, Manufactures, and Commerce, having advanced the Petitioner a Sum of £. 2000 to enable him to prove the

Practicability of carrying the said Plan into Execution; the Petitioner accordingly applied himself, with great Assiduity, to effect the fame, and moreover at his own Risque, advanced a further Sum of £. 1500, with which JointCapital he brought upwards of Eighty-nine Tons Weight of frefti Fish to the London Market by Land Carriage, from distant Parts of the Sea Coasts, between the 16th Day of May 1 762, and the 31st Day

ber following, both Days inclusive; and that, notwithstanding the many Difficulties the Petitioner had to encounter in his Attempt to ani’wer the Intentions of the Legislature in passing the said Act, he hath continued to prosecute the said Undertaking with unremitting Ash-

Vol. 29.

duity, at the further Risque of his own private Fortune; and that he humbly conceives, that the further Prosecution of the said Plan may lliew the Means of extending it to the furnishing several interior Parts of the Kingdom with Fish, in like Manner as the Metropolis is now supplied; and that the Consequence of this muff, in Time, be a considerable Increase in the Number of Fishing Vessels on every Part of our Sea Coasts, and of a Species of Industry which will raise an additional Nursery of Mariners for His Majesty’s Service in Time of imminent Danger or Invasion; and that notwithstanding the aforesaid generous Assistance of £. 2000 and the £.1500 advanced by the Petitioner, he finds the said Monies insufficient effectually to answer the good and great Purposes intended thereby; and therefore hopes, that the House will take the Premises into Consideration, and grant him such Assistance as the Nature and Importance of this Undertaking shall appear to them to require anddeferve.

The House was moved, That the Resolutions, which, upon the 18th Day of March last, were reported from the Committee, who were appointed to inquire into the Effectfi of an Act, made in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the better supplying the Cit ies of London and Westminster with Fish, and to reduce the present exorbitant Price thereof, and to protect and encourage Filliemien; and to consider of proper Methods for the further supplying the said£ities of London and Westminster with Fish, at moderate Rates; and to report their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time, to the House; might be read.

And the same were, as agreed to by the House, read accordingly; and are as followeth;

Resolved, " That the Cities of London and Westminster " have, since the Act passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the better supplying the " Cities of London and Westminster with Fish, and to " reduce the present exorbitant Price thereof, and to " protest and encourage Fishermen, been better, and in " a much larger Degree, than before the passing of " the said Act, supplied with Sea Fish by Land Carriage;

" and that the late exorbitant Price of many Sorts of " Sea Fish hath thereby been considerably reduced; and " the Cities of London and Wcfiminferhave been supplied with many Sorts of SeaFilh, not usually brought " there."

" Resolved, That the good Effects which the said Act " hath produced, have been owing to the laudable and " indefatigable Prosecution of the Plan or Scheme " concerted by John Blake, Esquire, for the better supplyine the Cities of London and with Sea

" Fith, by Land Carriage; and which hath, in Part, been " executed by him, notwithstanding the many Diificulties he met with in such the Execution thereof."

" Resolveed, That some Assistance ought to be allowed " or granted to the said John Blake, to encourage and " enable him further and effectually to carry into Execution the said Plan or Scheme, concerted by him, for " the better supplying the Cities, of and Westminster with Sea Fith, at moderate Rates."

Ordered, That the said Petition and Resolutions be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

A Petition of the Proprietors of the London Bridge Water Works, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth. That the Petitioners find by the Votes of the House, that the Trustees appointed by Act of Parliament to improve, widen, and enlarge the Passage over and through London Bridge, have applied by Petition to the House for a further Sum of Money for carrying on and perfecting the Purposes intended by the said Act; and representing to the House, that by taking down the Houses upon the said Bridge, which were supplied with Water by the Petitioners’ Works, the Petitioners are deprived of the annual Income of One Hundred Pounds; and that by taking away One of the Piers, in order to turn Two Arches of the said Bridge into One, near the Centre, where the Current is most powerful, the Resolutions of the Petitioners’Water Wheels were decreased to more than One Half; which Defect the Petitioners were obliged to remedy, by working a Fire Engine, at a great Expence, in Order to supply their Tenants with Water; and was also the Occasion of their losing to the amount of One hundred Pounds per Annum, and upwards: And therefore pray-, ing the House to take the great Loss and Damage, incurred by the Petitioners, into Consideration; and that Satisfaction may be made to them for the fame, out of any further Grant to be made to the said Trustees, for the Purposes aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Thor0ton reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, Gentlemen, Merchants, and principal Inhabitants and Burgesses of the Town of Kingston upon whose

Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the same as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed]; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of Parliament, passed in the 2d Year of His present Majesty’s Reign, to amend and render more effectual several Acts made for cleansing and enlightening the Town of Hull-, and for preventing Annoyances therein; was read. Then,

Mr. Carlton Monckton being examined, said. That the Rate allowed by the Act to be collected, being Eight Pence in the Pound, according to the Land Tax, amounts only to £.§1. 13 s.4 or thereabouts; which Sum is insufficient for executing the Purposes of the Act.

Mr. John Huntingdon said, That an Experiment had been tried of the Expence of lighting the said Town, by a voluntary Subscription, which amounted to £. 134. and which was found insufficient; and that it would require £. 150. to light the said Town effectually, for One Year.

That it would coll £. 100. a Year more to clean the Streets of the said Town; and that the said Acts have never been executed, from the Deficiency of the Sum rated for the Purposes of the Act.

That there is no Provision made by the Act, for a proper Place to lay the Soil in.

Mr. Monckton added. That it would render the Act more effectual, if certain Powers were taken out of the Corporation, and vested in the Inhabitants at large.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, for amending and supplying the Deficiencies of an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Regn of His present Majesty King George the Third, intituled, An Act to amend and render more effectual several Acts made for cleansing and enlightening the Streets of the Town of Kingston upon Hull-, and for preventing Annoyances therein: And that Mr. Thoroton, Mr. Charles Lord

Robert Manners, and Mr. do prepare, and

bring in, the fame.

To prove, the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. John Middlemarsh and Mr. Richard Some/fall being severally examined, said, That there is a Lane leading from a Place, near the Turnpike, at Comer,

to Lambeth, commonly called Lambeth Marsh Back Lane, which communicates at each End with the Roads directed to be repaired, and intended to be enlightened and watched by the said Act, and isabout Three hundred Yards in Length, and is very narrow and ruinous.

That the said Lane is a Retreat for bad People; and that Robberies have been committed therein at Noon Dav.

That if Provision was made for repairing, widening, enlightening, and watchitig the said Lane, it would be Yol. 29

a great Convenience to the Inhabitants of Southwark, and Lambeth.

A Complaint being made to the House, That the Hand-writing of a Member of this House had been counterfeited upon the Cover for a Letter, in order to prevent its being charged with the Duty of Postage;

And the said Cover being produced by the said Member; which he declared to be not of his the said Member’s Hand-writing;

Ordered, That James Boyes of Chatham do attend this House, upon this Day Sevenuight.

Ordered, That Fletcher, of the Band of

Music belonging to His Majesty’s Marine Forces at

Chatham, do attend this House, at the same Time.

William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Ditto. Moreing, was, according to Order, brought to the Bar, by the Deputy to the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

And the several Covers for Letters, which were produced to the House upon Friday last, beingshewn to him, he denied that the Franks thereon were of his Hand-yvriting.

And Mr. John Keith and Mr. Stockwell

attending, according to Order;

They were severally called in; and examined, and confronted with the said William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Moreing.

And then the said John Keith and were severally directed to withdraw.

And William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Moreing, was directed to withdraw.

Then the said William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Moreing, was again brought in, by the Deputy to the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

And Mr. Joshua Stockwell was again called in.

And the said Mr. Joshua Stockwell was further examined.

And then he was again directed to withdraw.

Then the said William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Moreing, was heard in his Defence.

And then he was again directed to withdraw.

Resolved, That William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Moreing, having counterfeited the Handwriting of several Members of this House, upon Letters, and several Covers of Letters, in order to prevent their being charged with the Duty of Postage, is guilty of an high Misdemeanor, and a notorious Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That, the said William Edwards, otherwise William Edwards Moreing, be, for his said Offence,

Mr. John Featherjtone said. He knows the Gravel Pits which supply the Road; that they lie on the West Side of Cottingham; and that One Third of the Gravel used in the Repair of the Road, at least, is carried through Cottingham, by Neivland Bridge, which is a very bad Road at some Times; and that Gravel cannot be carried that Way in Winter, or iii a wet Summer, so that the Trustees are obliged to get large Quantities of Gravel in Summer, and lay it on the Sides of the Road, by which some of it is wasted^ but if the Road from Newland Bridge to Cottingham was well repaired (which cannot be done by the ordinary Course of Law) the Trustees might get Gravel at all Times. ’ 4

That the Road from Cottingham to Netolarid Bridge is about'Three Miles in Length; and1 that the Inhabitants of Cottingham, goiRg to Hull, only travel over Two Miles of the Turnpike Road.

Being cross examined, he said. That he lived at -tingham, and knows the Difference of the Cottingham Gravel from that which comes from Hull by Water; but does not know' the exact Quantities of each used in the Repairs of the said Road.

That about Thirty Years ago, he was Surveyor of the Roads in the Parish of Cottingham; that the Parish is worth near £. 6000 a Year, in his Opinion, but an Assessment of 6d. in the Pound, according to the old Valuation, raises but £. 32 a Year, and that there are between Ninety and an Hundred Teams kept in the Parish, which do Statute Work on the Turnpike Road Two Days in the Year out of Six, being the Proportion settled by the Quarter Sessions; and that all Teams perform this Work, except where Persons keep more than One Team.

That there are Twenty Miles of Road in the Pafifli; besides the Turnpike Road; and that when he was Surveyor they raised 6d. in the Pound, and employed all the Teams, which was insufficient to repair the Roads* which were sometimes presented.

That the leading Gravel for the Turnpike has greatly damaged the Road from Cottingham to Newland Bridge; that a great deal has been done towards repairing it; and in some Parts there is a good Causeway.

Mr. William. WiUcii\fon, an Inhabitant of Cotting-ham, said. That the Gravel Pits which principally supply the Turnpike Road lie at the West End of Cottingham $ and that the Gravel is led through the Parish of Cottingham, and most of it by the Road from Cottingham to Newland Bridge, which is very bad> and only paflhble in dry Seasons: and if the Road could be repaired, it would save a great Expence to the Trustees, who are now obliged to lay their Gravel ' in Heaps, On the Side of the Road, by which Means it is much wasted, and damaged by Dirt from the Road getting amongst it; and that the ordinary Methods of Law will not repair this Road.

Being cross examined, he said. That some Gravel is brought by Water, but no great Quantity.

That the Gravel which is led in Summer is more expensive to the Trust, bccacufe they lay it on the Sides of the Road, and have it to lead again.

That he has seen Gravel often led in the Summer to other Turnpike Roads; but is not much used to Turnpike Roads.

That the Statute Work will not repair the Road, which is a clayey Soil, and much frequented by Carnages going to Hull Market; but that the Carriages employed by the Trustees do it the most Damage; and lie confirmed the Evidence of the last Witness, in regard to the Number of Carriages, Valuation of

I.ands, Amount of the Assessment, and Length of the Roads in the Parish of Cottingham, and likewise as to the Quantity of Statute Work done upon the 1'urn pike Road.

That the Labour of a Team is as cheap in Summer as Winter; and he believes the bell Time to lead Gravel, is between Hay Time and Harvest.

That Ten Miles of the Road, in the Parish of Cottingham, are very bad; and the other Ten wants Repairs sometimes.

That it is impossible to lead Gravel on this Road in Winter. That Sea Gravel might be had, but it must be carried a Quarter of a Mile by Land, and would be Three Times the Expence of Cottingham Gravel, as the Witness apprehends.

That the Inhabitants of Cottingham don’t think the Turnpike any Advantage to them at present, as they cannot use Carriages to Hull in Winter, unless the Road from Cottingham to Newland Bridge was amended; that the Gardeners and Farmers carry their respective Commodities on Horseback to , and go Twice a Day; but if the Road was mended, histead of employing Eight Horses to carry Ten Quarters of Corn in a Day, a Waggon with Four Horses would carry that Quantity at onefe, and bring back a Load of Dung.

That he has known from Forty to Sixty Pounds, within a Year, laid out Qn the Road, from Cot-
