Thomas Brewer, Inhabitant of Bank, formerly Collector of the Tolls, said. That the Gravel Pits from whence the Road is supplied, are at the Well End of Cottingham-, and that about 1500 Loads were led the Year he was Collector, from thence over Newland Bridge; and that the Gravel cannot be got by that Road in W inter, though never so much wanted.

That very little Sea Gravel is used, except in the Close Lanes, near Beverley, where they think it answer* better than Cottingham Gravel.

That Sea Gravel is more expensive, as lie thinks that it colts more a Ton; and that laving it down and taking it up is a great Expence. That he cannot fav the Tntftees ever wanted Gravel, for they lead it in Summer, and lay it. on the Sides of the Roads, which they would not do if they donld lead in Winter; and that Carriage at pressent is cheaper in Summer than in W inter.

Thomas Brewer was again examined; who said, That when lie was Collector of the Tolls at the Trustees paid 11 d.a Load for all Cottingham Gravel leading from the Pits, to any Part of the Road on the Hull Side of Beverley Bar; but if the Gravel was carried through Beverley Bar, which is Five Miles from the Gravel Pits, they pay One Shilling and Three Pence a I.oad.

That the Witness never paid for any Sea Gravel; but by the Book it appeared to be 20 a Ton; that it is led by Carts from the Place where it is landed, to different Distances, sometimes Haifa Mile, sometimes a Mile; that a Cart, drawn by Three Horses, brings a Ton of Gravel from Cottingham Pits, where the Gravel is measured, and the Carts marked.

That he never knew the Commissioners distressed for want of Gravel in Winter, great Quantities being led in Summer, which are laid on the Sides of the Roads: and that he is sure the Roads could not be mended without Cottingham Gravel, which is much the nearest, and cheapest; nor will Sea Gravel bind so well by itself, the Cottingham Gravel being always laid upon it.

That he never knew hut One Load of Gravel brought from llaffell Clitf, and that was to pave with.

That lie cannot say' whether if a Turnpike Road was made from Cottingham to Bridge, the

Gravel could be led for less than 12 a Toil; and that he never knew the Time when they could lead it in Winter.

That there are Eleven Miles more of Road in the Parish very bad, which he apprehends would cost £.250 a Mile to repair.

That the Inhabitants of Cottingham pay as much for going from thence to Hull, in which they only use Two Mil es of the Turnpike Road, asthofe who travel the whole Length of that Road, which is about Eight Miles: that they never come upon the Turnpike Road going to Beverley; and that Hull is their principal Market; and that the Witness thinks, that the Inhabitants of Cottingham pay £. 130, or £. 140 per Annum to the Turnpike.

To prove that the Exportation of Beaver Wool and Beaver Skins is prohibited in France:

Mr. Rojjiter produced a letter from his Correspondent in Paris, dated Parti, August 6th, 1751; in which the following Paragraph was read:

" Tire Exportation of Heaver is prohibited, by " reason it is preferred solely for the Use of the " Hat Manufeftory in this Kingdom."

By the said Letter it also appeared, that the befi Canada Beaver was, at that Time, fold for Seven and a Half Livres; which is about Six Shillings and Sixpence Sterling. (

When, about the same Time, the Bay Company Beaver sold to'England for Fifteen Shillings and Eleven Pence per Pound, on an Average; and that it was not possible at that Time to bring any of tijc Beaver to London.

Peter llaj'endever, Esquire, Merchant, informed yonr Committee, That lie hail been frequently in France, and is acquainted with the Beaver Manufeftory — -the chief P4rt of which is worked up into Hats; — that feme little has been made into Cloth, by way of Experiment; but t|ie Quantity has been inconsiderable.

Mr. Rojjiter being further examined, informed your Committee, That the Price of Labour in France is about One Half cheaper than in; but that iu

the North of England Labour is much cheaper; that lie had, on that Account, established his Manufactory there, as several other Hatters of London bad done.

That he had exported a small Quantity of Beaver to France; partly grown Skins, and partly Cubs, which cost him £. 128, and for which he received a Drawback of upwards of £. 13.

That the Cub Wool don’t work quite so well as the grown Beaver, there not being that Strength in it; and that it is inferior in Value about One Shilling per Pound.

Being aiked, whether the Charges of carrying the Beaver to Paris did not amount to more than the Drawback? He feid, he believed that the Expence of carrying it to the North of England was.near as great; — that a Merchant of London, who should fend Beaver to France on his own Account, must pay Warehouse Kent, Brokerage, and Commission; but that if lie was a Hatter resident in Parti, he should lend the Commission immediately to a Broker in London, by which the preceding Articles of Expence would be feved; and that the French can be suppliad with Beaver from no other Market.

To prove that the French supply the Markets of Spain, Portugal, and other Places;

Henry »Steers,| Esquire, Merchant, informed your Committee, that he had lived at many Years. —

That formerly large Quantities of Hats were imported to Lisbon from England, but of late very few; which was owing to the great Quantities of Hats furnished the Portuguese by the French, which are much cheaper, in respect to their Quality, than the Hats.

Lawrence Fowkes, Esquire, informed your Committee,

That he had lived Thirty Years in Portugal, and confirmed Mr. Steers's Evidence.

Then Mr. Roffitersaid, That he had taken Account/;

from the Custom-house Books; and found, on an Average, from the Year 1750 to the Year 1761, the Number of Hats exported annually to Portugal amounted to 13,948 Dozen of Beaver and Castor; and that in the Year 1762 the Number exported was only 2,397 Dozen; and in the Half Year, ending last only 92 Dozen.

That the Number exported to Spain, from 1750 to 1761, amounted yearly, at an Average, to 8,914 Dozen; and in the Year 1762 to 407 Dozen; and in the Half Year, ended at Midsummer last, to 67 Dozen: That the Quantity exported to the from 1750

to 1761, amounted, at an Average, to 2,105 Dozen each Year. — That in 1762 none at all were exported; and in the Half Year, ending at Midsummer last, to only 38 Dozen.

Which Calculations, upon Comparison, appear to agree with the Account from the Custom-house, referred to the Committee.

English Hats, an Extract of a Letter from his Correspondent at Lisbon, dated Lisbon, 26th August 1749, was read to your Committee, and is as follows; " We " again return you many Thanks for your further Promise of supplying no other House here with Hats, but " ours, while the Fleet is with us; the Obligation you " lay on us is great; and nothing we wish more than " your making of it complete, by favouring us in the " like Manner, on all other Occasions; in regard to " which, having expressed ourselves fully in ours of " the 12 th Ultimo, we have nought to add now, only to " give you fresh Assurance we can expend all the " Hats you can send to this Market; and that we " should be much more obliged to you to enlarge our " Quantity, by at least a Thousand Pounds a Year, " than be confined to what we are usually supplied " with. — The Consumption we meet with now for the " Fleets is cohfiderably more than we ever knew; " and we have reason to imagine it will encrease every " Year, in which same we fear you will not be able to " furnish us sufficietitly; we are sensible how much less " the Expence is when the said Fleets are not here; " however, we should have no Manner of Difficulty (if " obliged to it) to keep by us a Parcel of Cafes, as " we are sure of their not remaining many Months on " our Hands; in these Cjrcumstances we beg the .* Liberty of entreating you, in a very earueft Manner, " you will give up the Thoughts of supplying more " any other House in this Place with your Goods. We " are emboldened once more to aik this Favour, by 15

London Mr. Shiffner reported from the Committee, to whom Bridge the Petition of the Proprietors of the London Bridge Waterwor *' Water-works, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fast contained in the said Petition; and had directed him to report a State thereof . to the House; and he read the Report in his Place;

and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth;

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition is as follows;

Mr. Richard Hern, One of the Collectors of the Rents for the said Proprietors, produced to the Committee a List of Persons’ Names who occupied Houses upon London Bridge; and who, before their Houses were pulled down, in pursuance of the Act for improving and widening the said Bridge, were furnished,

with Water from the Petitioners’ Water-works; by

which it appeared, that the Rent paid to the Petitioners, by the Persons whole Houses were already pulled down, amounted to £.90. 10s. a Year; and he further informed your Committee, That Five Houses more were to be pulled down, which now pay £. 5 a Year; so that the whole Lots to the Petitioners will amount to £.93. 1 or. per Annum.

To prove the Petitioners’ Loss from the taking down One of the Piers, in order to turn Two Arches into One, whereby the Velocity of the Current was reduced,

Mr. George Foley, Secretary to the Proprietors of the Water-works, produced to your Committee a Book, wherein an accurate Account is kept of the Number of Resolution,s made by the Wheel in each Tide; which Account he informed your Committee was regulated by an Index fixed to one of the Wheels; and by this Account it appeared, that in December 1761 the Engine made from 2 and 3000 Strokes in a Day; and that in December 1762, at some times no more than 700: which Decreale of Power the Witness laid, was occasioned by removing the Pier.

In order to- prove the Loss incurred by the Petitioners, from this Deleft in their Works,

Mr. Rwhard Hern, Mr. William Hunter, Mr. Thomas . Willis, and Mr. Hugh Owen, Collectors for the Pro-

prietors, produced their several Accounts to the Committee, whereby it appeared, that the Proprietors had loft Tenants to the Amount of the annual Rent of £. 106. 18. o. on account of their Inability to supply them with Water, occasioned by the removing the said Pier.

the Roadisnotequallygood in Summer. — The Rains sometimes hinder Farmers for a Week. — Last Summer Coals were but 5$ per Hundred.

And being asked, at what Time they can most conveniently employ their Teams, he said — In Summer it is inconvenient, because they have Harvest in Hand; the Hay. comes in in July, the Rye Harvest, some of it, in dugufi-, — but that the Winter would be the moil convenient Time, as they are then at Leisure.

Coalheavers. Mr. Philip Fonereau reported from the Committee, to

whom the Petition of the several Persons, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, on the Behalf of themselves, and all other industrious Coalheavers, employed in the unloading Ships and Vessels bringing Coals into the River Thames, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; Where the same was read; and is as iolloweth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act of Parliament, made in the 31st Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, was read.

And Nicholas Jacob said. That a Coalheaver’s Office was established, in pursuance of the Powers given by the said Act. but that it has been discontinued for some Time; and that he thinks, if that Establishment had continued, it would have been beneficial to the Coal Trade. — That the Masters of Coal Ships approved of the Establishment, as they had less Trouble than before the Office was erected.

The Witness said, there had been Combinations amongst the Coal Undertakers, to prevent the Men continuing to regiller their Names at this Office; that they refuted to give the Men Work unless they would leave the Office; and that on this Account the Men had left the Office.

John Errington confirmed the Evidence given by Nicholas Jacob, as to the Establishment of a Coal-heaver’s Office; and added, that he thought that Establishment of great Service to the Men, and beneficial to the Masters of Ships.

That before the Office was established, and since it has been discontiinledj the Mailers are obliged to pay for Undertakers; and that during the Time the Office fubfilied they had no Occasion to employ Undertakers.

Then the Agent for the Petitioners acquainted the Committee, that the Act had been found deleftive iu many Respecis, for the Purposes intended.

Crackle/ A Petition of several Proprietors of Lime "Works, in the County of Salop, which supply the Town of Shrewsbury Shtewsbury, and several other Places in the Neighbour-

Road. hood thereof, with Lime, whose Names are subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice, That the Petitioners observe, by the Votes, that a Petition has been presented to the House, to enlarge the Term and Powers of Two former Acts for repairing she Road from Crackle}) Bank, in the Parish of Shiflhal, to the Town of Shreicsbury; and also for repairing other Roads tlterein mentioned} and alleging, that by the said former Acts, all Materials for building, not going to Market, (except Lime in the Winter Season) and Lime in the Summer Season, are exempt from Payment of Tolls on the said Roads; and that several of the Petitioners are Proprietors of several Lime Works lying near to other Turnpike Roads leading to the Town of Shrewsbury, and several other Places in the Neighbourhood, whereon Carriages with Lime are liable to the Payment of Tolls in all Parts of the Year; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if the Exemption from Payment of Tolls on the First mentioned Roads in the said former Acts, especially that for Lime in the Summer Season, shall be continued, it will be a great Injury to the Petitioners Lime Works, by occasioning a much greater Demand for Lime from the said First mentioned Works, than from those of the Petitioners: And therefore praying. That the House will take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration; and grant them such Relief in the Premises, as to the House shall feera reasonable.

Ditto. A Petition of several Persons inhabiting the Town of Shrewsbury, and the Neighbourhood thereof, in behalf of themselves and their poor Neighbours, was also presented to the House, and read; Taking Notice, That in the said Acts no Exemption is specified for Coal, which is almost the only Fuel made use of in that Town and Neighbourhood; and that much the greater Part of the Coal there consumed is carried along the greatest Part of the said Roads, and pays Toll for the same at Two different Places, whereby the Price of Coal is increased; and that the Carriage of Lime in the Summer Season with other Materials for building, exempted from Toll, is very great; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that if Lime, and other Materials for "building, were to pay the same Toll which is now paid for Coal, the Toll might soon be reduced on all Sorts of Carriages; and that thereby the Price of Coal might be greatly abated: And therefore praying, That the said Exemptions may no longer take Place; or else that Coal may be also exempted; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers of Two Act, of the Twelfth of King George the First, and of the Third of his late Majesty, for repairing several Roads therein mentioned, in the County of Salop; and also for amending and widening the Road from the Sign of the Horse Shoe in Uckingfan to Longnor Green; and also from the West End of Atcham Bridge to the Cross Houses upon the -

A Petition of the Mayor and Burgesses of the City of Gloucester, and County of the same City, in Common Council assembled.

And the said Petition was read; Setting forth, That the Mayor for the Time being, and Fleven other Aldermen, are Justices of the Peace for the City of Gloucester, and County of the same City, and that several of the said Aldermen having usually resided, and some of them do now reside out of, and at a considerable Distance from the said City; that therefore it is necessary for the better Execution of the Powers intended by the Bill now depending in the House for the more effectual Relief and Employment of the Poor in the City of Gloucefer5 and for lighting the Streets of the said City; that all the said Aldermen, as well as the Five Senior Aldermen, should be Guardians of the said Poor; and that they apprehend, it is the more immediate Office of the said Mayor and Aldermen, as Justices, to rate, assess, and levy, the several Sums to be charged upon the Inhabitants towards lighting the Streets of the said City, which the Petitioners observe, is very necessary to be enforced by Law, and ought not to be left to the Direction and Inclination of Individuals only to judge of the Manner or Necessity of doing it, provided the same shall not exceed a certain Expence, to be limited by the House; and observing, that several Petitions have been presented to the House against the passing of an Act of so much Necessity and Utility of that City; proceeding, as the Petitioners believe, from great Misapprehension, or Misrepresentation, of the View, Purport, and Intent of the Bill, and not framed by the collective Sense of the several Parishes, in their respective Vestries^ or upon real Circunillances and just

Informations; that the Guardians of the several Parishes in the said City had first a previous Meeting, to considerof an Application to Parliament for the Purposes in the Bill, with respecto the Poor; and after having consulted the Inhabitants of their respective Parishes thereon, at their several Vestries, at a subsequentMeeting or Court of the Governor and Guardians, holden for that Purpose, afterwards agreed unanimously to seal the Petition presented to the House, except the Guardians of the very small Parish of Saint Mary de Grace, not confiding of more than Twenty-six or Twenty-seven Houses, nor contributing more than about a Thirtieth Part of the whole annual Expence for the Relief of the Poor of the said City; and representing to the House, that the greatest Part of the present Debt from the Workhouse in the said City, was incurred, as the Petitioners have been informed and believe, in the following Manner; viz. About One Third Part, by a very ill-judged and mistaken Law Suit, unnecessarily entered into about Twenty-six Years ago, by the then Governor and Guardians of the Poor, most of whom are now dead; and the greatest Part of the Remainder of the said Debt was incurred by a Defect in the Pow ers of the former Acts, to enforce the Payment of the several Sums rated and assessed upon the Inhabitants, of the several Hamlets and Parishes, Two whereof are Petitioners against the Bill, and have never yet paid the fame; and thatfince the Workhouse hath beendiscontinued, the Poors Rates of the said City have been greatly increased; and as it is intended by the present Bill, that the Governor and Guardians shall be.restrained from railing any Sums of Money from the several Parishes, which shall exceed One Third, more than what has been paid, for any One of the five Years preceding the Year One thousand Seven hundred and Fifty-seven, the Petitioners hope, that the said Governor and Guardians may be enabled by necessary Powers; to put the Acts in Execution for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor; that the Petitioners apprehend, it will be expedient for the said City, that the Treasurer of the Workhouse, for the Time being, shall, at every Quarter Sessions to be held for the said City, pass his Accounts of Monies received and paid on Account of the fame, for every preceding Quarter: And therefore praying, That the said Bill may pass into a Law, with such Alterations and Amendments, as to the House shall seem meet; and that the Petitioners, if they think it necessary, may he heard by then* Counsel upon the said Bill, and have such further Relief in the Pre-mi fes, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the more effectual Relief and Employment of the Poor within the City of Gloucester; and for lighting the Streets of the said City; is committed.

Ordered, That Mr. Fuller have Leave to make a Motion.

And he moved the House accordingly.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties now payable upon Beaver Skins imported into Great Britain from His Majesty’s Dominions in America, do cease, determine, and be no longer paid.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That in lieu of the said former Duties, there be granted to His Majesty a Duty of One Penny, to be paid upon the Importation of every Beaver Skin into Great Britain, from His Majesty’s Dominions in America.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be granted to His Majesty a Duty of Seven Pence upon each Beaver Skin, or Piece of such Skin, exported from Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That there be granted to His Majesty a Duty of One Shilling and Six Pence per Pound, for all Beaver Wool exported from Great Britain.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, that the said Duties be made applicable to the same Purposes to which the former Duties upon Beaver Skins were applied.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Drawback be allowed upon Beaver Skins exported from Great Britain.

Mr. Dyson from the Committee appointed tq inquire Abufts into the several Frauds and Abuses in relation to fending p *n tre or receiving of Letters and Parcels free from the Duty 0 cc* of Postage; and to consider of the most proper Methods of preventing the same; and to report their Opinion thereupon, from Time to Time to the House; acquainted the House, that the Committee had come to a Resolution, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee, in the Course of their Inquiry into the Frauds and Abuses in relation to the Franking of Letters, having had a Letter from one James Campinott, of Ealand, inf Yorkshire, to Joshua Stockwell, produced before them; which Letter is hereunto annexed, ordered the said James Campinott to attend them.

And the said James Camjnnott having acknowledged the said Letter to be of his own Hand-writing; and the said Joshua Stockwell having also given Evidence, that he had, in consequence of the said Letter, bought for the Use of the said Campinott Fifty-six Dozen of counterfeited Franks, of William Edwards (the Person found guilty, by the House, of having counterfeited Franks) for which Fifty-six Dozen of Franks he paid the said William Edwards, at the Rate of Six-pence per Dozen; and which he had accordingly sent to the said James Campinott.

And the Committee having thereupon heard the said James Campinott what he had to say in his own Defence, who acknowledged, that he had bought great Numbers of Franks of the said Edwards, and fold them again; but alleged, that he took them for a

Debt

4 Geo. III.

Debt which Edwards owed him; and that he fold them only to make his own Money; and that Edwards had told him, that he had them of Gentlemen’s Servants, to whom their Masters gave Authority to make use of their Names.

Upon the Whole Mattel* your Committee came to the following Resolution.

Refobved, That it appears to this Committee, that James Campinott is guilty of Buying and Selling a very great Number of Franks, on which the Names of several Members of this House were forged; and that, at the Time of his buying and selling the fame, he knew the Names of such Members were forged.

Elland, December 13th 1763.

My Dr. Jos.

Don’t think it’s from any Indifferancy that 1 have not wrote to you before now, I have oftens enquired after your Welfare; as to John and his Wife, there is but a very indifferent Agreement betwixt ’em, for file’s a most notorious ill Woman, the Particulars I don’t doubt but you’ve heard for {lie’s almost a Countery’s talk here, very like your Brother John will convince you that I was not negligent about your Affair before he came down; I desire you’ll ask Timo: Pollard if he has got any of Dacre's,

Meredith's, or Ashburne ham's Franks by him, if he has buy ’em as low off him as possible you can, he perhaps may give them you as they don’t pass now, I want to return them for some that I had of a Person, otherways I mull pay for ’em, if I have not of them Sorts for him, but if he’ll not give them you get ’em as low as possible; also pray go to Jo: Lee, and ask him if he has any of those Sorts by him, if he has get all you can of him, for I have a matter of 100 Dozen to repay; and if I pay for them in Money I am to pay 3d\. per Dozen; I cannot make you understand how the Agreement was betwixt the Person and I in a few Words, but I desire you’ll get me all you can, tell them you’ll give them the Worth of the Paper, and they are worth no more, as they don’t pass; don’t mention my Name; you had bell indeavour to get them in a bantering Manner; I’ll further beg of you to go to one John Buckley at the Sign of the Christophers in Barnaby Street in the Burro and desire he*!! either pay you 5 Shillings for some Franks he had off me or return the Fks to you, they was all Dacre's.

I am fenfable your Time is not altogether your own, but pray my Dr. Jos: favour me as soon as possible with both what I require and' an Answer, and what Particulars you can on all Accounts;

I am yor. mo. affectionate Friend and Wellwilher,

Jsim7 Campenot.

Am sorry I coil’d not fend this in a Cafe, but I have not one that’s good.

To Mr. Jos' Stock well, to be left with Mr.

Timo: Pollard at the Bed Lion in, Alder/'gate Street. London:

A Petition of Samuel Touchet, of London, Merchant, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by His Majesty V. Command, acquainted the House, that His Majesty having been informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to the Consideration of the House.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; Alleging, That a Design having been formed, by his late Majesty’s Ministers of State, in consequence of Measures proposed to them by Thomas Camming, of London, Merchant, to attack the French Forts and Settlements at Senegal; and the said Thomas Gumming. having received the most satisfactory Assurances, both verbal and in Writing, that if the Attack succeeded he should have an exclusive Charter of the Trade to the River Senegal, for a limited Term of Years; and as a Number of Armed Vessels of a particular Construction was necessary, from the small Draft of Water on the Bar of Senegal, the said Thomas Cumming, with the Approbation of some of his Majesty’s then Mitiifters, applied to the Petitioner to fumish the fame, and for his general Assistance in this Armament; and that the said Thomas Cumming communicated the whole to the Petitioner, who, in consequence of a particular Agreement between them, relating to the exclulire

and that this Armament proceeded to attack Senegal; and in attempting to pals the Bar, One of His Majesty’s Busses, and One of the Petitioner’s Ships were loft, but the Four others, with His Majesty’s remaining Buss, got over, and, with the Marines, and some Sailors taken from on board His Majesty’s Ships, repulsed the Enemy’s armed Vessels and small Craft, placed within the Bar for the Defence of the River; whereupon the Fort capitulated, on the First of May 1758; and that the whole Expence of the Petitioner’s Outfit amounted to the Sum of £.10,223 5s. id. and the Loss thereon £.6,075 5 s. 6d. which hitherto remains unpaid to the Petitioner; and that the Petitioner having, with all Humility, laid his same before His Majesty, and met with great Opposition from the Merchants trading to Africa, to the original Idea of an exclusive Charter for a limited Term of Years; and His Majesty’s Attorney and Solicitor General having given their Opinion, that such a Grant would be inconsistent with the Statute of the 23d of his late Majesty’s Reign, for extending and improving the Trade to Africa; and the Committee of the Company of Merchants trading to Africa, having applied to the House to have the Fort of Senegal vested in them by Art of Parliament, in the same Manner as the other Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa are; he is now under the Necessity of applying to the House, hoping to receive from them such Indemnity for h’\9 Expences, and Risque, in the late successful Epedition for the Reduction of Sertgal, as to them shall seem suitable, upon a Consideration of the Circumstances of the Cafe, and the Evidence he has to produce: And therefore praying, That the House will take the same into their most serious Consideration, and grant the Petitioner such Relief in the Premises, as to the House seem meet.

A Petition of the Agents for the Colonies of South Exporter Carolina, and Georgia, on behalf of their respective Colonies; and of several British Merchants, and Owners of Ships trading to those Colonies, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth,. That the growing of Rice in the Colonies of South Carolina, and Georgia, has been productive of great Advantages to Great Britain, by increasing the Consumption of Bri-tifti Manufactures in the said Colonies, increasing the Demand for Negroes, and augmenting the Freights of British Shipping, besides contributing to the Increase of the Public Revenue, and that the Quantity of Rice produced in the said Colonies is already found to be hilly sufficient to supply the Consumption of that Commodity in the several Countries to which it may now be exported; and that in order to encourage a further Extension of the Culture of it in the said Colonies, it is necessary to open hew Markets for its Consumption; and that whilst the conquered Islands in the West Indies were ill the Possession of Great Britain, a very considerable Quantity of Rice was exported to them from Carolina and Georgia, for which Remittances were made to Great Britain, in Specie, in Payments of British Manufactures exported from hence to those Colonies, or of Negroes fold there; and that from the Suitableness of Rice for Food in Southern Climates, and from the Fondness the Inhabitants of those Islands, particularly the Spanish Inhabitants of Cuba, shewedfor it, there is the highest Probability that the Consumption of this Grain would have greatly increased in those Islands; and that still much larger Quantities would have been consumed in the other American Territories of France and Spain, had it been permitted to supply them with it; and that by the conquered Islands being restored to France and Spain, the Colonies of South Carolina and Georgia have loft the Consumption of so much Rice as the said Islands took off, because that, although it is permitted to the Inhabitants of the said Colonies, and of all other British Colonies, to send to the said Islands, and all other Territories of States in America; Lumber, Fish, <?orn, and -every other Sort

The Order of the Day being read* for the Second Reading of the Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of His present Majesty, intituled, An Act to explain, amend, and reduce into One Act of Parliament, the several Laws now in being, relating to the Raising and Training the Militia within that Part of Great Britain, called England;

Ordered, That the said Bill be read a Second Time, upon Wednesday Morning next.

Mr. Whately according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolution which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding One thousand Two hundred and Thirty-one Pounds Seventeen Shillings and Sixpence, be granted to His Majesty, for paying a Bounty for the Year 1764, of Two Shillings and Sixpence per Day to Fifteen Chaplains, and of Two Shillings per Day to Fifteen more Chaplains, who have served longest on board His Majesty’s Ships of War, provided it appears by the Books of the said Ships that they have been actually borne and muttered thereon for the Space of Four Years during the late War with France and Spain; and provided likewise, that such Chaplains do not enjoy the Benefit of some Ecclesiastical Living, or Preferment, from the Crown, or otherwise, of the present annual Value of Fifty Pounds.

The said Resolution being read a Second Time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House!

The other Orders of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, relblve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Resolved, That th i s IIou fe w i 11, u po n Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his Warrant to the Clerk of the Crown, to make out a New Writ for the Electing of a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City of Rochester, in the County of Kent, in the Room of the Right honourable Thomas Parker, commonly called Lord Viscount Parker, now Earl of Macclesfield, called up to the House of Peers.

And theu the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Exportation of Rice.

Mr. Cujt, according to Order, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Agents for the Colonies of South Carolina and , on behalf of

their respective Colonies, and of several British Merchants and Owners of Ships, trading to those Colonies, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, and bad directed a State thereof to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followetk; viz.

A State of the Matter of Fact contained in the said Petition, is as followetk;

William Knox, hfquire, Ageut for the Province of Georgia, produced to your Committee, an Extract from the Custom-house Books of Great Britain, containing an Account of the Exports from Great Britain to South Carolina and Georgia, by which it appeared that the Value of Goods exported in the Year 1740 was £.181,821, and in the Year 1761, was £.278,866.

To this Point your Committee examined John Nutt and William Greenwood, Esquires, Merchants in London, who said. That they themselves had, in the Course of the last Year, exported Goods to

Barrels of that Year’s Produce, in Payment for which Specie was remitted to Great Britain.

That from the Accounts these Gentlemen have from their Correspondents in Carolina and Georgia, they have Reason to believe, the Consumption of Rice in those Blands would have increased every Year, as the Inhabitants were fond of it.

Mr. Greenu 'oodfurther informed your Committee,

That au Agent, commissioned from France, lately applied to him to contract lor the Delivery of 40,000 Barrels of Rice, in Three Years, at Cayenne, the Value of which would have been upwards of £.40,000, for each Year: That he could not contract with the said Agent, because, that as the Law now (lands, he coaid not export Rice from Carolina or Georgia to Cayenne, or any other foreign Country in America or Africa, without bringing it full to Great Britain: That the Length of the Voyage would spoil the Grain; and that the Charges of Freight and Insurance would be much more than the Cost of the Rice.

Mr. Nutt also further informed your Committee, That the Quantity of Rice now exported to Portugal, and the Southern Parts of . from Carolina and Georgia, was 20,000 Barrels a Year: That before it was permitted to carry Rice thither directly from those Provinces, Portugal and were supplied with

Rice from the Levant, but that now the Levant Rice is beat out of those Markets.

That mow-burnt and broken Rice cannot be fold in Europe, but that such llice would do very well for the West India Islands; and that if the Carolina and Georgia Planters could find a Vent for their broken and mow-burnt Rice, it would enable them to fell their whole Rice cheaper, which would increase the Consumption of it in Holland, Germany, and Portugal.

That the Inhabitants of Madeira and the Canary Islands would consume a considerable Quantity of Rice, were they permitted to be supplied with it directly from Carolina and Georgia.

Mr. Knox being asked, if the Demand for Rice was increased. Whether there are Lands in the Provinces of Carolina and Georgia, sufficient to produce a greater Quantity ? said. That there was not near One fourth of the Land capable of producing Rice in those Provinces under Cultivation; and that the Addition lately made by His Majesty to the Province of Georgia, of I amis to the Southward of Alatamatia, contained a greater Number of Acres suitable for the Culture of Rice, than there was now planted with that Grain in both Provinces; and that there were now 80,000 Negroes in the Two Provinces. of themselves and others, was presented to the House, and read; Setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed that a Petition is now before the House, for obtaining an Act for making Turnpike Roads to the West and South of the Town of Bideford, in the said County; and that it is intended to erect a Gate at Rotherncy Bridge, about Half a Mile from the said' Town of Great Torrington; and that there are already Two Turnpike Gateserested in the said Town o Torrington, under the Barnstaple Turnpike Act, One of which Gates is at Great Torrington Town Bridge, about Half a Mile from Rotherncy Bridge aforesaid, and the other leading from Great Torrington, to the said Town of Bideford; that the erecting a Gate at

Bridge, will oblige all Persons travelling to or from Great Torrington to pay the Turnpike Toll, who will not travel the Roads to be included in the said intended Act, only by eroding the same; and such a Gate will be a grievous Burthen to the Inhabitants of Great Torringtonaforsaid, and others: And therefore praying, That aClause may be inserted in the said intended Act, that no Gate may be erected within Two Miles from Rotherney Bridge aforesaid.

And your Committee, for their better Information, as to the Maimer in which the Franking of Letters, by the several Persons mentioned in the said Account, is exercised, and the Extent to which it is carried on, examined Mr. Ma/callthe Inspector of the Franks at the Port Office, who informed them, " That the Letters and Packets from the Ofliee of oath of the Secretaries of St ate, are brought to tly Port Ofliee in " Bags fouled up; that in those Bags are included Newspapers Pranked by the Clerks in the Offices of the " Secretaries ol State; that those Clerks Flank in their " own Names; that they are also allowed to Frank " Letters about their own private Concerns; but that " of such Letters, they were required to write the " whole Superfeription."

And being asked, What Cheque there was upon them, to prevent their Franking the Letters of other People? He said, "That if the Superfeription vvaswritten by a different Hand, or if they appeared tocontain Inclosures, lie made it a Rule to charge them; " but that Angle Letters directed by them to whatever Extent, are allowed to pass free." He also said, " That there nlight be Letters put up with the NewsPapers."

He also informed the Committee, "That from the " War Office, and the Admiralty Office, the Letters " and Packets are brought in like manner, in a sealed Bag; but that the Clerks in those Offices Frank only " by letting the Names of the Secretary at War, and " Secretary to the Admiralty, respectively: That they " are not imderfiood to have the Allowance of Franking Newspapers; but that as to single L tters, " about their own private Concerns, there is no other " Cheque upon them, than upon the Clerks in the " Office of ti:e Secretaries of State."

LTpon the whole Matter, your Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Rejblvcd, That it appears to this Committee, That the Practice of Counterfeiting the Hands of Members of this House upon Letters, in order to prevent their being charged with the Duty of Pofiage, is become extremely frequent and notorious.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the buying and selling of Covers for Letters, commonly called Franks, signed with the Names Members of this House, is also become frequent, and is openly practised.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Practice of directing Letters to Members of this House, at other Places than the Places of their usual Residence, or where they actually are at the Time, in order to convey Letters to other Persons free from the Duty of Portage, is also become extremely frequent.

Rejblvcd, 'Flint it appears to this Committee, That under Colour of t he special Privilege or Allowance belonging or granted to, or e.xercifed by certain Persons, not being Members of either House of the Parliament of Great Britain, of tending and receiving the ir

Letters and Packets free from the Duty of Pottage, great Numbers of Letters and Packets, which ought to be charged, do escape being charged with the Dufy of Portage.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That by the continued increase of these and the like Frauds and Abuses, the Revenue of the Port Office hath been greatly defrauded, and if a speedy and effectual Stop be not put thereto, is likely to suffer rti further Loss.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the niort effectual Method of preventing a Practice so derogatory to the Honour this House, and at the same Time so injurious to the Public Revenue, as the Counterfeiting the Hands of Members of this House, in order to avoid Payment the Duty of Portage, would be, that no ’Member of this House should Frank any Letter, unless the w-hole Superfcrip-tion be of his own Hand-writing, except such printed Votes and Proceedings in Parliament, or printed Sews Papers as shall be lent without Covers, or in Covers open at the Sides.

4 Geo. III. 28* Martii.

999

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for preventing Abuses in relation to the directing of Letters to Members of this House, the Privilege of receiving such Letters free of the Duty of Pottage, iliould be confined to Letters directed to such Members at One of the qfual Places of their Residence, or where they actually are at the Time.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Allowance of sending and receiving Letters and Packets free of the Duty of Pottage, heretofore granted to or customarily enjoyed by certain Persons in respect of their Offices, has not been sufficiently confined’ to such Letters and Packets only, as should relate to the Business of their respective Offices.

Refllved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That such Allowance in respect of Offices ought not to be coutinued, without some further Restrictions and Limitations.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Counterfeiting of the Hand-writing of any Person in the Superscription of apy Letter or Packet, in order thereby to defraud the Revenue of the Pott Office, be made more penal.

Rq/blssd, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That* for a further Discouragement to the Practice of Counterfeiting the Hands of Members of this House, the buying or selling of Franks signed with the Names of Members of thi&House, should be declared a Breach of the privilege of this House.

A. 1764.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put.

That the said Report be printed j

It passed in the Negative.

Then the Five First Resolutions of the Committee being severally read a Second Time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Sixth Resolution of the Committee, being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Words, " unless the whole Superscription be of his own Hand-writing."

And the Question being put, That those Words stand Part of the said Resolution;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Then the said Resolution was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Seventh Resolution of the Committee being read a Second Time;

An Amendment was proposed to be made thereto, by leaving out the Word " One," and inferring the Word any," instead thereof.

And the Question being put. That the Word " One," stand Part of the said Resolution;

It passed in the Negative.

And the Question being put. That the Word " any," be inserted instead thereof;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

" Page 208; and that no new Alphalieticul Lift be " made, till all the Trustees, whose Names are therein " specified, have had their Turn of pr. poling or nomi-u nating anewTruliee for the Approbation of the " Board; and that every new Trustee be proposed " at One Board, and ballotted for at the Board following."

" Rejoiced, That no Trustee shall have a Right to " propose a new Trustee to fill up any Vacancy, ah " though his Name shall stand inserted in the Alphabetical List, unless such Trustee shall have attended some f< General Meeting of the Board within the Space of " One Year preceding such Vacancy."

Resolved, That in case any Trustee, whose Tijra shall be according to the Alphabetical List, to " nominate a new Trustee upon any V acancy, shall uegleet to make such Nomination at the First or Second

ft General Meeting of the Board, alter Notice given " him for that Purpose, such Trustee shall forfeit his " Right of Nomination for that Turn, which shall go " over to the next Trustee upon the Lift."

And, in another Book of Minutes, the following remarkable Order was made:

" That, for the future, every Trustee.do pay, on " his coming into the Board Room, Two Shillings " and Sixpence, towards defraying the Expence of the " Day."

Your Committee beg Leave to observe. That the above mentioned Orders are not warranted by the Act of Parliament, and tend to keep the Management of the Trust in the Hands of interested Persons.

Mr. Philips being desired to inform the Committee, what Proposals he would make for the better Regulation of the said Trust;

He said, First, I^e would propose to lower the ToHs: Secondly, Tq remove the Gates at Hyde Park and Westminster, near the Queen’s Palace; to make a five Communication about the Cityand Liberty of lpglmi»-fier: And, that if these Propositions were not approved oft he should then propose. That a considerable annual Sum should be taken from the Trull, to prevent the amazing Quantity of Matter, which lie apprehended WQuld,.by the present Trustees, be continually putting on and taking off the Road, whilst they are in ftyfeffioo of so large an Income.

And being aflted, What would be the Expence of keeping the said Roads in Repair?

He said. He thinks less than Two hundred Ppuiufc a Mile; but it depends upon the Gooduefe of the Materials: That he cannot lay exactly what would keep the Roads in Repair, but that a great Saving might be made: That he thinks the Trull could now sparp Five hundred Pounds a Year, and also pay off the Mopey borrowed within the Terqa of tl)p present

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee1, That no Persons for the future shall act as Trustees in any Turnpike Road, who are employed or inteicfled in the Works carried on by the said Trull.

tligh Price Mr. Torn nfmidreported from the Comm ittee, who w ere

of appointed to inquire into the Causes of the present high rovi ons. prjce of Provisions; and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; That the Committee had inquired accordingly, and had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at tire Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed); viz.

The Committee endeavoured, in the First Place, to establish upon Evidence what is the present Price of Beef and of Mutton in the several Markets of London; for which Purpose they ordered Mr. , Orton, and

Jones, Three considerable Butchers resident in London, to attend; and they also received additional Information from Mr. Hutchinson,a Gentleman who furnishes and victuals Ships for the East India Company, and from Mr. Capet Hanbury, an eminent Virginia "Merchant.

Mr. Winter, Orton, and Jones agreed in dating the present Price of the best Beef to be Three Pence per Pound to the Vender, which is about One Halfpenny dearsr than Beef of the same Goodness has usually been in the Month of March for forae Years part, to which Point, the Committee brought all the Witnesses in giving their Evidence, imagining it to be necessary, in determining a comparative Price, to adhere to the same Month, and to Meat of the same Goodness.

The Witnesses dated the present Price of the choice Pieces of the bed Beef to lie, to the Consumer, Four Pence, and Four Pence Farthing Pound; the bed Pieces of inferior Beef 3 d. or 3 and the Coarfe Pieces of Beef in general from Seven Farthings to Two Pence Ilalf-penuy and Two Pence Three Farthings, which is One Halfpenny dearer than the same have usually been in the Month of March.

Mr. Hutchinson agreed with the Butchers before-named . in their Representation of the present Price of Providons, and added, that he did not recollect that the same Sorts had ever been fold for a higher Price during the last War: And Mr. Ilanburyconfirmed this Evidence by . the comparative Prices of his own Charge, in victualling his Ships for Virginia, which he said he victualled in March, lad Year, at the Rate of 24 or 25 Shillings per Hundred Weight, Beef: Whereas he this Year gave 27 Shillings for the same Weight and Sort.

A Member present favoured the Committee with the comparative Prices at which the Hospital now and were lad Year served with Providons of the

«4

fame Goodnels; the Price of which this Year amounts to is. 3 hd. from the 2 % 111 of lad to the 2qt.l1 f

September next, a Stone, for Mutton, Veal, and Beef; but in the same Contract for the same Months of the last ear were charged only at the Rate of is. <^d.

The same Witnesses admit, the present Price of Mutton also to be higher than it uled to be in March, but they date the Increase differently from a Farthing to a Halfpenny per Pound.

To discover the Causes of this Increase of Price, the Committee examined Mr. iVildmun, an eminent Sales-inan, Mr. BarVoilh, and Mr. Broicnjicorth, who alleged the following Readies;

First, the greater Demand, which some Witnesses supposed to arise from an Increase in the present Consumption of London; but, upon drifter Examination, they produced no conclusive, or indeed probable Evidence, to prove any such Increase of Habitation or of Consumption as they supposed.

They then accounted for this Increase of the Price of Meat by the want of Pork at Market, proceeding from the great Plenty of Acorns in 1762, which, according to the Witnesses, induced all the Feeders to fatten their whole Stock of Hogs in that Year, which extraordinary Slaughter they allege is not yet replaced; and that the want of One Article in the general Providons of so populous a City as London has necessarily advanced the Price of other Species: The whole Demand acting upon the whole Quantity of the different Sorts of Provision as upon One and the same Subject.

They added also, that the wet Season had much h ffened the Weight of even Fat Cattle; that the great Scarcity of Fodder in 1762, had reduced the Breed and Stock; and that the Failure in the Crop of Turnips ia several Counties this Year, had prevented those Counties fattening the usual Quantity of Beads. They assigned also, the low Price of Hides and Tailow, as an additional Reason. But, upon further Examination, all the Salesmen and Butchers admitted, dial the present high Price is not entirely or exclusively the Effect of natural Causes, but an artificial Price, refuiting from Combinations, and the Want of better Regulations for the Sale of Cattle in open Markets.

In Support of this Opinion, they informedtbe CommitteeofaMethod now practised of buying largeQuan-tities of Sheep and Oxen upon the Road to Market, iu order to foredall the Market of that Day, and iixthe Price by the Will of a few Engrofl'ers; of another Species of r oreftallers, who buy great Numbers of Sheep and Oxen, and, after Slaughter, fell the Carcases whole to the lesser Butchers, and thereby set the Market Price to them, and advance the Retail Price; and all the Witnesses concurred, in declaring, that if tilde Combinations and arts for gaining and keeping the Command of the Markets in a tew Hands could he obviated and prevented, the Summer and Winter Price of Meat of all Sorts would be more reasonable.

They were clearly of Opinion, that, at. this very Time, there is no Want of Fat Cattle; and they urged, with great Force, in Support of that Judgment, that through the w hole Month of March, when Provisions have been so very dear at London, Beef, Mutton, and Veal, have been at a moderate and usual Price in the Markets of the several Counties within Thirty Miles around the Metropolis.

Upon the w hole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolution.

Kefolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the high Price of Provisions of late, has been occasioned partly hv Cireuniflances peculiar to Season, and the Year, and partly by the Deleft of the Laws in Force for convicting hud punishing all Pei ferns concerned iu ibreltalluig Cattle in their Railage t» Market.

The said Resolution, being read a Second Time, was.

Sir John Glxjnne reported from the Committee, vrho were appointed to inquire into the Causes of the present high Price of Hay, Straw, Oats, Coals, and Candles; and to report their Opinion thereupon to the House; that the Committee had inquired accordingly, and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Resolutions of the Committee were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Rrfolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the late high Price of Coals was occasioned by several natural Causes arising from the late tempestuous and rainy Seasons, whereby a Quantity of Coals, sufficient to keep down an extraordinary Price, have not come to the Port of London-, and that it did not appear to this Committee, that there were any illegal of unwarrantable Practices to raise the Price of Coals.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Growers of Hay employing Salesmen to sell the same in the Isondon Markets, gives an Opportu aity for Combinations amongst such Salesmen, and by their Management, Hay and Straw are now at an unreasonable Price; and that such Practices ought to be prevented.

Supply Bill; Exchequer Bill*.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill for raising a certain Sum of Money, by Loans or Exchequer Bills, and for applying certain Monies remaining in the Exchequer, for the Service of the Year 1764; and for Application of certain Savings of Public Monies, and of Monies arisen by the Sale of military Stores;

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to receive a Clause of Appropriation.

Ordered, That so much of His Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, upon the 15th Day of November last, as relates to the Produce arising by the Sale of such Prizes as are vested in the Crown, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That the Account of the Produce of French Prizes taken before the Declaration of War, be referred to the said Committee.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, that they have Power to receive a Clause for Relief of Persons who have omitted to insert in Indentures or other Writings, the full Sum agreed to be paid with Clerks, Apprentices, and other Servants.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Mr. Alderman Dickinson reported from the Committee, That they had gone through the Bill, and made several Amendments thereunto; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received Tomorrow. Morning.

of them were disagreed to, and the rest were agreed to, by the House; and several Amendments Were made’ by the House, to the Bill.

And the House being informed, that several other Amendments are necessary to be made to the said Bill;

Ordered, That the said Bill be re-committed.

Ordered, That the said Bill be re-committed to a Committee of the whole House.

liefolved. That this House will immediately resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of the said Bill.

The House accordingly resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir John Glynne took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir John Glynne reported from the Committee, That they had made several other Amendments to the Bill, which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Sir John Glynne accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the Bill; and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered the Bill, with the Amendments, in at the Clerk’s Table.

Ordered, That such a Number of Copies of the said Bill, with the Amendments, be printed, as shall be sufficient for the Use of the Members of the House.

And ttyyi the House adjourned till Tomorrow

Morning, Nine of the Clock.
